With the spread of ideas about how everything ought to be, the indolence of the established people, who always take everything as it is, will disappear. The enlivening power of ideas—even if they still have limitations in themselves, such as those of the fatherland, its constitution, and so on—will elevate the minds, and they will learn to sacrifice for them, whereas at present the spirit of constitutions has made a pact with self-interest and has founded its realm upon it. I always call out to myself from the course of life: “Strive toward the sun, friends, so that the salvation of the human race may soon ripen! What do the hindering leaves, what do the branches want? Fight your way through to the sun, and if you tire, so much the better! It is easier to sleep!”

To Mr. M. Schelling in Tübingen, free to Schaffhausen. My dear! The delay in my reply is due partly to various business matters and partly to distractions caused by the political celebrations held here. Every ten years, the sovereign council and the approximately 90 members who have departed during this period are replenished. I cannot describe to you how human it all proceeds, or how all the intrigues at princely courts through cousins and uncles are nothing compared to the combinations made here—the father appoints his son or the son-in-law who brings the largest dowry, and so on. To learn what an aristocratic constitution is like, one must have spent such a winter before Easter, when the replenishment takes place, here.

I am writing to you because I have heard that you have now arrived at your fixed place, and I first acknowledge receipt of your letter to me, which you wrote from Stuttgart shortly before your departure for Munich. I need not tell you how much your appointment, which is also very honorable in every respect, has pleased me. Jena, bereft of so many great men, has missed you particularly, and even among the common people your loss was considered the most significant, just as the people who do not call themselves common seemed to wish to possess you again.

You will have heard into which little streams your philosophical current divides here; I, too, have started reading again, and am getting along with it better than usual. The literary gazette now about to appear will become as common an institution as the previous one and any other; it was of no further concern to Goethe; since Eichstedt offered himself and money, the whole matter was handed over to him without further ado, so that Jena might have a literary gazette. Among the new developments is the fact that Ritter has been requested by the students to lecture on galvanism; he has bypassed the philosophical faculty and awaits a decision from the courts. — Fernow could find no auditorium large enough for those who were signing up; it is said that he reads Kantian definitions to them. — As for literary news, nothing has come to my attention except a scrap from Kotzebue, *Expectorationes*, a diarrhea which he still let loose in Germany); it is the old song about Goethe and the Schlegels; the anecdote is also used therein that the former, like Friedrich! with the Hores in the journal *Deutschland* dealt uncleanly with them /), at a dinner at Loder’s swore that these people should never set foot in Jena. — Goethe is very much set on the real and on apparatuses, not only did he have Schelvern set up a botanical cabinet, but a physiological one is also being established, and from Ritter he immediately demanded the

Other needs and circumstances will be communicated to you in part by Paulus, and in part by my most humble report to you. — P. has lodged me in the front house — the parson’s residence above the classrooms — also to allow the old, good Schenk the comfort of his change of residence. Please keep the room I am currently occupying; do you not consider it expedient for supervision purposes to move the Progymnasium to this building as well, and to relocate the Realinstitut elsewhere? Mr. v. Joli) now also has his standing quarters here; she will move here in the next few days and sends you, as well as the best of ladies, her warmest greetings. I have not yet seen Mrs. v. Siebein. — Please make my very best and most friendly recommendations to the best of ladies, and likewise greet Julius, who is probably also at the Progymnasium. Your devoted Hgl. Prof. Heller‘) asked me to convey his regards to you on this occasion. You have provided us with a fine acquisition in him, both in his own right and in contrast to the customary Nuremberg slowness. If you could arrange for a number of copies of the Normatives to be sent here for sale, this would be very important for publicizing the new course of study among the local public, which still has very little knowledge of it.

If I may express a wish, it would be for a few more hours of physics—without, however, taking time away from another subject; though this might perhaps be arranged in connection with the physico-technical institute. In general, however, it is still too early to speak of it. My thoughts on the matter in general would be to equip a gymnasium richly with apparatus for this purpose, so that young people, at the age when the non-theoretical observation of these phenomena and their applications to various games is still appropriate, can soon be done with it; whereas for the university, almost nothing of such apparatus should be allowed, because the scientific and mathematically treated theory of it requires almost nothing of the kind and is suitable for the university alone.

The long delay in answering your several kind letters, dearest friend, I could only partly excuse with the generally inexcusable manner in which I am accustomed to handle letter writing. However, part of the postponement is due to my intention to thank you more extensively for the kind gift of your writing. I would indeed have found the time, measured by the clock, but not enough leisure; a letter, if it does not concern a formal business matter, becomes for me a kind of journey to the friend, and in order to be able to allow myself such a journey, I want to wait for a mind free from other activities, cares, and distractions; so I often do not get around to answering dearer letters, such as yours, before the holidays, although in my thoughts I have answered them all winter long. An illness has also had its share in the delay; and let the first thing be for me to express my heartfelt thanks for your loving invitation, which you make to me in that connection, to spend some months with you; could it be so well with me that I could carry that out! Yet my health is generally getting better again, so that I am able to attend to my office, and spring will, I hope, do its part to finally consolidate it. That you and your worthy family, including the grandson, are in good health, I take with interest from your letters.

Your preface must have interested me particularly in this respect, personally, in that I find in it the satisfaction that you approve of the path of speculative cognition that I have taken, and indeed that you undertake the commitment to work in this field and to grace us with the fruits of your meditations. The point to which you carry your presentation has been doubly interesting to me. Since this point is of the greatest interest in itself, it may also be the point in which will fall what you designate by the name of our differences. But if the path that we are to walk together is so long, and if it offers so much in common in spirit and content, then those differences seemed to me, on the scientific side, to lie in such a wide distance of conception, that for the present I hold fast to the feeling of your loving friendship, and find in it intimate satisfaction, and at the close I ask for its preservation, as I am, with all my heart, yours, Hegel.

to the Royal Danish Steward, Mr. von Thaden, in Flensburg. As I first return the friendly and heartfelt greeting with equal friendliness and heart, which you, very highly esteemed Sir, already offered me a year ago, the next thing must be to say something about why I have let this return stand so long. Look for the cause in nothing else than in the desire not to answer your friendly participation in my philosophical endeavors with a letter that is, so to speak, devoid of deeds.

I see from this that the need for philosophy is once again drawing closer to the higher authorities and that I, too, have not been forgotten. A professorship at a university is the position I have longed for again for a long time. Such a position is, according to our customs, the almost indispensable condition for giving philosophy wider entry and dissemination, as it also provides the only form of lively face-to-face interaction, which in turn exerts a completely different influence on the literary form than mere conception, and I expect from this side a greater possibility to accomplish something more satisfactory in writings.

That it was you who, as you write, caused the delay in the execution of the decrees, I shall not flatter myself on one hand, for this vanity led to nothing at least, but on the other hand I wish that it had not been me, because if it had been me, I would have been the one to cause a new undertaking in addition to the troubles I have caused you. Paulus writes to me today with yesterday’s date that I shall now have the official documents from Nuremberg in hand; however, I do not yet have them; Stutzmann will arrive here in eight days, and then I can depart for there without any embarrassment; the curriculum, Paulus writes, has not yet arrived there; before its arrival, no official activity will be required of me, as it could only consist of taking over fragmentarily for a few days the school of the old Rector, consisting of 5 to 6 students, in its old form. Even after the arrival of the curriculum, at least a few days will be necessary, for the teacher of the philosophical preparatory sciences more than for others, who have a specific plan and thread in an author, but also for these—to survey their half-yearly syllabus in advance. — I also know nothing yet, neither about the philosophical subjects or sciences that are to be taught at a Gymnasium, nor about the books that are to serve as guides, nor whether my instruction will be assigned to different classes, and thus be different, as I must almost fear from the stipulation in Klein’s local appointment.

To Your High Reverence, Mr. Senior School Councillor Dr. Niethammer in Munich. If you call me a friend of little faith, then you yourself did not intend to call me little-faithful in relation to you, dearest friend, and likewise do not take it amiss if I am little-faithful toward a certain thing, in which you do not, like the thistle heads, the Spinotzists, represent man in general as a portion of seawater separated in a bottle floating in the ocean, but rather move actively in it as in an element, which everywhere recedes where you penetrate, but which, by its very nature, also immediately closes up again, and for individual moments can rise to the surface. — Whether I such an individual moment of

They told it to God, to the earth, even to Gusmann); I hear that the reply came back today, they found deaf ears. It has been written here from Munich that you have become a Church Councillor, and moreover the first one; is there any truth in this? I hope and wish that the prospect of living together with you on the scientific earth, in Elysium, should not be blocked by a gilded partition, a partition that for you would be nothing but a shining prison.

Dear dear Refugee! It was on September 24 that instinct led me to the distressed straw widow to collect the little sheet you had prepared for me. I greeted your flower-crowned portrait with heartfelt friendship, congratulated you on the happy outcome of your journey, and thanked you for your kind remembrance and its source, as well as for the notes provided from Munich. I spent 5–6 days in old cordial friendship with Schelling in Carlsbad (where I came on the tour through Töplitz, Prague, then Weimar, — to the eighty-year-old youth, — Jena). In Prague, please do not fail to visit Professor of History, von Henniger (pronounced: Hennigahr), a brother-in-law of my uncle there and aunt here), Broad Street, Schlichting’s house, whom I have announced you to, — he is by his own inclination very willing to help you in every way with researches and materials for your works. Please give him, and then also to Librarian Hanka, my best regards; it will be of interest to you to set aside a few days for Prague. The King has given a copy of your work to Count Waldstein as a gift. Farewell, soon a happy return, which the other vacant colleagues will also effect one after another. — Today the return of Madame Crelinger (in Gabriele) is to be celebrated, if it is not a beginning of the end (Vienna is said to have been very hard on her). Your faithful Hegel.

The main thing is that the departure of the entire manuscript will infallibly take place from me this week... Regarding my journey to you, the times do not permit it, much as I would like to accept your kind invitation; — the lectures are to begin on October 13th, or perhaps on the 20th; it will not amount to much, but independently of that, I would expose myself to the danger of not being able to return, or perhaps not even being able to come to you. — The mail coach is easily sent back earlier or delayed, compared to the riding post; so that if I were to deliver the manuscript, it might easily delay my arrival more than if it were sent by the riding post. — But the war has not yet broken out; the present moment seems decisive); in a few days, peace winds may blow just as strongly, and then I will not fear the October zephyr, and will travel to you.

I am writing to you, highly esteemed friend, for a twofold reason. First, I did not tell you the exact arrangement of the copies that you were kind enough to take with you; which I wish to supply now. Of the three bound copies, one on wove paper is for Goethe, the one on writing paper for Privy Councillor Voigt, and the other on wove paper is intended for you. Of the three unbound copies, you were kind enough to send one to Frommann; as you know, the time did not allow for having them bound or cased. Furthermore, I ask you to return the other two unbound copies; in exchange, I will enclose here an order for two printed copies to Frommann, which Göbhardt will send me today. You are to be kind enough to have one sent to M. v. Knebel and the other to Seebeck.

The reason for the present letter lies in your kindness toward me in general, as well as toward my brother-in-law, to whom you were so friendly and helpful during his stay in Munich. He has applied for artillery service for several months now. The lameness mentioned in your letter, which can be found both outside and inside the walls, now receives a vigorous spur in the flanks and sharp thorny bushes under the buttocks through the dispatches from Lyon, etc.; but unfortunately, the drastic power of such a stimulant directs itself in all other directions, just not in the desired one, and the lameness might first transition into a complete stroke and catalepsy of interest in sciences and scientific institutes, since I, like every other professor, schoolteacher, and section councilor, would have to take up the rifle on my shoulder if the matter were to become serious, which I do not believe at the moment, and cannot believe, even if the eagles were planted on the walls of Paris. — What could I therefore write about particular hopes and wishes that I might have had, especially now; until now, not, for the simple reason that there was simply nothing else to write, — as I generally find that reasons, especially non-events and non-fates, are very simple; yet I have reason to believe that it has not been decided negatively either. We all recommend ourselves most heartily. Your H.

You know what the theoretical philosophers say about the experience of everything bad, especially that one can use them for the most opposite claims and views; I had an example of this with regard to the latest organization. I expressed the good faith that from the experience now made in this regard in many ways, one had learned where it fails, and thereby must have learned to understand what the better is; what do you think another deduced from that? That the experience so far had only proven that the organizers do not understand organizing!

Dearest Friend! Julius’s arrival in these lands, and since it was not to be anything more, — at least his neighborhood has given us great heartfelt pleasure.... The very latest Munich organization is already becoming too old to say anything more about it; the essential point is your belief that things will not become so bad that we could not endure them; this comes quite close to my own, that we must not hope for anything so good that it would be particularly worth praising. This colorless and tasteless middle-of-the-road state, which allows nothing to become so bad and nothing to become so good, rules our world once and for all; I therefore praise myself, if one cannot be a minister, still for the sciences, where one’s affair, if one admittedly only brings about such a middle-of-the-road state, one has at least made it oneself, whereas in all other cases, perhaps even with the gentleman minister, unfortunately others mix in their share of mediocrity and badness. But the purely positive aspect in these other cases, which belong to practical life, is a good salary, insofar as thank God no paper money is mixed into it. Gradually, therefore, the instinct of sound human reason turns toward this tendency, and takes the further interests of the matter and of honor, if indeed into the hands and as far as it must and can be, also into the head, yet not so much to heart. The salary is still such a treasure that neither moths nor rust eat it, nor do the organizers dig it up or steal it.

That the Berliners hold no lower opinion of philosophers than the Bavarians do is a noble trait that honors both those and these; but as I said, setting honor and such things aside, I would rather cling to the nebulous twilight that you might perhaps see breaking in the distance for my sake. Have you not come across a Bavarian piece from the 1770s, Father Umgang? It seems to go with him as it does with the devil: when one thinks one has killed him, he comes back to life in another form. If Umgang, as a priest, is done for, it seems he rages all the more powerfully in another form, does not let his adversary, the Definitivus, get a foothold, and instead supplies his shape-shifters, the Provisoria. — Harle’s death, which the adversary perhaps wanted to seize upon to attach a thread of twine, will probably fall to Father Umgang to handle; and why not? one might ask, since there is no longer any Ludwig in Bavaria who would have been the one to tie on to this thread and no other. A pity, a tenfold pity!

You keep his memory vividly and firmly before you against the loss of the present; thus the son and the enjoyment you had in his possession are not lost to you. This is a moment in your life and in hard life experience in which your good nature and love of humanity, which in the calm course of life are to be valued at the highest, must also prove the inner strength of an even deeper foundation, so that the power of the spirit to endure even such things can be demonstrated. I press your hand with the deepest pain of friendship; — I will see tomorrow morning whether I can speak with you: please also convey to your highly respected wife my most lively sympathy. My wife, deeply shaken by such news, asks me to assure you and your wife of her most intimate concern. Your Hegel.

The specific reason you had for writing to me last time, namely to open up and offer me the prospect of a position near you, I acknowledge with heartfelt thanks. I am Professor of the philosophical preparatory sciences and Rector at the local Gymnasium. Besides the hope of eventually moving to a university, I have, which is the most excellent thing for me personally, a fixed career, and otherwise at least mostly official duties that are connected with my studies. If I were to throw away these advantages, or exchange them for greater ones, I would again bring a disturbance into my external actions that would set me back for a time. It would certainly be nice if we lived near one another, recapped old things together, and pushed through new things together. Come once to visit our old Nuremberg. Your situation probably allows you to make an excursion more easily than I can; I do not know if you have already seen our regions, Franconia, and our Bavarian state up close; it always has its curiosities. In the meantime, until I speak with you personally, I await your philosophical work. You have made a capable start, just as in the dramatic career with three tragedies, so in the philosophical one with three volumes; I look forward to it with great expectation, whether you are still the stubborn Fichtean and what role the progress into the infinite plays in it. That you want to have it printed at your own expense, I would absolutely advise against, if it were still in time and if I had a counsel to give you on the matter; you can only suffer significant damage from it. Finally, I am sending you a copy of my beginning, which I made a few years ago. See for yourself what you want to do with it; it is a concrete side of the spirit that is treated in it; the science itself is yet to come. How will your free, not to say anarchic nature receive the Spanish boots of the method, in which I let the spirit move?

Your account of the heroic death your friend Zwilling met has moved me deeply. I ask you to convey my most respectful regards to your wife’s mother, who has been kind enough to remember me. I also ask you to send greetings to Molitor, who once had the kindness to send me an essay of his on history, which I, due to my usual sluggishness, failed to acknowledge, and for which I can only apologize. Please also send greetings to the high Feldberg and Alkin, toward which I so often and so gladly looked from unfortunate Frankfurt, because I knew you to be at their foot. Farewell, do not hold my sluggishness against me, and let me hear from you again soon.

Above, I probably mentioned your gifts, but for all the trees, I did not see the forest; I have not, in fact, thanked you for these beautiful gifts. I will not, however, add a reviewing thank-you, since you also sent me the eggs without any cackling. As for other, i.e., un-laid eggs, you should not speak of them at all. In the case of every third person, it may perhaps be true that he cannot speak of them; but certainly not in the case of the one who lays them himself; at least only in the case of the one in whom only the dear natural instinct operates, which was precisely the case with the opposing wind-eggs, whose positors knew how to cackle a great deal, but had nothing to say, whereas others held the sermon, and indeed the funeral sermon. But he who has shot the geese into the grave, so that this burial becomes a production of swan eggs or the like, could not find it difficult to speak of it.

The urgent budget of the local educational institutions for 14/15 is to be processed jointly by the Administrative and School Council in accordance with regulations; it was not communicated to me and was sent to Munich without my co-signature. Since I believed for the first time that I could have a genuine influence on it (for a year ago I had only just entered the reference post a few days before it came up, and still had little knowledge of where the buck actually stops), I see myself equally deceived by that deprivation, as I can otherwise regard this stratagem as incurable. I have submitted my rectoral opinion on the matter to the Administration, and perhaps this might be the pretext to declare any further expression from me superfluous, since as referent I still had quite other things to bring forward than those on which I could call attention in the capacity of Rector. — Incidentally, I have heard from the administrative report that it — because of its insinuations against me — cannot be shared. The Administrator) has, since I have been referent, let no opportunity pass to bring accusations, insinuations, and slanders against me before the Commissariat; he is a rough, passionate man, — one of my Nuremberg colleagues characterized him most correctly as a fussy clerk. — His report may well not have been sent to Munich; but his budget, which I had a glimpse of, seemed to me likewise filled with insinuations or indirect accusations against the Rectorate, and in the matter at least he had the last word against me; I also do not know to what extent the local report was in his sense regarding the matter. It might well have been done partly out of delicacy towards me, to spare me the annoyance, but more to spare annoyance in general and to cut off the developments into which I would have had to enter, thus actually sparing the Administrator. — This Administrator is such a good Nuremberg patriot that he believes in his conscience to make a merit of himself by depriving the Royal Bavarian School and Study system of what he can, and the Nuremberg assets — rather advancing to the Service Urgency and Central Foundation Cash, and for a

I must first make very earnest apologies to you, dear friend, for my delay in answering your two letters, and I must ask you to be lenient with me; a peculiar misfortune hangs over me in this regard; every letter I write, I am compelled to begin with requests for forgiveness. However, as I now intend to proceed unalterably to the answer, I do not have your two letters before me, which I had recently set aside specifically for this purpose; in order not to waste time and pleasure again in searching for them, I must write only from memory. They are philosophical

From here I proceed to the representation you have formed of my thoughts, and regarding which you wish me to pass judgment. It has pleased me to see how deeply you have penetrated, and have seized precisely the point where the matter is most speculative. First, I wish to repeat from what has been said that I am not opposed to the content of Reinhold’s, Schott’s, etc. philosophy, but that I stand outside such a standpoint, and that I would only contradict them in that the standpoint of representation is the highest and final one. — Regarding your exposition of my intention, — which I find very exact and thoroughly grasped, I wish to remark only this: that if, as a result concerning the difference, which at the same time is no difference, you say that this apparent difference is the mere appearance of difference and the absolute truth of the spirit is absolute indifference, identity, unity, then the word: absolute, might easily acquire the sense of the abstract (as absolute, i.e. abstract space), and so the truth would be only the abstract indifference, identity, unity, — as above being was determined only as self-consistency. But in the sense of the philosophically Absolute I determine the True as the concrete in itself, i.e. (as you also cite), as the unity of opposed determinations in itself, so that this opposition is still preserved in the unity, — or the truth not as something standing, rigid (abstract identity, being), but as movement, life in itself, as indifference only as indifference appearing in itself, or with a difference in it, which as in it, in the unity, is at the same time no difference, as a sublated, i.e. annihilated and preserved one, which, because it is an appearing one, — is not. I now wish that these remarks may fulfill their purpose, namely to confirm to you the correctness of your representation of my concepts.... With heartfelt respect and friendship, your devoted Hegel. Orig.]

Since it is closely related, I wish to make the following remark here: if it is said of Being that it is a self-coincidence of itself, and yet it is then spoken of as something Unrecognized and Unrecognizable—so that the opposite is said of what has just been done—for the determination of Being, that it is the absolute self-coincidence, is a determination of thought, i.e., precisely thereby it is thought and, in this respect, recognized. However, I fully concede all those propositions insofar as they relate to the nature of representation; representation is indeed recognition that stands only in the relative, i.e., is burdened with a presupposition. For the same reason, however, I refrain from using the expression, for example, to designate the Absolute as the unity of representation and Being. Representation belongs to a different ground than that of the recognition of the Absolute.

Each of your subsequent letters, which arrived in quick succession one after the other, is more pleasing than the previous one and shows the goal to be in greater proximity. How greatly your kindness and zealous efforts have overwhelmed me with gratitude and joy, dearest friend, you can gauge from the length of my waiting and longing, which has already lasted for so many years and gnawed at me every single day of it. From your letter received today, I see that the matter itself still threatened to fail at the very entrance of the harbor; I will therefore not yet fully rejoice, as it does not yet rest on its anchors in the same place.

And now I may consider myself so fortunate as to be able to regard myself, in spirit and heart, entirely as yours; I proceed with a rejuvenated spirit to my vocation, to live for the university and the sciences, to the invitation to justify the friendly kindness you have been willing to show me, to the hope of your soon personal acquaintance, to my other dear friends, and to the image of friendliness and cheerfulness under which Heidelberg always appears; and I am, with the assurance of my most complete respect, your most devoted Hegel.

But what about theology? Is the contrast between your deep philosophical view of it and what is frequently considered theology not just as glaring, or even more striking? My work will also give me the satisfaction of being able to regard it as a propaedeutic to your science. I hope my, perhaps merely ostensible, answer will not cause any difficulty; only I do not have formal information on whether my announcement of lectures may appear earlier, before I have received my dismissal from my government. With unlimited respect and love, entirely yours. I ask you to kindly greet my other friends in Heidelberg for the time being; I am currently engaged in the most tedious examination of schoolteachers from morning until night, and have no free moment to write to them.

As for my lectures, since you do not consider Logic and Natural Law desirable for the next half year, I intend to lecture on the Encyclopedia of the Philosophical Sciences and the History of Philosophy; with the former, I believe I can most appropriately open my lectures, as it will provide a general overview of philosophy, as well as an indication of the particular sciences for which I intend to schedule separate courses in the future; I intend to speak more extensively on Nature Philosophy, i.e., as a part of the whole, and then not hold a separate lecture on this; a third

Invitation to visit me in the autumn, to become better acquainted; but under the present circumstances, I can all the less leave my dear wife alone; the solitude into which she has returned again weighs on her doubly now. Our examination will begin next week; Stephani, as I hear, will not be able to attend, the per diems having been cut; — because we have no examination hall, we must hold it in the location of the classes, so pretty much privately. Herr Oberfinanz Rath Roth told me that Herr Präsident Jacobi, with his sisters, has arrived back in Munich from his journey, and that it has been refreshing and pleasant for him as well; would you be so kind as to convey my and my wife’s most cordial regards to him; the lingering impression of your joint visit often cheers us, and the interest in the beautiful gift of Herr Präsident is able to draw my wife away from her pain. Live well for the time being. Your sincere friend Hgl.

Julius is therefore here for these holidays, and will return this afternoon to pick up the letter that has just arrived from Landshut for him, which he had been expecting this morning. He has visited us several times from Erlangen—not often—and has acquainted me with his life and activities there and the conditions among the students, as well as with his small interests here. He has also shared with us the concerns that you and the best lady have had regarding some of his tailoring and suit-making, both in content and in form. Given his open, on the one hand cheerful, but on the other hand very prudent character, and given his openness in keeping us informed about all those suits and outings, I believe I may earnestly assure you that you need have no concerns on this account. He has certainly kept himself free from participation in a crude tone and worn-out customs up to now, and will be secure from them in the future; I consider him to be so far beyond such things that he can only joke about them.

My dear! It is already eight days since I left home; I hope every day for a letter from you; my first will now be in your hands. I hope that you are well, apart from my absence, if you miss me at all—and apart from the weather. This is quite detestable here and offers no hope of improvement whatsoever; I shall probably not get further than here; there is nothing to be done but to sit at home in one’s little room, and from here I see the deep grey cloudy sky stretching far before me, and the awning is constantly banging against the window. However, there has been some entertainment at times; the day before yesterday I was in Pillnitz, saw the royal family dine, but above all we climbed the Porsberg, a one-hour walk—where one has the entire circle of the view of the whole surrounding area before one;—a ray of sun certainly did not come; but we also had no rain. On the gallery I was naturally also—and scanned the old dear acquaintances through—above all I was eager to see the Holbein painting, of which we saw the copy in Berlin), and I particularly noted the details that I had marked out there, the complexion of the middle figure among the three women, and the nose of the burgomaster, and the child in the arms of Mary. Regarding those two details, it was immediately clear to me that they are made by a pupil in the Berlin painting, however beautiful it is in itself;—the child in the one here is visibly sickly, and obviously intentionally, and I am entirely convinced of the correctness of the statement of the inspector here, that it is supposed to be a deceased child of the donor, whom she sees here in the arms of the Mother of Heaven, and which sends them comfort and resignation from this place. This statement proves its correctness by the child standing almost in the middle at the bottom, which is very beautiful here.

This alone is what I have to write to you in this matter; it comes down to referring you to the ministerial reply, one of which you will in any case receive. So much for this time; I have barely had time to write this; my wife has been lying down for nearly three weeks with a severe illness, and I have had bitter days and nights of suffering; we still dare not harbor any certain hope of improvement. My best regards to Daub and Creuzer; has the former seen the second part of Schleiermacher's Dogmatics? Yours, Hegel.

As for me, I am reading three courses this winter, which take up almost all my hours; I am only a newly appointed university professor, and since I actually have to mostly create the sciences I lecture on, you can understand from this the otherwise blameworthy rarity of my written communications. All the more often do we speak among ourselves and with Julius about you, of whom I can write to you nothing but favorable things. It is becoming increasingly evident in him what can only occur after a period spent in absorbing information, namely that he is intrigued by perspectives and questions.

I ask you to convey my very best wishes to Ms. Niethammer; that is, in my name, for from your side this is done anyway. May I also ask you to recommend me to Mr. and Ms. Hufeland as well as Mr. and Ms. Paulus? I do not know whether I can entrust you with a compliment to the Schelling family, because I do not know whether it would be appropriate. On this margin: Natural philosophers and professors in Bamberg. The dispute and complaint of Kilian against Marcus was triggered by an article which the latter wrote in the 'Newspaper for the Elegant World' about the University of Würzburg. Dr. A. F. Marcus according to his life, and I recommend myself most highly to your esteemed friendship and am your sincere Dr. Hegel.

My dear Doctor! Your letter of the 19th of September, which I received through Mr. D. v. K., gave me much pleasure, as I gather from it the good progress of your undertaking to hold lectures; I am very glad that you have begun with such good success — it has not gone so well for me. Just persevere patiently for a few years, though this of course also depends on the economic side; in the meantime, with such a large audience — which, as I hope and wish, will have increased further this winter — you will certainly have a pecuniary supplement from it. There is now a great lack and need for capable university teachers, particularly also for philosophy. People have finally come to regard this science in general as a necessity — and indeed a capable science. The Friesian and other such stuff is beginning to seriously fall into disrepute due to its inner emptiness and then externally due to its political tendency; I therefore do not doubt at all that this career is also externally advantageous. You know, I advise no one to enter this career, rather I advise against it, but since you have nevertheless taken it up, and with good success, I now seriously believe I can advise you to continue. However, it is necessary that you, as said, patiently endure it for some time and do not immediately expect salary and appointment. A government must necessarily first see how things really go with the lectures of a private lecturer. That the philosophical faculty in Heidelberg (Mr. Munke at the head) does not do much to advance philosophical study is of no consequence and will have little or no influence on the government....

I ask you, in this connection, first of all not to write anything about it to Munich; as soon as something is certain, I shall be the first to know; further, not to say much more in Berlin than that there are intentions regarding me in Heidelberg. I should very much like to receive something formal from Berlin, so that this prospect, which would have been of use had it arrived only half a year later, passes by perhaps not without advantage to me; perhaps also, although my wife does not want to hear of it, the position there is the preferable one, and it would be foolish to pursue the former. From Erlangen, Thiersch is said to be proposed; Julius thinks he will probably accept it. It was said that the Secretary had presented the pen to the Minister to sign the new general organization, with the remark that it was awaited with longing; but precisely this remark had induced him to reply: it cannot be yet. Upon your return, you will probably find the whole gift. Your

Yet perhaps the opportunity might arise thereby to earn the merit of getting me away from Munich again, since in Bavaria a removal of mine (as the people are indeed fine) is customarily transformed, graciously, into a promotion, and thus the double advantage of the transfer to Erlangen—getting me there and away from Munich—could be made valid. Regarding your other thought, which is as friendly as it is honorable, to entrust me with the drafting of a logic of the land, I would almost be even more grateful and entirely agreeable. But!—I must confess that I would be most unwilling to see this sole opportunity slip away from me to bring philosophical views to general teaching or examination; nothing could be more desirable (also in economic respect, both with regard to such a book itself and indirectly to other writings) than to raise one’s philosophy in this manner at once to the ruling one in a kingdom. However, such a sovereign means does not help itself if the matter does not carry and hold; Weiler’s philosophy) will, notwithstanding, not become the ruling one, or even be so. — In truth, however, I do not quite know how to grasp the task. The main concept of a textbook seems to me to be that it contains what is generally recognized in its science—chiefly and essentially for a textbook in gymnasiums;—for university textbooks, which are used primarily only by that professor, particularity is rather permitted. But the avowed logic is something for which enough textbooks already exist; but at the same time it is also that which absolutely cannot remain so; no one knows anymore what to do with this old logic; one drags it along as an old heirloom, only because another substitute, whose need is generally felt, is not yet available. What one might still let pass as valid determinations in it could be written on two pages; what goes beyond two pages, a further detail, is considered entirely unfruitful scholastic

Subtlety—or, to make this logic more durable, it has been extended through psychological wretchedness (cf. Steinbart, Kiesewetter, Mehmel). A new science cannot be presented in a textbook for secondary schools. One cannot hand teachers a book that would be as foreign to them as to the students, and which, as a compendium, could not contain the necessary developments that complete insight. A middle ground, an old logic that simultaneously contained the beginnings and pointers to further progress and to views going beyond it, can certainly be thought of, as it is called, and seems at first glance to be the most fitting, precisely what is required. However, Fichte could perhaps read Platner, i.e., say something entirely different for each section than what stood in the section, and tear that section down completely; but I would like to see the compendium he would have written for such lectures. I would certainly hold similar lectures on every logical compendium, but how I should connect the old, the transition to the new, i.e., the negative of the old and the new positive, in a manner that would be universally valid, as in a textbook—I do not yet know how to manage that. If I had spent a few years reading my logic, as it is beginning to become, on which I laid barely the foundation in Jena and have not read in detail, I might perhaps know how to help myself sooner. If it were possible for you to suspend this commission for a year and a day, i.e., not indefinitely, that would be something for which I would ask you very earnestly. In the meantime, I completed my more detailed and comprehensive logic, and by subsequently making a more popular excerpt from the relevant part—the excerpt can be made more easily after the completion of the whole than before—I could together

Now, thanks for your tidy Bavarian-literary presents; they are indeed tidy, as they were condemned to the sweepings corner when you were tidying up your study. I ask you for more such contributions; I intend to build up a patriotic library. I have just received a Bavarian original piece, Rittershausen on Schelling’s speech; that is quite a crude fellow; he speaks somewhere of lectures on the arts that he has given and had printed; if this also falls under your department, you will be able to assign him his place in the learned world, perhaps by employing him as a journeyman book printer; he is hardly fit to be a typesetter, but as for writing, that will surely forbid itself to him in the end.

It is, dearest friend, the wealth of materials I have to write to you that has delayed this reply to your two, so to speak, letters. As for the first of them, which, though not a letter, was a word of friendly remembrance, it has been greatly enhanced by the good opportunity it brought with it. I cannot tell you enough how much it pleased me and all the friends here to see this good opportunity again. The best of women has become much stronger, fresher, and more lively in appearance than when she left Bamberg, and she bears very good witness to the Munich climate. That she has also taken a certain view of the ministry currently in the seat of government has likewise come to light, as the two gentlemen, the Provincial Director and the Consistory Councillor, who had her to themselves—for I could not intrude upon them—presented to her, with complaints and recommendations, the hangover caused by centralizing the assets of the charitable foundations in Munich. She could do nothing else in response to this presentation by the provincial estates than give good advice and promise better things. When you yourself come, as the best of women has given us hope, you will then have to hear a bitterly complaining report. Since I had no such official concerns to bring to her, she only whispered a friendly word in my ear, in which I well heard the name Munich, but your second letter contained the further clarification, and you kindly ask for my opinion on your generous idea. The opinion is necessarily, even if my exposition of it should become more lengthy, very simple. Whatever one may be in a state, it is best to be in the capital; a stay in a provincial city can always be regarded as a banishment, even if one is oneself the one who banishes oneself. Only a university, which likewise makes itself the supreme center of activity and interest, can rival a capital and make itself one.

In fact, however, I believe that at least in my case it is necessary that, while you speak of Munich or a major provincial capital, I should, at least in the beginning, have support in the new situation in which I would be placed at the head of an institution, such as you, or an immediate superior commissioner who could be roughly the same to me, perhaps like Paulus; for I have no idea how I would manage with a superior commissioner à la Wißmayr or Graser, whom I would not understand and who would not understand me, N.B. if he were otherwise willing to take on the matter. — As for the specific duties of the office, I have perhaps not yet been able to learn much from your presentations of Bavarian educational products, since you promise us a new school plan; if you allow the public occasional speeches to remain, these perhaps will not have to be exactly like those of Rector Beyschlag; with regard to instruction, the Rector perhaps has a certain choice among the subjects of instruction, which are otherwise already more pleasing in the Augsburg trial than in the other Lyceums and Gymnasiums. The supervision and administration that the Rector must conduct will also be determined by your new statutes. — The number of hours that fall on the Rector in Augsburg is not large, nor is that which falls on the Professors; I fear that you will be more severe in this regard; yet you have enough subjects to employ, among whom the work must be distributed. Since the appointment would primarily go to Munich (should not a literary journal be established there?), and since you express that you do not lose sight of Erlangen in this, I know no relationship that I would wish for more, and that I would at the same time have more reason to thank you for. — Since you mention Erlangen, it seems that the university is indeed to remain on this patch of sand. But is this taking of possession being delayed so much? Should not this, and thus the greater possibility, in the initial setup, of getting something through regarding Erlangen, and the new organization and with it the study plan, coincide in time quite closely?

That you should suggest to me the editing of the so-called new Berlin monthly journal makes me all the more suspect that many others, who know me less well than you do, will accuse me of the same; it is true that much is said about me in it, but all the less should one harbor the suspicion that I have any part in it; — also of my thoughts — and occasional whims, perhaps some run through it — but at least I have not expressed such things for the use that is made of them there; the idea is, however, good in itself; the matter must always be brought to the public in various ways.

B. right from the start, what you say about feeling must not be taken as a deduction, — rather you presuppose the concept (— or deduction) of feeling, and here you merely state what it contains; I would explicitly distinguish this; (— in the same place I would wish for a closer specification of in what respect and in which direction feeling is at the same time the indeterminate — i.e. which mode of determination is lacking to it) — the elucidation by examples would be in its proper place here, where you speak presupposingly, —

What is it, dearest friend, that has caused this long silence, which you have observed both in letters and in rescripts? At present, there is really not much to write. As is known, our educational foundation administration has been dissolved, as it has happened due to the insufficiency of the fund for the regular maintenance of an administrator, so there is initially no prospect of an increase of the same being brought about. At the same time, it is reported that the administrator has been put out of business regarding the use of incoming capital—for our salaries—on the condition of a settlement against what should have been used for us from within; so he has declared that from now on he can no longer pay us anything; at the same time, so much is required to be sent in from him, that everything perhaps coming in within two years would barely be sufficient for that necessity. Thus we are on dry land; but all the closer must we also believe the help to be.

Paulus) traveled to Schweinfurt yesterday to process as much as possible of the 650 florins for this year, i.e., for 6 weeks. — Fuchs' child is very dangerously ill. While I ask you to recommend me to Mrs. Centrälin, this expression carries the meaning that I feel, with heartfelt joy, that I possess no better friend than she, nor any better friend than you. Your sincere friend Hgl. P. S. I must also now, with greater composure, make up for it by asking you to convey my most respectful and friendly recommendations to President Jacobi, Schelling, and Breyer. Mr. von Asbek) will visit you in Munich in a few weeks; he had the extraordinary kindness to pay me a visit just now. See that he becomes General-Krais-Kommissär in Nuremberg. Second P. S. Monday; I have just had Fuchs' child inquired after: it is better this morning. — A courier arrived here this morning, who, in addition to the 10,000 men announced for Thursday, announces another 25 thousand; 4,000 M. will arrive here tomorrow; they will be transported on 1,200 wagons; the day after tomorrow 6,000! — Let us hope that they arrive in time enough, before the Austrians are in Munich, as last time!!!

Otherwise, with this fine weather, everything is going well here. Children are a great acquisition for me; I go almost exclusively to that house. Mrs. von Pflaum has been on a fourteen-day journey; she is returning the day after tomorrow. It has been a great pain to her that the best of women has not yet written to her; I have long since lost track of what to say about it to comfort her; she clings to this best of women with great trusting tenderness. If you could at least have some influence on her willingness to write—for the others you will surely want to leave alone—you would be doing a good, friendly deed. Mrs. von Joly was very pleased to receive a letter from you and, without flattering you too much, was almost even more pleased to receive a letter from Madame Nieth. The town says, and the people here say it to my face, that I am paying court to Mrs. von J.! Otherwise, there is nothing new here. However, if it were not too tedious, I could tell you a long story about the Hoffeten, whose kind and nature you will have seen in my newspaper—for I hope you read it—about the harassment that His Excellency the President has made against me, which I almost believed was because he had something, though I do not know what, against me, otherwise out of pure zeal for duty and submission (which, however, took such an unnecessary turn that I almost came to that suspicion)—but as it often happens with him, without any consequences—shelved! The best of it was, between us, that Mr. von Bsayard had written the entire article (i.e., both that appeared), who was no more pleased by those Hoffeten than by the attempted derivation of the retroactive effect of their clumsiness onto the newspaper. The divine satisfaction was that the Court Marshal was buried today—his coffin passed by the newspaper office—the Duke himself attended. Mr. von B. is generally still very well-disposed and even open and trusting toward me.

If I receive the final commission, I shall see how I can extricate myself from it, and you will have to watch how you extricate yourself from my work. I have taken on my business; the matter is not difficult and, in terms of workload, not much more than before; however, I intend to expand it, and especially to build up the bookselling business over time. I have free lodging, and if the matter remains as it currently stands, an income of 1300 florins. What more temporal things do I want in this world? — Only the damned peace! The peace treaty, for example, certainly already fills its page, but the year is long, and I hope to be supported particularly by you, since the peace works will then be the page-filling ones in reality and thus also in the narrative, and you have such a significant share in such an important part of them. But from Munich, it seems that publicity is neither loved nor sought; not a single word is heard about the Academy, its purpose and instructions. And yet publicity is such a divine power; in print the matter often looks quite different than when spoken and done, its crookednesses come to light just as much as its excellence first receives its luster thereby, — to maintain this clear and impartial mirror in its purity, I have also already contributed my part, since I am now having whiter paper taken for my newspaper.

But the greater the triumph and the honor, the greater the difficulties and the worse their nature. In one of your letters you speak of your honorable intention to secure for me the commission to work out a logic for the lyceums. I hope that you will at least not make the demand so soon, nor for a hasty completion. I am working on my general logic as much as can be done, and I will not be finished with it soon; I feel that it will cost me even more effort to master the subject so that it becomes elementary; for you know that it is easier to be incomprehensible in a sublime manner than to be comprehensible in a plain way, and instruction for the youth and the preparation of a subject for it are the final touchstone of clarity. Insofar as my views are new, there is the added necessity that the teachers must first study the matter even more than the dear youth. But if I

I have also been introduced to Countess Rotenhahn; she is a particularly respectable lady, and her daughters are just as natural and good-natured, as well as educated and full of talents. Bamberg has also made a new acquisition; Liebeskind from Ansbach has come here; I do not know whether you know him; but his wife at least will not be unknown to you. Her friendship with Schelling might perhaps, depending on how one judges the latter, bring a certain timidity to the curiosity of getting to know her. She has seemed kind to me; and he is indeed a very charming man; the rest of Bamberg's manners and education are perhaps not quite suited to this family, are perhaps somewhat against them; so I think all the more that I find an unreserved and interesting company here. — Paulus's family is not yet here.

I was greatly pleased by what you further said in your letter about your diligence in work, and that you promise me a fruit of it soon. Nothing could be more desirable to me than to hear from you again, and along with that to hear you philosophize about my philosophizing. But it is equally necessary for the public that the men who are philosophers make themselves heard again; they can certainly not take the lead back into their hands, for the power and the spread in which the presumption of the bald, shallow, and even senseless has established itself has become too great. If you also perceive differences between us two, I know at the same time that that in which we are in agreement is greater and more powerful, and in relation to those others we shall be infinitely more collaborators than opponents; it is a matter first of all of having gained the common ground, the speculative standpoint; the two approaches to it, on which the world of itself already stood, mysticism and thought, are now more or less blocked up or made inaccessible by overflow. — That you gave Dr. Esser a good scolding may in any case have done no harm; but whether you washed a Moor’s head, you will know better... With love and reverence, yours, Hegel.

On the other hand, it is gratifying to those who look deeper and penetrate the mystery from a higher vantage point that the postal service is so highly cultivated, and that its revenue is so greatly increased by effective and far-reaching means. It is said that the income has increased by several thousand guilders over a short period, and the most gratifying thing is that, as is assured, this surplus is to be applied to our local school fund, and first of all, our arrears of salary are to be paid from it. For this purpose, which also interests me so closely, I am writing this letter to you, in order to increase, on my part, the number of those who flow in from all sides to the center. Before that payment is made, I cannot and must not undertake anything more or further, to steer personally toward the center, and thus to contribute to the promotion of the Hauderer trade, which is in high bloom; because here and elsewhere in our country no grape harvest takes place, this is fairly replaced every autumn by another turnover, and the circulation of both money and people is activated, at a time when substitutes are needed for everything.

In this regard, my request is that you would like to find out, if you can, what the cause of that measure was, whether a requisition from the French Ministry, or something else (namely that affair). This affair is probably of such a nature that legally nothing can well be done about it; but the simpler the matter often is, and the less often what one expected and which presented itself as a more probable suspicion can be established and investigated, the more vexing one can become about it. — I therefore make this request to you, for the sake of my peace of mind, to which it belongs that that investigation not be taken up again, which is not likely if the reason for the ban is some other one; I desire this peace of mind so much that I cannot desire anything more earnestly. — From a notification on this matter, a direction will perhaps at the same time emerge, which I could advise the newspaper owner to take in order to save his property; I am very much indebted to this man, and even without this I would be willing to do everything I am able to do for his integrity. He deserves to the highest degree that one exert oneself for him, and I am doubly bound to do so, whether it is that that affair was the occasion, or a later article, which is by another author, which I however brought to the newspaper, — Stutzmann, who is once and for all predestined to have bad luck in newspaper writing, must himself despise this business; he is necessarily in the greatest embarrassment, and certainly not useless; could he not be of use at a school seminary, since he devoted himself particularly to the school subject? — But what more I could say on this matter is superfluous with you. But once more give me soon that desired peace of mind; if what you could let me know were not reassuring, I would have to look further into what is to be done, and to consult with you about it.

I have now, dearest friend, two letters of yours to answer. One was dictated by your friendly concern regarding the possibility that remarks on the constitution of the Academy might appear in the newspaper. I do not wish to claim outright that your concern was unfounded—setting aside the Censorship; I would not have wanted to make a mere reprint or, since that would have taken up too much space, a mere dry excerpt without any praise; but you have rightly drawn my attention at the right time to the fact that praising certain parts might seem to imply—entirely unspoken—criticism of others, and I would hardly have refrained from praising some things and placing alongside them, in a tone opposite to that of the praiseworthy, other things that are written in that manner. Even the act of praising can already appear disrespectful in our states.

Not yet in December; if we are to wait until those funds are exhausted, that will still take a long time. — I have already spoken with Paulus earlier about Heidelberg; namely with regard to myself; he himself has the idea that a philosopher is still necessary there, and considers the matter very possible and feasible; I shall recommend it to him again all the more urgently. — When you both are out of the country, I shall have no further point of support or prop, and my Marie will go everywhere with me. Farewell, a thousand, a thousand greetings to the best lady. Your H.

The journey and personal presence proved all the more useful, meritorious, indeed necessary; Cotta is entangled in so many complications and interconnections that it is difficult to extract and secure a significant matter cleanly, which itself is such an extensive complex; he had previously remained dark about such further connections; had he not given us, or even his agent, the spice merchant Küffner, any indication of them, we would have sailed over reefs and shallows where we saw a clear course. — For indeed, Munich’s glorious pregnancy is threatening to us; there are three requisites with which such a scientific epoch must be equipped — and woe! perhaps at our expense; famous names — you will probably learn of their fame in Munich; an active publishing house, that is, one that pays considerable honoraria to poor authors and has them printed on white paper, and with enterprise, with or without capital, makes a spectacular bankruptcy after a year; a literary newspaper, namely one like none has ever been, that is, if God now sees the damage, as daily or even more daily than any others have ever been. Cotta, whose iron head has seen many of these glorious university pregnancies and their publishing houses pass by and harden therein, has not yet managed to strike broadly for the new South German Zion of science.

All this, then, as a friendly return for your kind bulletins, for whose friendliness and pleasantness I am most grateful to acknowledge, insofar as it is possible from a distance, as well as my thanks for the kind handling of the matter with my sister. Now, what I have gathered since then in local news: Grillparzer was here, a very plain, sensible, and zealous man; then Raupach’s Night Watchmen did not crow to their advantage; they blew in Potsdam the day before yesterday; whether less harm came to the gentlemen there is still unknown to me. Professor Blum is currently here on his way through; Leo was appointed in yesterday’s session at the Library with 400 thalers. Professor Abegg from Königsberg is here; he and I miss your presence; he has joined Schunke’s and thus Puchta’s Journal in a criminalistic and criminal manner, and has one or two moralities in petto for you, but we do not let him get away with them. Von Hülsen departed today. My bust is as good as finished. Carové will come here in a few days; one could have plans for current, busy, routine secretarial work with him. The art exhibition has begun ten days ago. With your return home, we hope to receive a report on the beginning and the prospects for our first issue. The warmest greetings to Hotho and to my dear, beloved Munich friends, and to you, my dear and esteemed friend, whose company I so often miss. Your Hegel.

However, it is time to close, and I therefore add only this: I hold that this content is present in all genuine consciousness, in all religions and philosophies; but our present standpoint is to recognize it in its developed form, and this can happen in no other way than through a scientific method, which is at the same time the only way in which it can be proved. I have taken it upon myself, in my position, to work toward elevating philosophy to a science, and my previous works—though partly imperfect and partly incomplete—have only this purpose; I have attempted to provide an overview in my Encyclopedia, which, however, greatly needs revision. You should therefore consider my past and future writings in light of this purpose; a Logic and then the Philosophy of Right (which has given great offense to the demagogic people) are to be such scientific treatments, the former of the Universal, the latter of a part of the Idea that reveals itself in reality, which is the One in all; you will be able to see my method more closely from these, which is to develop nothing but the necessary progression from the concept, and otherwise to look at and concern itself with no good reasons or opinions. I now wish that this little may serve to give you approximately the requested acquaintance with my view and manner of philosophizing; in this attempt you will at least recognize how much it has pleased me to know in you a friend of philosophy (there are many of the superficial self-conceit). With all respect, your most devoted, Prof. Hegel.

My view is that the Idea must be expressed and grasped only as a process in itself (as Becoming is an example), as motion; for the True is not merely a resting, being, but only as self-moving, as living; — the eternal distinguishing and the reduction of the difference, existing in the One, to the point where it is no longer a difference; — what, when conceived as a mode of feeling, has been called eternal love; only as this motion in itself, which is equally absolute rest, is the Idea, Life, Spirit.

Life experience is initially manifested, but the further need is to grasp it in the form of thought — he wishes, to use the expression you quote, not to believe the truth, but to see it with the eyes of the spirit, for it cannot be done with the bodily ones — to see it, i.e., to know it. —* And since the interest of your mind has long since placed you on the standpoint of this need, I am spared the task of pointing to that first form, as well as of speaking of its transition into the second — of faith into knowledge —; only allow me to remark that it immediately makes an important difference whether faith and knowledge are distinguished according to their content, or whether they are regarded only as different forms of one and the same content — and in this regard it is my view, and I consider this one of the most important, that religion may well have deceived individuals, but not peoples and generations, and that philosophy has not been completed, at least in its execution, as long as it has not succeeded in perceiving that reconciliation and harmony. — I have recently spoken about the relation of these two forms in a few sheets, of which I take the liberty of enclosing a copy (only I ask that the indicated printing errors be carefully corrected beforehand), and which are the preface to a work by one of my students, Dr. Hinrichs, on religion in relation to science.

The more immediate causes of this long delay were that last year I wanted to let the writing stand until I could report to you the completion of my Logic, the second part of which, as I gather from your letter, has arrived according to my instructions—and since the negotiation of my transfer to a university then arose, until I could report to you the decision on this matter; I had been appointed professor at Erlangen by the Bavarian government, and at the same time I received a call to Berlin, just as I had given my binding word for Heidelberg—a decision for which I have not yet found a single moment to regret. Above all, I wish you, although I shall be among the last of the congratulators, very great good luck on your new post in Brussels; I imagine it to be very delicate, especially since you are a Protestant. I know some of the professors who have been called to Belgium; Becker, who studied here, attended my lectures last winter; Stahl, from Landshut, who was formerly in Jena, is, as far as I know, Protestant. You do not think it good that the Dutch and Brabantine universities have not been amalgamated any longer; I must be of a different opinion; by the sharp separation and careful preservation of what each party may consider its right, the first evil, which opposes all improvements and approaches, namely mistrust, is removed; once trust has been gained by that means, it becomes, like all the palliations of mistrust, superfluous in time and destroys itself. I have also seen in several German states the deception that the supposed impartiality of partiality removed all external barriers, and thereby gained the possibility of being partial under the pretext of impartiality. You mentioned in an earlier letter Friedrich Schlegel, who might well be inclined to be active for freedom from ultramontane principles; but I have all reasons to suppose that the exact opposite is the case with him.

Dearest Godfather and Friend. I will not delay in thanking you for the friendliness with which you accepted and granted my request to serve as godfather to my recently born son. My [wife] and I likewise hope and wish that, according to the general custom, not only the rightful portion, but also a good deal more from his worthy godfather may pass over to him. At the baptism I took your place; I endeavored to remain negative in doing so, and not to place myself between the influences of your godfatherhood and their effect on him, but to let everything flow through unimpeded and honestly. His name, which you inquired about, is — Thomas Immanuel Christian; — the last from my sister), the first from Seebek, and the middle one, by which he is called, from you; the former he has because he is a Christian and baptized, the latter because he is also to pass over to the other extreme, unbelief; the middle one, which is to fuse these extremes in friendship and philosophy and temper and balance one in the other as a point of indifference.

Your first letter contains, with regard to the state of the Bamberg newspapers, a great comfort for me, for which I am all the more grateful to you, since your friendship in this matter had to contend not only with the unpleasantness of the affair but also with illness. — In general, I also recently heard from Rößler that you had been unwell on several occasions; I unfortunately have the notion that, given the heavy burden of work that lies upon you, it cannot be otherwise; tu sacrificris pro nobis. However, you will surely take time in the summer for the necessary rest; I scarcely dare to say it, but the order has been preserved and the commanderies and estates of the same located within the borders of Bavaria have been gifted to the King of B.

You recently asked me until when I believe I will be able to finish a philosophical textbook for secondary schools; if I receive the commission for it, I cannot promise to have it done before next Easter. If I can look further ahead and get to the actual work, I will submit the general plan to you beforehand for your review and decision; until then, I will say no more about it. You have sent me Schubert and Kanne, who are fine men for friendship and companionship, and very capable people for the Realinstitut; moving the Realinstitut and the Gymnasium to different locations would be of essential benefit. It would also do no harm to our Gymnasium to have a few of that sort, for bare Latin and Greek words cannot acquire the Kingdom of God.

Mrs. von Joly and Mrs. von Siebein send their best regards to you and, above all, to the memory of the best lady; the husband of the former has taken his leave from the military and will move to Mannheim with his wife; the latter speaks of the hope of visiting you in Munich. — When shall I be able to attain such happiness? — In eight days we take our vacation; if that alone were the case, I would be with you in a single leap. — For the time being, therefore, my warmest greetings to the best lady and Julius, as I commend myself to you. Your Majesty.

The sciences receive their concept from philosophy, which makes use of the sciences as its own property, just as it in turn receives its nourishment, matter, and wealth from them. I cannot say how far I might be able to contribute here; what each person is, he must prove through his deeds and his effect on others; I can only refer to unfinished works. If I am to speak of what I might accomplish in science, then, after the first excursions that lie before the fair-minded judge as attempts (in the critical journal), I have remained silent before the larger public and have delivered lectures to a smaller circle on the entire science of speculative philosophy, the philosophy of nature, of spirit, and natural law. In addition, I would read in Heidelberg on aesthetics in the sense of a course of literature, and I would consider myself fortunate to be able to enjoy your support in this. A larger work (the Phenomenology of Spirit) I will present in the autumn as a system of philosophy; I hope that at least so much will result from it that it will be clear that it is not my intention to promote the nonsense of formalism, which ignorance currently drives particularly with the help of a terminology behind which it hides. Luther made the Bible, you Homer, speak German, the greatest gift that could be offered to the people; for a people remains barbaric and does not regard the excellent as its own property as long as it does not know it in its own language. If you wish to forget these two examples, I will say of my endeavors that I will try to teach philosophy to speak German. Once it has come to that point, it will become infinitely more difficult to give the appearance of deep speech to shallowness.

Your Excellency will do me the honor if I yield to the impulse to address you in these days of autumnal sorrow, which could still be decreed upon Your Excellency, with these lines. What feelings of veneration and gratitude, what acquaintance with the beneficial activity of Your Excellency in your high position, with the labors and difficult circumstances thereof, with the high virtues of public and private life, which are the object of general esteem, and then with the severe sufferings and trials to which Your Excellency has been subjected by higher power, what such sentiments and recollections have gathered in the mind, unite at the sight of such a hard turn in life into a concentrated realization, which feels driven to expression; and the pain of sympathy over the immeasurable loss which Your Excellency has suffered presses itself into its center, to settle in the place where it exists in its full extent and strength, and thus in its full right; but such a place is in the heart, from which the full, detailed, value of the object of this sorrow, proven throughout an entire life, is known. To have been permitted to gain an image of such value belongs to the best and rarest experiences of my life regarding people. In the image of Your Excellency’s immortalized sister, memory is occupied with all the virtues that adorn a female soul; and if it is moved and delighted by the idea of a cultivated mind, the acquaintance with the seriousness of life and the great circumstances, and the even earlier acquaintance with the pains and sufferings thereof, but the heavenly simple patience and resignation, the loving compassion with all who suffer, the sympathetic friendship, the infinite love for the brother—this strongest feeling of a noble female breast—by the series of individual virtues, it finds the highest value and the most peculiar grace of this richness in the fact that it has been found closed together in unbroken harmony into the simple bloom of cheerful naturalness and straightforwardness of mind, indeed of a maidenly youthfulness of a noble nature.

A concluding remark is still missing, which I have not added because I am still undecided about it myself; — namely, that perhaps all philosophical instruction at secondary schools might seem superfluous, and that the study of the ancients is the most suitable for secondary school youth and, in its substance, the true introduction to philosophy. — But how can I, the professor of the preparatory sciences of philosophy, argue against my own field and position? Dig up the bread and water from under my own feet? On the other hand, however, I — who should also be a philosophical pedagogue — would indeed have an official duty to do so, even as Rector; finally, there is also the closer interest that the professors of philosophical sciences at secondary schools be declared superfluous and either given a different workload or transferred elsewhere. But one thing also draws me back to the first side, namely the purely scholarly philology that tends toward verbal wisdom. The Church Fathers, Luther, and the old preachers cited, expounded, and handled the biblical texts in a free manner, in which, with regard to historical scholarship, it did not amount to a farmer’s shoe, provided they could put in all the more doctrine and spiritual edification. The aesthetic dabbling in phrases like “pulere! quam venuste!” (to shine! how elegantly!), of which we still hear significant echoes, has now been replaced by word-critical and metrical scholarship; I do not know whether much of this has already crept into your subordinate staff; but it will also befall them, and in one case or another philosophy will come away quite empty-handed.

I will not trouble you much with our local troubles; things are going as usual. The fundamental evil, however, is that we are without advocates against the administrative authorities, because we have no district councilor here to whom nothing is communicated that has a particularly administrative aspect.... There is complete silence regarding the arrears for 1810/11, and we must now come forward with a lithographic petition. All this and other things have so completely destroyed my hope without works that I must again speak to you of the idea of taking a step from my side in Württemberg.

Gloke was! — If the latter were well-founded, what a connection there would be between the blind instinct of time division, which seems arbitrary, and nature! What could be more welcome to Ritter for his study of time periods?
