His attempts will, however, sometimes be so transcendent that others are unable to follow, and he will have difficulty getting his magnetic needle made of 2 metals, which you mention in the writing against Fichte, accepted by other physicists; at least, as far as I hear, there is still great disagreement about it. — Regarding the sidereal experiments, I have therefore heard with pleasure that he writes to have indicated a device by which the accidental factors that can interfere with these experiments are removed — without this, I would not dare to consider one successful in my own case — admittedly, I have also only been able to experiment with lead weights, coins, and the like — not with golden or silver dice.

Highly esteemed Sir and Friend! Your kind intention has finally been fulfilled, and Jakob Böhme, along with the other enclosures, has reached me safely. I offer you my heartfelt thanks for this beautiful gift of remembrance and friendship; it has greatly pleased me; the edition and the copy are very excellent. — I can now study Jakob Böhme more closely than before, because I was not myself in possession of his writings; his theosophy is always one of the most remarkable attempts by a deep, yet uneducated man, to grasp the innermost nature of the absolute being. — For Germany, he has the particular interest that he is actually the first German philosopher. —

You do not deserve to be left in quiet repose by us in Jena, since you only wished to stay with us so briefly and only appeared to us like a fleeting vision. As fleeting as this vision was in terms of time, so powerful was it in contrast, like lightning, and it has left behind in us a resonant uplift. Your activity and even your physical energy completely astonished us through a packet of letters written during the night before your departure, from which Madame Paulus still has not recovered. — For years we had expected you as our savior, who has at least also healed me, namely from the craving and longing for the things and upheavals that were to come, from that restlessness that does not properly settle in their presence and in the things as they are, because it is awaiting something else, or only because it wants to know how it really is with them, and supposes an unknown reserve and background therein; even if the object would have no influence on the whole of the situation and one knows its limitation very well, the fact that it is expected gives it a breadth into the darkness, so that it seems to overreach the whole therein. — Thus I would now be at peace and would regard the state of affairs that is as the one that will also be more or less so — if your statements about your personal circumstances had not driven me again from that lack of expectation into the opposite and into fear. These statements, lastly a broad nocturnal letter to Mr. v. Zlentner! make me believe that you have made the period of your absence the decisive moment regarding your circumstances.

I have submitted my report on the Real Institute; it was only necessary to send this one to Jena as well, in order to keep the school system sufficiently before your eyes from my side; however, I have spoken to you enough about my views, and you will, God willing, find it in Munich. Jakob's family passed through here a few days ago; he himself is expected to follow in a few weeks. The imminent announcement of the merger of the Financial Directorates with the General Commissariat, the reduction of the districts to 10, and the subordination of the foundation administrations to the General Commissariates is expected; Lerchenfeld is definitely coming to Innsbruck.

In your next letter, and hopefully a soon one, I hope to find the date of your arrival fixed. The duration of your stay cannot be less than 4 weeks, given the many affairs awaiting you. In any case, your inclination for building, which will not have rusted and has since then only exercised itself in offices, will find a great scope here; and in fact, I am assured that the local planners will not agree and come to a conclusion with something comprehensive, and that a higher authority coming to the spot is absolutely necessary to bring it to a firm decision and to a thorough arrangement, for if such does not occur, then (only] provision will be made for the immediate needs; the higher authorities believe that everything and even more has been done, and a quarter or half remains in the old rubble, which has accumulated over a hundred years, and at the clearing away of which) one will not get around to it again for a hundred years.

To His Highness, the Provincial Directorial Councilor Dr. Niethammer in Bamberg.

I postponed writing to you until I could report to you, dearest friend, the execution of the commission regarding the review. Next Monday I shall begin my lectures. The necessity involved is this: that there will probably be listeners, but a middle number, whom one cannot refuse to read, and who yet do not bring in much, which finally sinks to a trifle through the uncertainty of payment. — It has been given me the hope, after I had raised the matter last autumn, to receive a salary this spring; the good will of the ministers seems not to be lacking; but before the next autumn, I fear, they will not muster the courage to speak to the Duke, who does not like to hear of such things, about it, and then perhaps next spring it will be resolved that I might receive something in the following autumn. In any case, in the uncertainty in which the political independence of this Prince also stands, there is now no time for favorable hopes. So much for my situation and circumstances here. — But how is it with you, both with yourself, and Madam Niethammer? Your devoted Hegel.

Yet I wish to write to you now about a different subject. I will, namely, in accordance with my recent promise, share with you the epigram by Mr. Kästner on Kepler. Here it is: So high has no mortal ever climbed As Kepler climbed, — and died in hunger. He knew only how to please the spirits, Therefore the bodies a) left him without bread b). How strikingly here the inexhaustible wit of Kästner stands out, which otherwise gets along so little with mathematical heads. Another one is:

To Mr. Haag, Mathematics Student, in Stuttgart. Mathematikhausen.

Dearest Friend! I am very grateful to you for your last letter. Regarding insects, I only wish to note that you do not call them by the shameful name of vermin. I also want to contribute to this topic: it has been observed that all insects do not breathe through openings in the head (nose), but through small holes in the abdomen, 3, 4, 6, etc., on each side. If one now covers these with something sticky, e.g., oil, the insects die because they no longer have air. I read this in a natural history book, so I checked it myself and found it confirmed by experience; in particular, I could observe the little holes in the hard skin of beetles.

The spirit by which Euler became great fits into no binding and rests on no order. In praise of mathematics, he says the following in another place; he wrote it, namely, to a friend in his memorial book. Oh, could a shadow move you of the delight that hearts feel, which have devoted themselves to the art of measurement! You demanded from fate the empty hours back, which you had spent with songs! I will tell you the following anecdote about his deep thinking:

To Mr. F. W. Schelling, Professor of Philosophy in Jena.

I think, dear Schelling, that a separation of several years should not make me feel awkward about asking for your favor on account of a particular wish. My request concerns some addresses in Bamberg, where I wish to stay for some time. As I am finally in a position to leave my current circumstances, I am resolved to spend a period of time in an independent situation and to devote it to the studies and works I have begun. Before I dare to entrust myself to the literary bustle of Jena, I wish to first strengthen myself by staying in a third place. Bamberg occurred to me all the more because I had hoped to find you there; I hear that you have returned to Jena again. In Bamberg I know no one, nor do I know how else to obtain an address there, so allow me to ask you for this and for your good advice; it would be of the greatest service to me to find an arrangement regarding board and lodging, etc.; the more specific information you give me, the more grateful I shall be to you, and the more time and useless expenses I shall save; it will also be very pleasant for me if you will make the way open for me to some literary acquaintances. If your local knowledge prefers another place, Erfurt, Eisenach, or similar, I ask you for your advice; I seek cheap food, because of my physical condition a good beer, and a few acquaintances; the rest is equal — I would prefer a Catholic city to a Protestant one; I want to see that religion up close once. — Forgive my request due to the lack of acquaintances who would be closer in this matter, and forgive my fussiness over such particularities to our old friendship.

I have watched your public, great stride with admiration and joy; you spare me the necessity of either speaking humbly about it or wanting to show myself to you; I make use of the middle term, that I hope we shall find each other again as friends. In my scholarly education, which began with the subordinate needs of men, I had to be driven to science, and the ideal of youth had to transform itself into a form of reflection, into a system at the same time; I ask myself now, while I am still occupied with it, what return to intervening in the life of men is to be found. Of all the men I see around me, I see only in you the one in whom I would also like to find my friend with regard to expression and effect on the world; for I see that you have grasped men purely, i.e. with your whole soul, and without vanity. I therefore also look, with regard to myself, so full of trust upon you, that you may recognize my disinterested striving, even if its sphere were lower, and find a value in it. With the wish and hope of meeting you, I must, however far it may be, also know how to honor fate, and expect from its favor how we shall meet. Farewell! I ask you for a prompt answer. Your friend Wilh. Hegel. Recommend me to our friend Breyer. Address: with Mr. J. N. Gogel on the Roßmarkt.

Above all, I am behindhand in thanking you for the multitude of productions that your assiduity has succeeded in bringing to light and that your friendship has wished to send to me, and for the dedication of one of them by which you have wished to honor me; this dedication, a monument of your friendly sentiments toward me, finally contains your manifesto against our police, for the omniscience of which, by the way, Plato is presumably a dark corner into which it has probably not penetrated. The interest that the Fragments have inspired in me has led me to undertake writing an article on them for our critical journal; I have not renounced it, but its completion will be late; besides, being out of season is one of our German qualities. It is a fine present that you have given me with your complete edition of Descartes; the naivety of his method and exposition is admirable; one may regret not being endowed with the power to force men to receive the initiative of philosophy through the study of these so simple and so clear treatises, but what is still lacking to make the edition complete is the most interesting part, your work on Cartesian philosophy.

The young Ampère is here, and has the kindness to come and see me from time to time; in order to penetrate completely into the heart of the romantic world, he plans to visit Sweden and Denmark as well. I, who am not very at home in these mists, am in a position to contribute to the advancement of his views. I have recently received some news of yours from Mr. Panofka, who will have the kindness to deliver this letter to you, as well as, finally, the volumes of Mr. Hotho.

I am told from Württemberg that I have also been mentioned regarding the refilling of Abel’s position in Tübingen; as I generally have no great hopes, I also look without strong hope to see whether anything will come of it. Perhaps our petition to Your Royal Majesty’s Department of Studies, concerning the state of our salary arrears, has come to your attention. The local foundation administration calls upon the financial department, we call upon Your Royal Majesty’s Department of Studies, so that the scripture may be fulfilled: the deep calls to the deep. Things are going badly here, very badly, too badly.... Your Royal Highness

Regarding the journey, I foresee that the costs will not exceed 10 Carolines, and I would wish that you would speak with Mr. Gogel about this provisionally and, as you deem appropriate, ask him to send me a bill of exchange through you—or to reimburse me for the costs when I arrive in Frankfurt. Although it pains me that I cannot set out immediately, it is impossible for me to leave the house in which I am staying before the end of the year, or to arrive in Frankfurt before mid-January. Since you have already begun to take an interest in this matter for my sake, I must ask you to share the essential content of my letter with Mr. Gogel and to assure him of my high regard. He will surely realize that a part of what you may have told him about me, in order to inspire the trust he accords me, is more to be credited to your friendship for me, or that one friend cannot always be reliably judged by another; nevertheless, assure him that I shall make every effort to deserve your recommendation. I shall say nothing of how much longing for you contributed to my swift decision, or how the image of our reunion and the happy future of being with you would hover before my eyes during this interim—farewell. Your Hegel.

I have long set aside a copy of my brochure, as well as of my dissertation, which I intend to send off shortly. Something new is again coming off the stocks, namely the first issue of a critical journal of philosophy, which I am publishing in association with Schelling (with whom I live, and who sends you his best regards), and which has the tendency, on the one hand, to increase the number of journals, and on the other, to put a limit and measure to unphilosophical abuses; the weapons which the journal will use are very varied; they will be called cudgels, whips, and goads; — everything is done for the sake of the good cause and for the glory of God; people will perhaps complain about it here and there; but cauterization has in fact become necessary.

To His High Reverence, Mr. Ober-Schul- und Kirchen-Rath Niethammer in Munich. Nuremberg, 12 February 1809.

You, highly esteemed friend, recently had Paulus send you my regards, and at the same time mentioned the cause of your long silence, namely the files, of which I do not believe the piles to be too great if I compare them with Etna and Atlas, and of whose weight I do not fear that you are crushed, but that you are thereby too much pressed and burdened. From here, there is undoubtedly no lack of contributions to make life bitter for you. My general report on the gymnasiums, along with a supplementary report from the district commissariat, will be in your hands. If the whole already stands in a flourishing state, there are nevertheless many circumstances in it which cry out for help. You will find them in the report, and I will not fill your ears here with complaints about them either. However, I cannot remain entirely silent on two things. One is the arrangement to provide students with cheaper schoolbooks through the schoolbook shop; this is the last time I believed in it when a relief through public provision was announced; I had the books brought, sold them at the discount that Frommann gave; and now that the account of the schoolbook shop follows afterwards, it turns out that only a swindle and fraud lies behind this arrangement.

A second circumstance is the external condition of our schools, though it is superfluous to say a word about this in general; only this I cannot pass over, that in the two premises, the Sebald and Lorenz schools, that is, in the Progymnasium, the primary and collaboration schools, there is no privy. This state of affairs is far too shameful and, so to speak, dreadful. I have repeatedly approached the Cultus Administrator, under whose authority these buildings still stand, and the Building Inspector, both in writing and orally, to remedy this disgraceful defect; as of today, nothing has been done. They have, as Paulus told me, decreed a double middle class in the Gymnasium and a second primary school; two privies would be a much greater benefit to us, but one that is made, not decreed. — In the admission of pupils, I must now each time also ask the parents whether their children have the skill to relieve themselves without a privy, by their own strength. — This is a new part of public education, the essential nature of which I have come to know, namely the rear part of it. — Since I have now turned to the General Commissariat to obtain relief through the police — because in one of the premises the military and the night watchmen have taken possession of the necessary place — it is now to be expected how far we will get with this. But you will imagine for yourself how greatly this sloppiness of the external conditions, which even extends to that dreadful defect, prevents the public from gaining any confidence, — since no care has yet been taken for anything and money is lacking everywhere.

We were all unanimous in our opinion of the merits of your work, namely that it combines the thoroughness of speculative insight with the precision and clarity of development and presentation. In particular, I consider the excurses in which you treat Herbartian and, on this occasion, Aristotelian philosophical propositions as models of exposition. How welcome it would be if you were to treat other matters, which are currently on the agenda, in this manner; the tangle of ideas, as well as the shallowness and, on top of that, the ignorance, is equally glaring in much that makes itself thick and broad and good-humored and speaks in grand terms; this cannot be countered by declamations, but only by such expositions that closely follow the assertions, as yours are. It is equally necessary to go directly at this coal, to disturb it in its rest and in its ignoring, by which it maintains its well-being against more profound science. Such expositions have their difficulties, but you have this manner in your power, and it will be very pleasing to me if you will soon put it into practice in our Berlin Yearbooks, in which even fewer of this kind than declamations have been received. The review of your work in them has been assigned to Hinrichs in Halle and is to arrive soon /).

That I gave Tholuck particular consideration in my second edition of the Encyclopedia is, on the whole, accidental, and was only determined by the local commotion insofar as he came into my hands earlier than anyone else as a representative of the chatter about Pantheism. Your exposition of the appearance, which you particularly mentioned in your letter, where without doubt the note to § 89 is meant, I found excellent; it is one of the most difficult points, and if one fully grasps the relationship, the exposition remains the most difficult, which you have accomplished perfectly. Once again my urgent apology for my long delay in answering; my wife, who has been much plagued by ill health this winter, is now well again with my two boys, and she sends her warmest regards to you and your family, as I also commend myself to your continued friendship — as your most devoted Prof. Hegel.

I recently wrote to you about the expected domestic events that were to come, and since the pleasing part of them has reached its happy conclusion, I hasten to give you brief news of it. My wife was delivered of a healthy boy the day before yesterday—or actually already on Monday night—and since then both mother and child are doing very well. Thus, at least, the hope awaited with anxiety has come to its happy end; I know that you and your wife take a heartfelt interest in it.

I have instructed the bookseller to send you, dearest friend, a copy of the second part of my Logic (1 volume, 2nd section). Please excuse the long delay in my reply to this work; I have a good excuse for it; but in truth, the printing of it had already been finished in December... We have at last received the salary arrears from two years ago; it was a matter of bread, for naturally I had to borrow so much; it had taken no small effort to get them paid out; but our help was also no small power, — several hundred thousand Cossacks, Bashkirs, Prussian patriots, and so on, were approaching; then it went through. The best thing is that we received this money without the Cossacks, Bashkirs, and the other excellent liberators. — Three years ago, no such effort was necessary; a few hundred Austrian Landwehrmen procured our arrears for us at that time. — So we are only well off when the enemy comes.

My father-in-law has been ill since the beginning of December; his weakness has now progressed to such a degree that all hope is lost, and he has little coherent consciousness left. You can imagine how hard this is for my mother-in-law and my wife in their circumstances; he has not yet acquired any property, partly because his father is still alive, and partly because the main revenues depend on the family foundation and his person, so these will cease with him. Jena, too, must have had much to endure. Farewell, Your Highness.

By chance, I spoke a few days ago here with the author of the letters in Archenholz’s Minerva, which are well known to you and signed with an O, supposedly by an Englishman. The author is, however, a Silesian and is named Elsner. He gave me news of some Württembergers in Paris, and also of Reinhard, who holds a position of great importance in the department of foreign affairs. Elsner is still a young man, and one can see that he has worked hard—he is studying privately here this winter. What is Renz doing? Has he buried his talent? I hope not—it would certainly be worth the trouble to encourage or urge him to compile his certainly thorough investigations on important subjects. This might perhaps compensate him for the vexation he has had for a long time—I have some friends in Saxony who would be helpful in furthering his placement. If you do not consider him entirely averse to it, encourage him to do such a thing, try to overcome his modesty—in any case, give him my regards.

A main aspect of the circumstances of your stay, it was said, should be that you obtain direct influence over university affairs; this is for me at present the main point! — Has this point, has Erlangen — or even I myself — already come up for discussion? — In the summer, in Munich, everyone usually goes to the spa — you on commission; for the autumn you intended to go to Swabia. — We have organizations dated October 1, and calculated for that date, to be seen announced late in November; — others, which were to take effect around April 1, were assured on March 30 that they were still to be drafted, but on April 2, because it is now too late, to be seen postponed by half a year, if luck was good, — or else by another year. — What a future of uncertainties, expectations for this day, for the next day — hopes and so forth — and all this in the state of betrothal and in such a way that the marriage is tied to all these uncertainties, deceptions, and expectations. — This is a tangle of a different kind, which requires a main stroke and can only be hacked apart.

I also have to thank you for another project, which was supposed to already be in progress, namely for provisionally entrusting me with the management of school affairs here; it would indeed have done something in the opinion of the people; but how I would have honored this honorable commission, I do not yet know exactly. — My small-mindedness gave me for a moment the suspicious thought that you had the project of opening a hole in my career in business, in case or out of concern that difficulties might arise for the academic one. — But I call to myself: away with this fear!

Bless the Academy’s presidency that they found him just as you described him to me; the picture you have drawn of him has surprised me, for I had not imagined him to be so! — The addition, however, which was meant to confirm your impartiality, namely that you ought rather to look askance at the amiability that the wife also finds in him, has seemed to me rather suspicious, for in truth one does not quite know whether you are not merely following the wife’s judgment bon gré malgré, which, as I admittedly cannot know with complete certainty, is said to occur sometimes in marriage; experienced people have assured me, however, that things do go that way here and there. What might serve to confirm this is that this wife demands that you find J.’s sister charming. This demand is truly too jealous; here in Bamberg the wife has been more liberal toward you! Here she has left you a range of choice among three — I do not know how many — pretty young ladies; in Munich she wants you to stick to a sixty-year-old spinster! That is, as I said, carrying jealousy too far! — I can hardly believe it, given her known goodness! and I now see that I was indeed only deceived by first appearances, and that this wish is rather the pinnacle of her generosity; for since three times twenty makes sixty, she allows you, in a single sixty-year-old, three twenty-year-old ladies at once; — a truly selected generosity and concentration of goodness.

The other side has sought to cover itself in its own way with formal freedom, and has taken great care not to expose its vulnerability; the assertion of this so-called freedom has in itself immense popularity, and is also so defiant against an attack because it is immediately at hand to give such an attack, which defends the dogma and the form of the Church, the odious turn of an attack on the office and livelihood of individuals; it is a similar relationship that those who defend the rights of the rulers and the state are accused, in regard to themselves, of servility towards state teachers and orators who are just as shallow as the rationalists are in religion, and of the intention to make them suspicious to the governments and to draw their punishment upon them. — But at present the enormous political interest has swallowed up all others, — a crisis in which everything that previously counted seems to be made problematic. As little as the philosophy of ignorance, violence, and evil passions can oppose itself to this loud clamor, so do I hardly believe that it can penetrate into those circles that have made themselves so comfortable; it must become aware of itself, — also for the purpose of reassurance, — that it is only for a few. As I have accustomed myself to seek the satisfaction of my mind in the activity of the same, it is at the same time most pleasing and refreshing to me when some of it resonates in others and I meet them on the same paths; how valuable the encounter with you is to me, I express with deeply felt thanks and with intimate veneration; with this I allow myself to recommend myself to your further kind disposition. Your obedient Prof. Hegel.

It has already been a considerable time, over a year, since I received your kind letter, which informed me how graciously you had viewed the liberty I had wished to take in personally expressing my high regard to you, and whose benevolent content and such weighty words regarding the temporal relation to speculative knowledge made me whole for the failure of that attempt. I must ask your forgiveness most earnestly for such undue delay in my thanks and make my very great excuse. What must you think of such negligence, — I have indeed often had to say to myself, — while I, filled with intimate veneration for you, am so much concerned with the preservation of your kind disposition toward me. I cannot entirely pass over it without citing the reasons for my excuse; as the main one, I must name an idiosyncrasy that does not allow me, who am not a businessman to begin with, to dispose of the answering of a valuable letter, such as yours, as a matter of business: it counts for me rather as an intercourse with the man to whom I am writing, — as such a conversation, for which I need composure and quiet and wish to wait, but of which I am not capable in a state in which the mind is overfilled with external distraction; in such a state, however, I have been for the past year, and while I wished to use the first time of leisure for such conversation, I have been afflicted from the very first moment with a cold fever, with which I have been struggling for a quarter of a year.

At last, most esteemed friend, I have reached the point where I can begin sending the manuscript of the second edition of my Encyclopedia today or tomorrow. I inform you of this in gratitude for the kindness you are showing me by willingly taking on the revision of the printing in a most friendly manner. As much as I am indebted to you for this, I also have a certain bad conscience about having relied too much on the state of the manuscript, for it is indeed of such a nature that it requires an attentive typesetter, and that you will therefore be put to more trouble than I am justified in demanding. Otherwise, I have endeavored to mark the changes, insertions, etc., very carefully and precisely. Otherwise, I give you full authority to correct, strike out, and supply whatever you find to be obscure, unintelligible, or repetitive, entirely according to your own judgment. I must wish that you might be somewhat entertained or compensated by the interest of the content; it is only the friendly encouragement you have allowed my endeavors to receive that can permit me to accept these kind efforts on my behalf as well.

It is said that if the Devil once grabs you by the hair, you are his forever; I do not think that you intend to let the hair grow into a lock with me, but rather to pull it out again as soon as possible and to reorganize it, for which, if so, the opportunity should be found at present; I commit the matter to God, to you, and to the lady. I told Roth and his wife upon his departure today that the enjoyment of his friendly presence also contained this pleasing wealth, that it thereby includes a half-presence of the dear circle of which he is a member, and thus, as he travels here with his wife to a homeland, he also carries with him one of the best plots of land from my homeland... Your H.

Fichte tires me. Beer glasses and state fathers' swords have thus resisted the power of his spirit); perhaps he would have accomplished more if he had left them their roughness and had merely set himself the goal of attracting a quiet, chosen little group. But it is still shameful, the treatment of would-be philosophers by him and by Schiller; my God, what letter-worshippers and slaves are still among them! I hope to receive Niethammer's Journal every day and look forward especially to your contributions. Your example and your efforts encourage me anew to keep up, as much as possible, with the development of our times.

Since you will soon leave Tübingen, please be so kind as to notify me soon of what you intend to do and of your future place of residence, as well as of all your circumstances. Above all, for the sake of yourself and your friends, spare your health; do not be too stingy with the time you should devote to recovery. Greet my friends warmly. Next time I will enclose a letter to Renz for you; it would delay the departure of this one; nevertheless, please greet him warmly from me when you write to him. Farewell, answer me soon, you cannot imagine how much it comforts me, in my solitude, to hear from you and my other friends from time to time. Your Hgl. Schelling's answer from Jan. 1796 see From Sch.'s L. 1, 81.

The spirit that the previous government threatened to introduce, I have recognized in your description); it is founded in hypocrisy and timidity (a consequence of despotism), and is itself again the father of hypocrisy; the spirit that must prevail in every public constitution that has the chimerical notion of wanting to examine hearts and kidneys, and to take virtue and piety as the measure for estimating merit and for the distribution of offices; I feel most deeply the pitiable nature of such a state, where the state descends into the holy) depth of morality and wishes to judge it; pitiable it is, even if the state meant well, yet infinitely more sorrowful if hypocrites get the office of judge into their hands, which must happen, even if it was meant well at first. This spirit seems also to have had an influence on the completion of your college of repetents, which, if it consisted of well-organized heads, could bring true benefit.

Forgive me that I am entertaining you with such matters, or rather asking for your help in them. — A few other things. — I hear with pleasure that you look forward to a speedy final decision regarding your position; best of all, to Munich itself — Lord, when You come into Your Kingdom, remember me, I shall pray! — I hear that Fichte is not in Erlangen, but in! in — Göttingen; a better proof of Prussian) affection for Göttingen than the gift of the Wolfian Homer. — I have finally received a salary here, of? of! — 100, I say: One hundred thalers. — I have not yet read the Salatsches) review in the Haller newspaper; it will probably not appear — it has, among other things, the fault of being too large. — I hope, although the best source is here, to learn something from you about the state of our dear fatherland,“) which women cannot be expected to pay attention to. Mrs. Niethammer promised me today to send you a letter; in case it does not come, I will finally tell you that she) arrived very well. In) hope of some answer, your devoted friend Hegel.

From the fact that your wife is not currently in Bamberg, it has become clear that you, dearest friend, are there again — what a marital situation! By right, you should be where she is. I have also seen that your journey has achieved its purpose; Julius arrived here quite lively and healthy, and larger than last time; I unexpectedly met him on the street as he was coming out of a lesson from his brother). — I had hoped to receive from you some reports on what you otherwise saw and learned on the journey, but now Miss Niethammer will have the kindness to do this in a more pleasant manner — though your letters are also very dear to me.

Ammon in Erlangen is said to be speaking very badly about the fact that nothing has yet happened regarding the promises he received, and that he has again entered into negotiations concerning Greifswald, or intends to do so. How much my Marie lets herself be recommended to you is already evident from everything that has gone before; she is truly glad to come closer to you and your wife, and you will certainly be glad to extend your friendship for me to her; I also love her for this reason, because in her nature and disposition, in the benevolent cheerfulness and naturalness of her mind and feeling, she bears so much resemblance to the best of women; I kiss her beautiful hand and am your faithful Hgl.

As for why the content of your earlier submission to the Ministry is to remain entirely disregarded, I still do not quite understand. If, in our Gymnasiums, which have no Lyceum alongside them, the two upper classes are to be abolished, then we need a substitute; — a student who recently arrived here from abroad brought the rumor with him that a Lyceum is to be established in Nuremberg. — The Lyceums currently in existence show themselves, through their low attendance, to be superfluous in themselves, and you would have long since abolished them. If one wishes to keep them, then a proper consistency is the abolition of the two upper Gymnasium classes. It then concerns itself with a mere name, whether the final preparatory classes for the university should be called upper Gymnasium classes or Lyceum classes. But how is it with us? What is being done about it? Is there any truth to the aforementioned rumor? Or are the students in our Gymnasiums to go over to the currently existing Lyceums, in order to gain the preparation of the last two years, before they attend the university; or are they to go directly from the lower middle class to the university? — These are the three possible cases, which is one thinking of? Or is one not yet thinking of us at all? All three will arouse the common outcry over the eternal variability of institutions, — a main source of annoyance; the last is of such a nature that it cannot stand; against the second one will become very indignant, and without doubt will oppose it. — The first is still unlikely to me, because no reports on funds, localities, etc. have been requested, or is it to be treated as something general, and to be paid for from the debt fund? — That seems unlikely to me.

The earlier entry into the Progymnasium is also something that cannot stand; age is in any case not a positive measure; it depends on knowledge, and in application such things must of their own accord, in accordance with the nature of the matter, settle into balance and proper proportion. — Only two things come into play here: the first is that vanity is satisfied in having done something different — that it was the makers themselves who did it, whose vanity had hitherto lived in suppression, but the matter makes itself for itself, i.e., it adjusts itself to the old order. The second, however, may be the confusion into which the makers place themselves and the matter; — the greater this confusion is, the better satisfaction and, so to speak, Schadenfreude one can have with it. — What strikes here is what I recently cited regarding reactions; — the Excellent, freed from their captivity, come with terrible outcry and the opinion that everything must become different; as they engage, one thing after another slips from their hands, and apart from the vanity that attaches its etiquette to it, the matter has maintained itself by its own weight. If you have seen my report on the separation of the primary schools, you will have found how I there took the distant occasion to speak of the spirit of our gymnasium constitution; the main charge is always that so much time is spent on Latin. Here lies the difference between the Catholic and the Protestant; we have no laity, the Protestantism is not entrusted to the hierarchical organization of a church, but lies alone in the general insight and education. I would like to add this point of view to that of the need for superior mental formation of the Protestant clergy; it seems to me even the most essential. I will take the opportunity to insert and develop it somewhere; our universities and schools are our church; the pastors and the divine service do not suffice, as in the Catholic church. — But enough and too much.

to be entrusted solely to his service, the fruits of which a better genius will have to enjoy. I had long hoped—indeed, as early as last Easter—to be able to send you something of my work—and that, too, was the cause of the prolongation of my silence—but now I finally look forward to the end of the printing, and I shall be able to send it to you—though it is only the beginning, yet certainly voluminous enough for a beginning—this Easter. It will be of particular interest, provided you do not disapprove of my thoughts and manner.

War Time 1806—1818 p. 55. have been waiting, and at the same time to prove it by deed, but I could not get around to carrying it out, and so that too was omitted, which I at least should have replied to. That I have greatly enjoyed your exposition of Fichte’s renewed syncretism, “the old hardness with this new love,” and his stiff-minded originality with the tacit picking up of new ideas, I need not tell you. Just as much has it pleased me that your manner, so vigorous as it is moderate, has discredited his personal attacks. That he otherwise, when he let himself go, often behaved foolishly, of which we have plenty of examples, but I think this is the first time he has gone so far as to descend to vilenesses, which are at the same time flat and parroted. — The purpose of the writing, which, apart from the necessary explanation regarding the latter aspect, confines itself to the truly philosophical, makes it that you have treated Fichte’s renewed appearance still with some leniency; for at least that one of these popular works, *The Spirit of the Times*, which I alone have seen, contains enough absurdities to allow and almost invite a similarly popular handling. To bring out such stuff with such self-conceit — without which it would be quite impossible — can only be comprehensible through its public, which, as before, consisted of people who were not yet oriented at all, and now of those who are completely disoriented and have lost all substance, as has also recently been sufficiently shown in another field.

What you tell me about the theological-Kantian (if the gods permit) course of philosophy in Tübingen is not to be wondered at. Orthodoxy is not to be shaken, so long as its profession, linked with worldly advantages, is woven into the whole of the state. This interest is too strong to be given up so soon, and works, without one being clearly aware of it in the whole—so long has it had on its side the entire, ever more numerous troop of thoughtless and higher-interest-less repeaters or shouters—when this troop reads something that is contrary to its conviction (if one will do the honor of calling their word-mongering so), and whose truth they perhaps felt, it is said: yes, it is probably true—then they lay their head down, and in the morning one drinks one’s coffee and pours it out for others, as if nothing had happened. Besides, they are content with everything that is offered to them, and what keeps them in the system of idleness. But I believe it would be interesting to disturb the theologians, who fetch critical building materials to fortify their Gothic temple, in their ant-like zeal as much as possible, to make everything [difficult] for them, (them! to whip them out of every angle of retreat, until they found none more and they had to show their nakedness entirely to the daylight. Under the building materials that they carry off from the Kantian pyre, to prevent the fire of dogmatism, they also always carry home burning coals; they bring the terminology better into circulation, and facilitate the general spread of philosophical ideas. To the nonsense, of which you write and whose conclusion I can imagine accordingly, has undoubtedly Fichte opened door and window through his Critique of Revelation; he himself made moderate use of it, but if his principles are once firmly adopted, then there is no limit to theological logic and

I had continued my writing to this point when it was interrupted by the infamous occurrences that have since taken place here. On Monday, the Austrian patrol corps arrived here; the citizen militia did not make a single move, even to maintain order; its commander was infamously mistreated, beaten, and disarmed by the rabble at the gate; this rabble opened the gates and, amid the most dreadful shouts of joy, let the Austrians in; they stormed the police headquarters and destroyed windows, documents, and royal coats of arms, which were torn down everywhere by the people, and everything else; Count von Thürheim, who was being led on foot through the streets from his residence by Uhlans, was grabbed by the chest by the rabble (saying: "you damned dog, you shall not get out of our hands alive, etc."), pelted, and covered with every kind of insult; the night before last, he, Police Director Wurm, and Chief Postmaster von Axthielm were taken away by the Austrians, who themselves marched back early yesterday morning at 2 o'clock and carried off 50,000 florins in contribution, along with bonds for another 50,000 florins, in addition to requisitions for cloth and the like, amounting to some 20,000 florins. Yesterday at 12 o'clock, 600 French dragoons arrived here, who set out again in the evening at half past 5 o'clock to search for the Austrians — a total of 700 men including the Landwehr, of whom 200 were mounted —; another French dragoon regiment is said to have taken a different route at the same time. We are expecting the results today. — The citizens immediately said of this appearance that these were Frenchmen who were in the midst of a retreat. In short, the attitude and behavior of the citizens cannot be conceived of as more contemptible. — The first thing, after the citizen militia had reassembled in the night following the departure of the Austrians and is now proud of its uniform, but not of its deeds, was that they occupied our Sebalder School, so that no school has been held there since yesterday; this school is generally considered the privileged watchroom, and such a violation occurs at every moment, against which Paulus has not yet known how to take strong measures to maintain order.

The latest item I have received is the vacation rescript; from it I see that our District School Councilor here, too, intended to skim something off the top, as he applied for five weeks, although he had allowed six weeks here with us; but that you parried that and have thwarted his intention for the Gymnasium; however, you have let another so-called trick of his pass, namely, to load two more hours onto the Gymnasium class teachers. On the one hand, I find it unfair that the teachers here should have this distinction over all others in the Kingdom, that a Gymnasium Professor should be expected to teach three hours in a row in the morning; on the other hand, our students are bombarded with hours; besides, I do not know what norm we have, if it is departed from on every occasion. Private study cannot be spoken of with our students; our District School Councilor considers it, when this consideration is touched upon with him, to be entirely superfluous, and has no other concept of youth education than that it consists in the misery of eternal instilling, haranguing, memorizing (but not by rote learning, but purely by eternal miserable repetition), driving, stupefying—in the eternal pre-chewing and pouring in, to which it is incomprehensible that a youthful mind must and does behave actively in learning.

Fate seems to have it as its method at present to keep us in suspense with our expectations until, whether they are fulfilled or not, they have become indifferent. With so many other things it achieves its purpose; only the desire for your presence it has not been able to blunt, and I hope—though I will not count on it—that you will leave it at the beginning of September. If it remains at that, you will still partly make it in time for the examination of the Real Institute; ours begins on August 13. I associate your arrival here primarily with the examination, because that is the objective subject which has the greatest interest for us here at present, not knowing how you stand with it. Other subjective interests are cast so much into the shadow by this and other objectivities, or by the aforementioned method of fate into the past, that I leave it to your arrival to awaken them again, and regarding the rest, to the quality in which you come here, whether only as a friend, or also in a commissarial capacity—that I value only in every case higher than this more—not as a mere passing shot, who sees our city for nothing but a mere post station. I also sense your commissarial quality from the circumstance that of so many determinations to be made concerning our institutions, not a single one has yet been decided; I suppose that everything has been left to your personal view; but as said, these determinations also belong to the subjects about which expectation has blunted itself. So it was also with Erlangen and Bayreuth—generally, whose surrender at the end only made a pleasant sensation because the news of the effected surrender ceased to arrive. Regarding Erlangen, it was assured here that the King had promised the Bayreuth deputies the maintenance of the university;—but will they maintain it only insofar as they do not overthrow it; do they concern themselves with that? or do you have to do with it?

As for the matter itself, I find this development very pleasing, as I may regard it as the consideration presented to the public for your plan, which I hope will appear and be implemented in the Lyceums and Gymnasiums; and, independent of this hope of immediate effectiveness, we shall receive something instructive and stimulating; the latter we certainly stand in great need of. My newspaper life proceeds in its merely usual course without further disturbance, quite calmly; what a rescript—or general order—insinuated yesterday from Munich might have stirred up as difficulties, Mr. v. Bsayard has again calmed, whose kindness generally makes the otherwise often difficult relationship of a newspaper with higher authorities quite easy and smooth. If only it were in equally good standing with scholarly pursuits, but against that I find it rather intolerant.

I have, moreover, as I am proud to claim, foretold the entire upheaval; in my work (completed on the night before the Battle of Jena) I say on p. 5475, “Absolute Freedom (it has been previously described, it is the purely abstract, formal freedom of the French Republic, which, as I showed, emerged from the Enlightenment) passes out of its self-destroying reality into another country (I had a certain country in mind) of self-conscious spirit, where it, in this unreality, is taken for the True, in whose thoughts he delights, insofar as he is and remains thought, and knows this being enclosed in self-consciousness as the perfect and complete essence. The new form of the moral spirit is present.” Of the sea-currents that must follow those great events like rain showers follow lightning, the brown little stream of coffee nevertheless already flows for us more pleasantly and wittily from the pot, since we are relieved of the surrogates tax, and from the report allowance we can now procure a proper Java, which God and good friends may wish to preserve for us for a longer time.... .... May relief from all this catnip perhaps be obtainable for me from all that great and small of the time! Yours

Since I was so deeply immersed in realities and temporal matters, my imagination could not come to dream; on the other hand, it was all the more lively in my wife; she dreamed that she found herself in a great camp full of wild soldiers, Cossacks, Prussians, all mixed together near Paris; she was full of terror, but you rode through the tumult, making your way everywhere; my wife walked on foot beside you; if she was to be crowded, you kindly reached down from your horse to give her your hand and showed that she was under your protection; thus she came through safely and full of joyful thanks, and then found herself with you in a temple where joy and contentment reigned. — I was not indifferent in this account to the circumstance that I had not appeared at all in the whole story; my wife wanted to excuse this by saying that I was included in her; and I am well willing to accept it, that under her vehicle I was protected by you against all Bashkirs and Tschuwasches and brought to the harbor of peace.

Dear Friend! I was greatly pleased to see your friendly disposition toward me in your kind letter, and thereby received the immediate occasion to tell you how much I value it and how grateful I am for the earlier proofs of it. You have been so kind as to occupy yourself so thoroughly with my literary work and to give the public such an extensive account of it, as is contained in the Jena Literary Gazette. With philosophical writings, one knows—or rather, in our times least of all, or does not get to see—whether they, I will not say, find an audience, but only a few individuals who take an interest in them and pay them attention; all the more valuable it has been to me that my work was not indifferent to you. Schubert had already conveyed to me what you had been kind enough to have said to me regarding the non-publication of your remarks on the preface; but he has, as it now appears, neglected to convey what I had asked him to write to you on the subject. Given the arbitrariness and intentionality that so frequently shows through in the direction of that newspaper, both toward the writers and in its conduct toward the contributors themselves, I was more surprised that so much and so many things from the review were taken up. — I am returning herewith the communicated part of the review of the preface, and thank you for this communication, which has been valuable to me and contains so much that would be right good if it were often said before the public.

I am very eager to see your work on magic, which you are currently engaged in. I confess that I would not dare to approach this gloomy aspect and manner of the spiritual nature or of the natural spirit, and I am all the more pleased that you will partly illuminate it for us and partly take up again and restore to its honor so many things that have been neglected and despised. — But no work requires health and a cheerful, and indeed a firm, cheerful mood more than this one. Be assured that your state of mind, which you have described to me, is partly due to that work. This descent into dark regions, where nothing appears firm, definite, and secure, where everywhere flashes of light sparkle, but next to abysses their brightness rather clouds and deceives, misled by the surroundings, casting false reflections rather than illuminating, where every beginning of a path again breaks off and runs out into the indeterminate, gets lost, and carries us away from our own purpose and direction. — I know from my own experience this mood of the mind or rather of reason, when it has once involved itself with interest and its intuitions into a chaos of appearances, and when, though inwardly certain of the goal, it has not yet passed through, not yet arrived at the clarity and detailing of the whole. I suffered from this hypochondria for a few years until I was exhausted. Every person probably has such a turning point in life, the nocturnal point of the contraction of their being, through whose narrowness they are squeezed through and secured and assured of themselves, of the security of ordinary everyday life, and, when they have already made themselves incapable of being filled by it, of the security of an inner, nobler existence. — Proceed with confidence; the science that has led you into this labyrinth of the mind is alone capable of leading you out and healing you. — If it is possible for you, cast off all this brooding for a while; if you keep your distance from it, you will return to it with renewed strength and greater power over it.

A creation of Stephani’s, a local higher girls’ school, has collapsed these past days, and the money spent on it—however unjustly and improperly, God knows—has been thrown out the window, so to speak; our Chief had taken an interest in it, and in that respect I would have liked to help. — You know the relations with the Chief best yourself: he sometimes does something for himself, as with the girls’ school—(since my time, in fact, only its abandonment)—in administrative terms; since such things happen without connection, one has to make up for contradictions and obstacles afterwards. But in truth these are trifles, and my small tasks have hitherto met with approval, and I have not had the slightest annoyance, and what more can one ask to be content?

I am enclosing herewith the substantial letter you shared with me); I have already thanked you for it and expressed my complete agreement. — The final major decision has still not been made; yesterday another victory from the 25th arrived, which is supposed to be the decision; but we have been promised this so often, and always in ever more brilliant terms the worse things stood, that one does not yet know whether this victory does not signify that the Allies have merely pulled themselves out of their downfall to some extent. — Our government has now exercised possession of its acquired freedom, and shown the world and its subjects the sovereignty that had been offended by the French yoke. The French Emperor had not tolerated that smaller powers (even his King of Holland had to withdraw it) have a Field Marshal; but now, after such a complete overturn of things, after such brilliant victories, such heavy burdens and abundant blood, we have one). Whether we shall receive any other consequences of the liberation and fruits of the burdens besides this, we shall calmly await. In the meantime, I only wish for this consequence, that the beautiful hope of seeing you passing by us in the autumn, even if it is to remain only a passing by, be fulfilled to us. Live well with all my heart. Your most faithful Hgl.

For the time being, some examples have come into your hands showing that I had to justify, excuse, or correct previous deficiencies and disorders;—you have perhaps seen with what injustice and sloppiness the presentations have been handled—(for the Castellers, Schwabachers, and the like, provision could indeed have been made)—and perhaps you have also seen that I seek, if the matter cannot otherwise be changed, to proceed objectively in the matter. I will further mention the discovery that, among other things, the means for studies and school purposes are always insufficient, and that whenever something is requested for them, a cry is raised about their inadequacy, because advances have been made from the education fund for the maintenance of the clergy; provision was made from available means for the immediate need; it seems to have been remedied; no one complains; the law is an abstract and silent person, the end that uncovers the treasury is then precisely the end, and those who truly suffered need and injustice have become accustomed to the view that everything is to the devil anyway.

to see Hölderlin still, so I ask that this be communicated to him). Fernow will arrive here soon). Now I would also like to write to you about scholarly matters, or about myself; but there is not much to say about either; it would please me to receive something from you about Jacobi; Frommann expects other news from you. Schad) is having a physical apparatus made, and will read experimental physics in the winter; others think he is on the way to going mad. — One more thing — Oberthür wrote from Würzburg to Böttger") that, despite the note in the Merkur, you will still get there; these Würzburgers, Loder or Böttcher Schütz, seem to be all connected in the most exact way.")

Here one has hardly been able to keep up for some time with all the new things that are happening. The latest is that the Literary Gazette, after having been in Würzburg for a few days, and upon its return having categorically assured that it would move there under certain conditions, is now certainly moving with all its belongings, Ersch and others, to Halle; Loder brought the definite arrangement regarding this a few days ago from Potsdam, where he traveled to see the King — though he probably did not see him. — Thibaut had four calls, but remains here with an allowance of 300 thalers. Hufeland received very advantageous offers in Würzburg; 200 thalers in allowance have been sent after him from Weimar; however, it seems that he, just as Paulus if an official call is sent to him, will accept the call in Würzburg. — Finally, Mereau is to become Senior District Commissioner in Coburg, and Martens from Göttingen has been called to his place. Sömmering did not accept; his first condition was that no students were to come to him; he proposed Ebel, who has written about the mountain peoples of Switzerland and is currently staying in Frankfurt, as his replacement. (Should you have gone ahead, which at the Prussian government secured compensation of 10,000 thalers for the relocation of the Gazette and its editorial staff. Cf. the letter from Paulus, Jena, January 9, 1803 (printed in v. Reichlin-Meldegg, G. Paulus und seine Zeit 1, 35, which touches on Hegel’s letter in many ways and partly supplements it, as well as Goethe in Tages- und Jahresheften 1803 (Works, 1st ed., vol. 31, 15.

To His Excellency, Professor Schelling in Murrhard, to be delivered via Stuttgart at the Red House. First of all, let me congratulate you on your marriage; I ought to send you at least a sonnet on the subject, but you are accustomed to making do with my prose in general, and this does not allow one to be more prolix in such matters than a handshake and an embrace. The accompanying package was sent to me by Dr. Assal, and the letter by the post; I hope that both will still find you in Swabia; had your positive assurance to me, as well as to Schelver, not preceded this, we would, based on everything one hears from Franconia, have believed you to be in Würzburg rather than in Italy by autumn.

After the most exalted authority has taken the praiseworthy and grateful step of ordering that the budgets be prepared through the joint action of the District School Council and the Foundation Administration, the Royal General Commissariat, in place of that, issues decrees for the drafting of budgets on the one hand to us, whose unilateral drafting will be neither right nor proper; and on the other hand to the Foundation Administration, which is already full of work and is not informed of the data regarding the needs, and therefore, although threatened with a fine of .. thalers, can do nothing about it either, because it is instructed to submit a budget jointly with the relevant Council, which does not deign to do so, to the General Commissariat; so that, as the matter stands now, the Administration, which is otherwise very willing and would be, has partly already complained here and will have to complain in Munich, — and the old delaying ship’s course will set in, with the General Commissariat sending its unright and improper budgets to Munich, which will then have to be sent back from there to the Foundation Administration here for review. So one holds the matter and the other does not let it go. But we are the Achivi, qui plectuntur.

But now I must definitely close this letter, which, as I see, contains complaints or vexations with which I should least burden you, since you have enough of them anyway; as for me, however, do not consider them as something that strongly affected me. By no means! At most for a moment; I then do not let myself be further troubled by it and can calmly watch everything of that kind that goes awry around or with me; I am interested in it only to the extent that I believe I can achieve something thereby; the rest is none of my concern, and so I am actually content overall. — Live very well once more. Your Majesty.

Among the legends here it is said that the three local foundation administrators intend to resign their offices, alongside rumors that thirty others in this region are minded to do the same. It appears as if, at last, matters are about to grow beyond all formalities. One of those administrators states that he is currently tasked, among other things, with producing 9,000 tables; however, he does not know how he will manage to accomplish this, etc. D. 4 Sept. Yesterday I made a detour to Altorf with Mr. Market Mayor Merkel and Mr. Finance Councillor Roth, who will marry the former’s daughter in 8 days, and saw this university for the first time; I found that the professors there wear a hairstyle of powdered pigeon wings and a Kattogan, have a botanical garden which cannot be compared to the vegetable gardens between Kamsdorf and Wenigen-Jena, for it is not so large, and I saw no horseradish in it; the houses, on the other hand, are quite similar to the houses of Kamsdorf and Wen. Jena (with the exception of one of the latter). The surrounding fields are otherwise quite pleasant, and especially the promenade spot Grünsperg is enviable. Roth will hardly be able to resolve himself to university life any longer; each of us looks forward to your distant determination regarding me with confidence as well as patience. Your greeting: Vale interim, I extend to all our interim status....

One can undoubtedly still expect fine clarifications from Kilian and Markus; the former does not seem to be lying quite so flat against the latter as it appeared, and is at least still able to bring the latter down. But a good story is the origin of Weiler’s philosophical work, which has been introduced as a textbook in the gymnasiums, which you will have found in the Leipzig newspaper; the vehemence with which the school plan is defended in the Munich newspaper proves that these gentlemen did not expect such a reception of it, and the clarification regarding Weiler’s book cannot fail to increase their annoyance.

In these parts, there are no such brilliant, enviable movements. Akermann is going to Heidelberg, and Weimar seemed very surprised about it; upon a private notice from a friend of Akermann’s, Voigt himself immediately came over here. It is said that offers have also been made to another great man here from the same place and were not unfavourably received; if this is finally brought about, if this stroke is carried out, the surprise will be like that of butter in the sun. Finally, all four decrees regarding my professorship here, which is jointly conferred upon Fries and me, have arrived. Krause, as I hear, has already declined last autumn. That Goethe was very dangerously ill and Schiller also very sick, you have probably heard; behind such great examples I could not remain behind, and I too have had a fourteen-day setback. You will also know that Mrs. Seebeck has safely given birth to a son.

Finally, most dear friend, I am paying off a debt of so many kinds that I owe you, which I must remind you in advance is only a small return for your kindnesses. My main thanks is for your invitation to the sermon at the beginning of the church year, for which I am very grateful to you. I have already written to Mde Niethammer about how much I was edified by it; the boldness of choosing this subject pleased me just as much as the execution. But one thing: please do not let Nitribitt print it any more; his name begs for salt, as it lacks the proper way of printing.

I must ask your very sincere forgiveness for not having answered earlier the letter you kindly addressed to me on the 5th of last month; what I could offer regarding this delay, namely that it is my usual habit to be equally neglectful of correspondence in general, would serve more as an expansion of my fault than as an excuse. It could not but be very pleasing to me to see from your letter that what I have attempted in philosophy has found your approval; however much one who has long been occupied in solitary thought might find satisfaction in his own course, it is all the more a pleasing confirmation and strengthening to see approval coming from the minds of others. Such participation, as you attest, must be all the more valuable to me, as a deeper interest in the great subjects of our mind and the seriousness of the thoughtful study of them are usually limited to few. It is also a rich compensation for the disparagements you mention; against these nothing else helps but to be hardened against them, and one does this all the more easily, as it soon shows that those who allow themselves such things do not even fulfill the reasonable requirement of having knowledge of what they disparage.

The content of your letter, highly esteemed friend, has stirred up such extensive feelings and thoughts in me that I would not know where to begin or where to end, were it not for the fortunate circumstance that I may assume these are already known to you, and were it not that the result is so very simple, namely my intimate, continuing, and ever-renewing thanks for the much good that you always do for me. The prospect of the function salary has so struck my wife’s eye that, before its radiance like that of a star, everything else that might make me pale has faded; and I intend to attach myself to her as much as possible, and to take the rest, with the exception of the new duties, on the lighter shoulder. For that prospect is approximately what, according to the experience of a year, would make up a supplement to household needs that would be difficult to miss for long.

We have, as is proper, begun with the beginning, and conducted ourselves methodically enough in doing so. — But I hold in general that, however much difficulty there is usually in making a beginning in philosophy, and rightly so, one should not make too much of it on the other hand. Foolishly, especially the non-philosophers demand a beginning that is an Absolute, against which they cannot immediately chatter, an unassailable First Principle; — foolishly, or rather cunningly — for they would have to be very far gone if they did not know beforehand with absolute certainty that one cannot bring them anything against which they cannot object and bring to bear the wisdom of their soundly reasoning common sense, and it would show little wisdom on the part of a philosopher if he allowed himself to be deceived or led astray by honestly attempting to make such a beginning. For the beginning, precisely because it is a beginning, is imperfect. Pythagoras demanded four years of silence from his students. At least the philosopher has the right to demand such prolonged silence of the reader’s own thoughts until he has gone through the whole; he can assure the reader in advance that he himself has long known and better everything that the reader will find to object to; he will let it arise for him in due course and appear at its necessary place; his entire philosophy itself is nothing else than a refutation, rebuttal, and destruction of his beginning. — I certainly agree with you entirely that one must not begin out of the blue, but that the beginning must essentially be the beginning of philosophy, and one may and should not hide the fact that what one does is philosophizing; I therefore demand for the beginning even more than you, namely, that it itself be philosophy in deed and in substance and acknowledge itself as such, thus more than just the need for philosophy, but also not more than what it can be as the beginning of philosophy. Those who have at the very outset the idea of philosophy itself, the Absolute, and our Lord God with all his glory, certainly know little of the matter. Doubt, I concede to you, is a great and worthy beginning.

Your Excellency, I have reserved for the free holiday days the task of thoroughly enjoying the pleasing gift you have given to the public with a new scientific journal and to me, in addition, with a copy of it and such a kind letter, and of returning that gift with some of my incidental thoughts—thereby at least testifying to the interest I have taken in it. At the time, I believed I could well defer the expression of my thanks to Your Excellency until then, as I could assume you were convinced of how valuable your kind remembrance, this new enrichment of my insights, and how refreshing the other more serious expressions of your genius would be to me. However, I have not been well during those holidays, and I can no longer delay giving a sign of my gratitude.

Regarding the primal phenomena, I am reminded of the story that E. E. added to the Theory of Colors—namely, the account of how, when you and Büttner were already hurrying down the stairs, you still looked at the white wall and saw nothing but the white wall; this story greatly facilitated my entry into the Theory of Colors, and whenever I have to deal with the whole matter, I can hardly know what to be grateful for, yes, your own views might even get the catchword: Naturphilosophisch, thereby, and yet allow us to behave tolerantly with your stuff in our innocent manner—it is still not the worst that has befallen you, and I can rely on the fact that E. E. recognizes the nature of human nature, that where one has done something substantial, the others rush in and in doing so also want to have done something of their own. — But in any case, we philosophers already have a common enemy with E. E.—namely, in Metaphysics. — Newton has already put up the great warning sign: Physics! Beware of Metaphysics! The misfortune, however, is that, while he bequeathed this Gospel to his friends and they faithfully proclaim it, he and they have thereby accomplished nothing else than to give the countless repetitions of the state of that Englishman who did not know that he had spoken prose his whole life long. This man eventually came to insight, but the others are not yet so far as to know that they speak abominably bad Metaphysics. I leave it, however, to say something more about the necessity of ruining this their Metaphysics for the physicists. I must return to one of E. E.'s teachings, as I cannot refrain from expressing to you my heartfelt joy and appreciation for the view you have given of the nature of doubly refracting bodies; this counterpart of the same thing, once represented by external mechanical means—another time an inner damask weaving of nature—is, in my opinion, certainly one of the finest strokes that could be made.

This damask weaving, by hand of light and dark, must lead further; the living in the beautiful is at the same time the fertility it possesses. But since there is something to lament in all things, I would indeed have to lament that I have not been able to go through the instructive series of phenomena with physical eyes, preferably, of course, under the guidance of Your Excellency. Yet perhaps I may still promise myself this favor in a year or two, and this hope itself dispels that lament, and in order not to claim Your Excellency’s patience any longer through further chattering, I allow myself only to repeat my pleasant thanks for Your Excellency’s kind remembrance and for the rich instruction obtained. Hegel.

Honourable Vice-Chancellor! Your valued letter of the 20th informs me of the Grand Duke’s approval of my appointment. Now, then, this last matter is also in order, and I am truly delighted that this too has been added so quickly and happily; I also gratefully acknowledge the kind and lively interest that Councilor Eichrodt has taken in the matter. Following your hint, I have already enclosed a letter to him, in which I express my grateful respect, as well as my willingness to accept the position. But how can I express to you the joyful longing with which I look forward to my journey to you....

Agamemnon, German science is called. This small expression, which vibrates almost as an afterthought to those preceding letters, you will surely not merely forgive me in your truth, but for this time—allow it to the sick one. I know this, because I know that your goodness is equal to your justice. And who could also exercise greater forbearance over that German writing! I well knew, when I handed it over to the press, that I released it from the workshop or furnace of my life at that time in Berlin only as a slag, but I also knew that that furnace was something different than a Faustian witch's kitchen, for which many among us might hold it, unable even to guess at that irony in which I was convinced that a certain public indeed requires such slag castles, as one is being built here in the country by a half-mad master mason, in order to have bad wine set before it within them, when it, having grown weak as it is, has first laboriously climbed the small height. This here only insofar as, insofar as perhaps later a likewise long since finished, detailed part of this partly intentionally chaotic writing, determined by documentary historical facts, might occasionally appear. Only in the system itself is there healing. Only in truly scientific thorough working-out do I find my satisfaction, and yet it is precisely only this that is the root of those vibrating expressions of reverence, as the beginning of wisdom. Yet I would not gladly let anything of such attempts at definitely scientific work appear publicly in written form except in very late years. Although my body is older than my years, although I am far from that vain modesty that would out of self-love be ashamed, but I also know what that means, after your works are partially already present. But precisely these do not give the impotence of mere imitation, but the holy spirit of self-creating knowledge. In this self-consciousness alone could I take upon myself to step onto the lectern. Therefore that rather orally, yet, if it must or may, with time partially also in writing!

Most Honored Professor! At this very moment, I am receiving here, at these unhippocrene springs, your letter, which is beneficial to me in every respect. I remain silent regarding my thanks for this as well. You alone understand this exactly as it is, even as it remains unspoken here, in every respect. — My health is currently fluctuating anew. You will also see this fluctuation in the letter. However, I know this fluctuation to be essentially temporary and mention it here on the one hand as an excuse, and on the other in the sense that I consider it permissible to tell you that I therefore do not yet know with complete certainty whether I will be able to spend this entire winter in Erlangen. For there I lack (for financial reasons) all the care that I have in Bayreuth, and which, given my constitution, will probably be necessary this winter as well. Nevertheless, I will, even if this relative separation becomes necessary for me, know how to maintain my position in Erlangen, at least being invulnerable in science against all wasp stings of non-Aristophanic vulgarity. This is all too certainly omnipresent in a very particular way. However, with perhaps the exception of Greifswald in a certain sense, so far as I may presume, no Prussian university has a Senate with such power as in Erlangen currently does. Yet I know very well that this position cannot be of lasting duration. In science I have learned to embrace and comprehend every real relationship as one that is welcome in itself, but in it I have also experienced what kind of state that is which gave birth to Kant, which thereby gave Schelling spiritual nourishment, which summoned Fichte to itself, and which, after longer hesitation, finally also recognized, if not identified, yet honored, whose name and spirit alone call themselves to us, and whom I only in relation to the significance that Greece had in world history compared to the dizziness of the East, with a certainly not exaggerated, rather only very weak little image, in a letter to my Rabenau the

Shall I now say a few words of paternal joy in confidence, yet without foolish reserve? I believe I have grounded the knowledge more deeply than has been done before and deduced it from life itself. I believe I have derived the method from the subject itself and followed it consistently. Up to now, however, it seems to me that the method has been chosen arbitrarily, and followed even more arbitrarily: for example, Spinoza’s geometric method. One also made gratuitous premises everywhere and omitted the most essential distinctions, for example, between expression and the expressed, and hurried only to the results.
