In contrast, I believe I have presented a system from beginning to end, and had my premises been false, they would not have been able to lead me back to life, and my results did not agree with the most common truths, for example, as will not escape you, that this is the case in my presentation of the applied sciences. Therefore, I also do not believe that anyone will be offended by the apparent formality, for this seems only so because the strictness of my course did not allow me to think about my ideas as if from outside my ideas, and thus to fill the gap of the first with the second. Every freedom in the detail fell away and exists only with regard to the whole. Although there is no trace of polemic in my work, and I have not donned armor for battle, I am nevertheless aware that I have not been daubed over with oil, but have exposed myself to every attack as an honest fighter for honor and not for reward. Therefore, I have also appended a table of contents and even an index, and divided the whole into paragraphs. But I notice that my statements go too far; do not view them as if I wished to preempt your judgment, but only as an invitation to go into the details: just as I am very willing to go through yours in detail and share my opinion with you, as soon as you wish, so that we, who touch on so many things, may also make communications to each other that could not be replaced by any others.

What Schelling wrote to you about the wonders of the dowsing rod and the effects of the will on it, etc., is approximately the same as what Ritter also revealed to me—after he had not concealed from me that he knew me well enough to know how much secret mistrust had taken hold of me regarding the whole matter—namely, “that the stimulus of the will has the same dignity as the ordinary physical stimulus.” “Already,” he says, “I am able to place my fingers different, indifferent, or conversely different for frog preparations of a specific level of excitability, by the mere will.” Can one demand more? He has also communicated to me some main and fundamental experiments, which would be somewhat lengthy to describe; therefore, I would rather speak of them orally. You will surely have already received the first fascicle of the Siderismus. The plan he submitted to the Academy’s Commission for the examination of Campetti is probably good and could have already led to results, had the members of that Commission been at all equal to the investigation. But the gentlemen seem to have lost the courage to clarify such a troublesome matter. The Commission has been dissolved, and Ritter now has to deal with this matter solely with the Presidency of the Academy and, through it, with the government. It went no better with the Parisian Commission during the investigation of Bleton (in Lavoisier’s time). A member elected to this Commission even answered: “I have written against Parangue (a predecessor of Bleton), I belong to three Academies, and you want me to believe in these nonsense things!”

As I learned from you, my dear friend, that the local literary journal is not known or read among the barbarians, and that you must therefore unfortunately do without it, you will probably not yet know what has been announced in it, namely, “that I have succeeded in obtaining 48 layers of 36-inch plates of Davy’s metal, and that these combine with ½) to form a fairly firm, silvery-white amalgam.” Furthermore, that I, as you have already expected from us, immediately set about the earths, and have indeed found them just as combustible as the alkalis are, namely talc, clay, lime, silica, and baryta. All the aforementioned substances emit specific, distinguishable, particular pungent odors when burning. The odor of baryta comes closest to that of caustic potash, and, which will be of particular interest to you — because of the natural-philosophical paragraph — the somewhat less easily burning silica really has some similarity in odor to gold leaf burned by means of the column through a drop of water (otherwise in the usual way). This was observed on the 19th of February, at 4 o’clock and 25 minutes in the afternoon, by our city clock, which unfortunately never keeps quite correct time. You will not fail to notice that this was one of the periodic hours (9, 4, 11,), and also that the moon had entered its last quarter the previous evening.

Niethammer has traveled to Augsburg and Ulm himself to mobilize the organization. It seems that here everything is to transform itself into a perpetual motion machine. God only grant first the guiding spirit of the coins or "of the money." It also occurs to me that my order for relocation funds from the Court has probably now arrived at Mr. Financial Director von Grau. Would you not ask him about it, and if it sounds as desired, collect the 300 florins in my name, so that as a good Nuremberg housekeeper, you can bring them here to me free of postage. I ask my friend Graser to send me the school status tables of the district courts of Neunkirchen, Pottenstein, and Vorchheim as soon as possible, or to give them to you. Many greetings to Mrs. Fuchs and other friends who are in your house. Everyone greets you, and wishes wings to the time that brings you. Your P.

After the kitchen gift that was sent to you a few days ago, I find, in sorting through the wealth that has accumulated around me, an opportunity to serve you up a few more solid dishes. I am sending them to you as proof of our tireless literary activity in Bavaria, which you once took a liking to or, as one would aptly put it if it were serious, have swallowed a fool! You will surely take the best care yourself not to spoil your stomach with the solid fare.

In my widowhood, things are going rather poorly with me at the moment, because I am giving myself some holidays from the pleasant activity of work, which I spend fiddling around in my study and bedroom. But these holidays end today, for I must now seriously get to work to bring the new curriculum to a conclusion during the course of this month of May. For this reason, I also have two things to ask you: How is the logic going? Can I count on you when it gets serious? I at least intend to apply for you to be given a commission for it. I do not know if my application will succeed, but I would not make it in any case without being certain that I am doing you a service by it. 2. How would you feel if you were proposed as a Rector of a Gymnasium? The idea is still so foreign to me at the moment that I cannot come to terms with it myself. It only flashed through my head that we could get you here in this way. However, this plan is still subject to so many difficulties that I am for now holding only to the general idea of employing you in one of our main provincial cities, as they say in this country!

What you will write to me as your opinion on the matter will itself give me some light on the subject. I still do not lose Erlangen from sight. — The inquiry itself is, as can be understood, absolutely not to be communicated further. Farewell. P.S. I may not let a joke pass you by. Please read Reg. Bl. St. XIX p. 916 a rescript "concerning the Lyceists Kopp, Mittermayer and Meinel" which I drafted, that came into the Reg. Bl. through a chancery error.

It is said that the King of Saxony is already there; also, the Crown Prince of Bavaria, the Archduke of Würzburg, and Archduke Karl are expected to be there, or they are already there. Our princes are likewise present. However, the Prince-Primate is not expected. Three different residences have been prepared in Erfurt for Emperor Napoleon, among them the Government House, in which the Russian Emperor will probably reside. The Duke of Weimar is arranging a large hunt on the Ettersberg in honor of the Emperor.

Honored Friend! I have calmly continued and finished the first reading of your Logic and Encyclopedia; I have thereby become convinced that a love of truth and good will are not sufficient to understand such works as they ought to be understood in order to arrive at one’s own conviction. These works, written with strict scientific rigor for the school, are beyond the powers of a lover of truth educated outside the school, and I have had to contend not only with the difficulty inherent in the nature of the subject itself, but also with that arising from the uncorrected printing errors. Given the insurmountable difficulty for me of following your view in its full development, of fully comprehending your reasons, and therefore of testing them with my own powers, I would at least like to learn from you, Honored Friend! whether I understand you correctly or incorrectly in the main point.

I believe I grasp his standpoint most correctly if I consider it distinguished by its decisive difference from the Reinholdian one, namely as absolute rationalism (the science of reason, which becomes conscious of itself as all being) distinguished from relative rationalism. Reinhold, along with Dugald Stewart and other thinkers, conceives that: 'Knowledge in no way constitutes these truths, which are its objects,' and this thought seems at first glance satisfying to reason. According to this first friend, true being and the truth of being are independent of human representation; being is—in itself true—whether represented or not; it does not presuppose representation at all in order to be what it is. On the other hand, human representation is true only insofar as it is the pure representation of true being; representation presupposes its object, which is independent of it, and so on. In this way, for Reinhold, truth, as the absolute: the—distinguished from the relative truth of knowledge—agreement of being in itself, which agreement man can know only relatively, namely in its generality purely.

Thus I still find no less conflict and strife in the church than in the school; and you see from this that although I have indeed grown old with philosophy, I have nevertheless not yet reached that happy apatheia. It was suddenly destroyed — everything has risen en masse against the new hierarchy, and the Consistory, which hatched the neat plan on the proposal of a Calvinist member, Consistory Councillor Heinz, now stands as it were abandoned by its own church, ashamed and powerless there — How strange do these passionate outbursts sound in contrast to such excellent men and best-intentioned Protestants as Niethammer and Heintz, who, as Consistory Councillor in Zweibrücken, had materially contributed to the adoption of the church union in the Palatinate!

I have nothing new to write, as far as I know. We are now all settled, those of us who have had the good fortune to belong more closely to the Jacobian circle: Roth, Thiersch, and I. I have bought the house in which you visited us; Roth has built himself a new house in the same row, three houses from ours, which he has been living in since May of this year; and Thiersch bought a house and garden behind us, in the street of Minister von Zentner, already in the autumn of last year, and moved in immediately. We are therefore not only property owners in Munich, but also, by virtue of this, close neighbors. .... I also greet my dear godfather, of whom I hear much good, but ask you to let me know about him at the next opportunity.... In old, faithful friendship, Yours, Nh.

I have to answer a letter of yours, dear friend and godfather, which was doubly pleasant to us through its bearer.... Better that the return of your friendly visit of 1815 remains postponed until it can be done properly and completely; what is currently quite impossible on my side, since the unfortunate Presbyterial war is to be fought, and moreover, in the midst of this war, a General Synod is being prepared, which is to be held this year, so that the word of the Constitution, whereby 4 years are set for the assembly of the Synods, is fulfilled according to the letter, on which we insist.

For the gift of the preface, as for the preface itself, my sincere and warm thanks. Before it came into my hands as your gift, I had already read it and taken pleasure in it. One needs healthy, solid food, but disguised stomachs cannot tolerate it. The book itself, apart from the author, is hardly read through by anyone. I at least, who took it up with good will on the good credit of the preface, and who am accustomed to demand something of myself, could not endure it. I seize the occasion of your preface to remind you of the book you had in mind to write for me and my schoolmastering. It is very close to my heart that you may find time for it and retain the pleasure in doing so. Do let me know how things stand with it.

I have come to the view that war and peace are equally valid, and that war is in fact preferred to peace, as war is the animating force, even if not the bliss-giving one, and one neither hopes for nor fears a victory of the warring powers. What your letter says about me from former times still holds true, notwithstanding the years I have reached: that I am indeed "occasionally irritable"! I only think that this "occasionally" is decreasing. I could well return your mockery of our opposition men, "the good ones." If yours are devils, they at least seem to be very stupid devils. Others than such would hardly have placed themselves in the stupid alternative of April 12th, either to drive their best teachers away, or to stand there themselves as absurd or malicious snoopers; the latter, after a long-elapsed peremptory quarter, seems in fact to have occurred. But it seems to me perhaps harsh to have to submit to such a judgment. — A rumor that has spread here these days says: Schleiermacher had come to Regensburg during these holidays to visit his sister, and perhaps also wanted to visit us here again, and had already made all arrangements for the journey, but his leave had been refused "for compelling reasons." Such a thing is hard to believe, and even harder, if it were true, that such men would not be entirely granted leave! —

Help me, my dear friend, by immediately sending me your two notebooks on the philosophy of history and the history of philosophy, without having them copied. Mr. Hotho possesses them perfectly written. He had them with him in Paris, and one of my friends who knows German perfectly well had begun to copy something. But Mr. Hotho having assured me that one would easily find a copyist in Berlin, my friend interrupted his work. He is ready to resume it. Therefore, obtain from Hotho that he send the two notebooks to his uncle; I will have them copied exactly, and return them to him two months later. To refuse would be a proof of distrust that I do not deserve, and he cannot need his notebooks when their author is here. See to it, my dear friend, that this shipment suffers no delay; I will measure your friendship by your activity in this circumstance. Day by day, I take more pleasure in the history of philosophy, and I see in it the comforting confirmation of the ideas that are dearest to me.

By the way, Gans and Hotho had told me that you were planning to write something about my fragments in the New Berlin Journal? What happened? Has your much-feared and much-desired article, like the judgment of the master, appeared? And could you not send me the issue in which it is found? Alas! I want to educate myself; no one here is in a position to be of use to me, and my friends in Germany are abandoning me. Do not forget me with Mrs. Bloch and Mrs. Milder. I remain very attached to them, although they give me no sign of life. I am inclined this summer to take a trip along the banks of the Rhine. Could Berlin and Paris meet there? Farewell, my dear friend, remember that I will be angry with you as long as I have not received the two issues of Hotho. I embrace you with all my heart, Vict. Cousin. P.S. Mr. Grouchy, of the French legation, could take charge of your errands.

The little book of the Heol. [Hebrews] has indeed been delivered by me; but now I must, because the typesetters will not wait, still produce an Epiméetrum [supplement] during this first week of the holidays, because I only recently received some Specimina varr. lectt. [specimens of various readings] from 3 other mss. [manuscripts] and Taylor's English translation of that book. Now, those [manuscripts] indeed yield little or no harvest — but you know the German public, which likes to count the codices. Taylor, however, in himself insignificant, did use the old Latin version of Fr. Patricius; and the latter I, despite all the effort applied, have not been able to track down. — In this Epimetro, then, your remarks will also find their place; for which I am most gratefully indebted to you. You show me how much better my edition would have become, had I been able to make it in your vicinity; and I still regret that I did not take up that little book while you were here. But that can no longer be changed; and I must now count on your friendly forbearance. You have at least been more than forbearing regarding the symbolism. I must take a little care of myself in this point before you, and always keep the consideration present to me: how much share friendship has in your lettered expressions about this book. All the more arrogant am I, however, in the face of Voß's philistinism. In the certainty of being able to learn nothing from Voß, I have indeed not read his review. What I know of it, I have from oral reports. Consequentially, I should have remained entirely silent — and you have lost nothing if you have not read that silly, scurrilous little sheet. A few friends here thought I should send something into the world — and so I did. In the preface to the 4th volume (which will now presumably be in your hands), I have indeed no longer mentioned Voß; but at the same time, although also without naming names, I have taken into account the exegetical nonsense that Paulus has recently been driving again in the Heidelberg Jahrbüchern [Yearbooks].

Thus, by excusing my long silence, I have been led into a bit of chatter about myself. But now not another word — except this one thing: that I shall now say farewell to this excessive writing for a few years, and devote myself all the more earnestly to Plato, Aristotle, and Plotinus. Your intelligent conversation and instruction would be of great service to me in this. That you have divined correctly, and that Berlin has indeed offered you a larger and more consequential sphere of activity — I can only be very glad about this. With lively interest I often hear the students coming from there tell how, with each course, the number of your listeners grows; and how there are not a few there who also possess the ability to delve into the depths of speculation. Our Daub had many listeners in his summer lectures on the Phenomenology — but not so many who went along with him for more than half the way. Hinrichs is very diligent, and his approval has not diminished. But his external situation demands a speedy change. It would be a real comfort to us if he were to obtain a fixed position! We had great trouble with his book until we found a publisher. Finally, Varrentrapp in Frankfurt has decided, and the first sheets have already been handed over to the press. A few days ago, Prof. Heller from Erlangen was here — still the same restless man. He knew a great deal about Döderlein and his family

Your trusting, open-hearted letter, my dearest Professor, I would have liked to reply to with more than good will. Mr. G. R. von Reizenstein, to whom I communicated it, immediately expressed that, although such a proposal had previously been very desirable to him, the Academy’s treasury restricted it to the most urgent need. It was the hope of a fresh influx that I wanted to wait for. Now it is clear to me that, for the time being, until the necessary positions are filled, one must think of nothing extraordinary. May the Genius of Germany bless your resolution to bring philosophy back from the clouds to friendly intercourse with eloquent human beings! It seems to me that intimate understanding and feeling are not even possible outside the intimate language of the heart; and that our rich native language either has formation, or flexible formability, for the freest and most delicate movements of the spirit. An Olympian in shepherd’s form would perform greater wonders than through superhuman appearances. With sincere respect, Your Devoted One, Voss.

In these beautifully composed and well-balanced words, I certainly do not find the somewhat displeasing expression of “concealment,” but I do find the matter itself presented in the most agreeable manner. That Goethe is moreover mistaken in saying that Fichte submitted a letter “to the Ministry” is irrefutably evident from the letter itself; it has been printed and clearly bears the character of a confidential letter, such as hundreds are written to the person in charge of an authority in business matters, without thereby being addressed to the authority itself. In general, the documentary evidence and explanations that Fichte’s biography provides on this matter deserve careful attention, and to me at least they have only confirmed the earliest impressions, according to which the entire affair always seemed to me to be to the discredit of the Weimar government and, insofar as he had a share in it, also not to the glory of Goethe.

I have also checked regarding Rudolstadt. It is certain that a gathering of students from Jena there for Fichte's sake could not have been a reason to demand his removal from there on the part of Weimar, for Fichte did not come to Rudolstadt at all, but only inquired in writing; whereupon he received a negative reply. A possible following of students was undoubtedly feared, but it did not happen. And in this respect too, the Weimar government, even if one cannot exactly blame it, must be said to have taken advantage of its university, yet this does not reflect very favorably on its side. What Schiller wrote to Goethe on June 14, 1799, about the Rudolstadt project confirms at most that Fichte had not actually attempted a stay there yet). I think I have read another passage for the same matter in the letters, but I cannot find such a one now in any way. Forgive me, Most Honored Sir, that I burden you so extensively with these proofs, but the name Fichte must excuse it, since every circumstance connected with him will always be of significance to the world. With the most intimate reverence and devotion, I remain most faithfully Your Most Well-Born's most obedient K. A. Varnhagen von Ense. Forgive the (not by me) splattered tea stains!

Most Honored Sir and Teacher! You will kindly forgive me if, after such a short interval, I again trouble you by sending you another of my works. However, as I may suppose that you are perhaps just now engaged in judging my treatise on your system—if you have not perhaps already completed it and submitted it for publication—it is indeed of interest to me to have the first part of a new work, which has just been finished, in your hands as soon as possible, by means of which I wish to be able to convince you that I did not merely write carelessly the objections I ventured in that treatise against various of your doctrines, without having previously thought through what I would set in place of what I opposed on my part. The systematic treatment of Aesthetics, the beginning of which I permit myself to send you herewith, had long since been conceived in spirit and provisionally thought through when I wrote that small book, and I believe I may say the same of several other philosophical disciplines, the written treatment of which I hope to be able to undertake next. That I did not express this against you with any other intention than to meet the reproach you expressly made to me, that I had made it easy for myself with my objections, needs no further remark.

How greatly I always and unchangeably revere you, and gladly owe to you the best that I am able to accomplish scientifically, this work, I hope, will also bear witness to. In no way would I have permitted myself what one might call attacks in the earlier as well as the present writing, but rather would have concealed the actually existing differences or let them reveal themselves through themselves, if those who currently call themselves your students had not, in a manner that must necessarily appear narrow-minded to me, asserted that which you yourself, in a magnanimous manner, recognize as a limit drawn for the individual in contrast to the never-stationary development of the human race, as an absolute final and insurmountable thing against all further striving; — and one, if one announces oneself from one side as your student — in order not to be misunderstood, must expressly protest against that which is commonly, but entirely unjustly, considered the truly essential thing of your school. With renewed assurance of my unchanging reverence and gratitude, your most obedient H. Weiße.

Thank you, thank you, thank you. First, your trip to France had no bad influence on your health. Next, your recent indisposition has completely passed. Finally, you still like me well. That is excellent. Now it is my turn. The old ministry rushed into action itself: it could have dragged on an existence without honor for a few more sessions; the dissolution of the Chamber killed it. The result of the elections was certain, and only surprised the ministry. The new administration is a transitional administration. It is clear that it lacks the strength and the brilliance that would be necessary for it to sustain itself against the two extremes of opinion, in France, in the public, and at the court, and to intervene dignifiedly in the general affairs of Europe. I do not believe it is sufficient; but at the same time I believe in its good intentions; I understand the difficulties of its position; it must be pushed a little, but my conviction is that it must be done gently or even amicably. Let us not precipitate anything and not believe the enemy destroyed because the battlefield is ours. I insist here with force on the necessity of being wise, measured, conciliatory, to prove finally that liberal opinion should frighten no one, neither private individuals nor governments, and that it is capable of holding the reins of affairs. One must sit down and one can only do so in a strong moderation. But I spare you my politics. Let it suffice for you to know, as a symptom, that all the youth is excellent, the public in general quite well, the directors of opinion not too hurried; that finally the future of France has nothing that can frighten. Be sure that one will be wise. We must relegate our enemies into the impotent furies of defeated parties and leave them all the odium of the violence and the recklessness that have so long dishonored and ruined us. Be tranquil about France, whatever you are told and whatever it seems to you from afar.

It is now that I am in great need of your advice. I shall measure your friendship by the number and severity of your criticisms. That is all for our correspondence. There is more. I need, even for here, a little success in Germany. See, therefore, Hegel, whether it would be impossible for Proclus, Plato, Descartes, or the Fragments to receive in your Journal the honors of a small article. From you, my Lord, that would be too much; but have a few pages written on the subject by Gans or by the excellent Hotho. Think about it; and let German philosophy support one of its friends. I thank you very much for your remarks on my partiality toward Plato; that is the misfortune of occupying oneself too much with an individual. The whole, the whole! You cannot make too many remarks. Do not develop them; I understand half a word. I have spent the whole winter on three dialogues of Plato: the Phaedrus, the Meno, and the Symposium, which, with a very large number of notes of all kinds and an introduction, will make up the sixth volume of my translation. I have finished everything, and the volume will appear in the first days of August. You will have it immediately. It will contain things that will perhaps not be unworthy of your attention. That is not all: on my return, I have reworked my article on Xenophanes (you will easily notice that this piece is an extract. I had to sacrifice the details and the philological and critical apparatus); and I have worked on another on Zeno of Elea. I am sending them to you by Schlesinger. I am joining to your copy another for the person who will be kind enough to take charge of making a small announcement in your Journal or elsewhere, for example, if it were possible, Mr. Böck, or Mr. H. Ritter. I see with infinite pleasure that people are busying themselves with ardor in Germany with Greek Philosophy. Try, I beg you, to tell me your opinion on these two small dissertations.

The misfortunes of my friends have ended with the old ministry. Mr. Lainé backed down in the face of real but not insurmountable difficulties: his refusal is probably definitive and deprives the country and the King of an honorable servant; but his position in the Chamber of Peers will be no less elevated. Mr. de Chateaubriand will sooner or later enter into an eminent post. Mr. R. Collard is well where he is. In the second ranks of the administration have already arrived and will successively arrive honest and enlightened men who wish me well. I come to myself. I have made up my mind. No, I do not want to enter into affairs; my career is philosophy, teaching, public instruction. I have declared this once and for all to my friends, and I will uphold my resolution. I have begun in my country a philosophical movement that is not without importance; I want with time to attach my name to it, that is all my ambition. I have that one; I have no other. I desire with time to firm up, enlarge, and improve my situation in public instruction, but only in public instruction. What do you say, Hegel? — Consequently, I have asked the new administration only for my reinstatement in my chair, but with a more solid title than that of substitute professor. For anything in the world I would not have suffered Mr. R. Collard to give his resignation: his name on the notice board of the Faculty is for the Faculty an honor and a strength that I would never have consented to take from him. That is how I am neither substitute nor titular, but adjunct, which is better than the one, less than the other, and confers upon me independence and inamovability. I therefore no longer have to reckon with authority, nor with the public, but with myself, with science and my projects. I resume my courses on April 15; in a few days I will reappear on my old battlefield and make my return with general considerations on the history of Philosophy as an introduction to the history of ancient Philosophy which will occupy me next year.

I am all the more in need of being informed that I intend to write a dissertation on Parmenides next winter; and you can imagine how much service is rendered to my future work by criticizing my opinion on Xenophanes or Zeno. I therefore expect something from you on this point by August or September. I do not speak to you of my course. It can only interest Germany through its ultimate consequences; for the moment it is good that it be very superficial so as not to discourage. I will speak to you of it when it is finished, that is to say on the 1st of August. Until then, I will not write to you. And Logic? You are quite right to think of it. All your reputation lies there. Leave the details and applications to others; it belongs to you to lay the foundation for all subsequent developments. Tell me where you stand with this great project. Farewell, a thousand heartfelt affections to you, to your children, to good Madame Hegel, and to all those who remember me in Berlin.

After having acquired all the works you have published, I should also like to possess the Difference between Fichte’s and Schelling’s Systems; however, I must unfortunately fear that this little work is already completely out of print, as I was only able to obtain the Phenomenology of Spirit in the bookshop with difficulty. The time has come when this philosophy wants to emerge everywhere; therefore, even its persecutors must bring it friends. With all my heart, I wish that God may grant you further health and strength, so that you may be able to remain active for a long time yet; although you have already acquired immortal merits for science and thereby secured the memory of your name for centuries. Although I am convinced that you do not need such assurances at all, it might nevertheless be pleasing to you, amidst the manifold defamations, to learn that the honest striving for the recognition of truth is nevertheless progressing irresistibly here. This is mainly the tendency of this letter, whereby I dare to count again on your lenient judgment. Finally, I have been instructed by Dr. Hügel to repeat to you his sincerest assurances of his great respect, and for my part, it is likewise the highest esteem with which I have the particular honor to call myself, Your Excellency’s truly devoted student Ravenstein, Premier Lieutenant and Adjutant of the 2nd Cuirassier Regiment.

To the extent that a person is capable of recognizing and judging himself within his earthly shell, I consider myself a friend of truth. I have often tested myself in various periods and circumstances, and I have found myself—despite all the instability of a very agitated and mobile temperament—always constant, and increasingly so, in my love of truth. About 15 years ago, I was lying ill in France and was haunted by skepticism, a disease that could only be worsened, not healed, by the empirical manner of philosophizing that prevailed there!—While we did not want to lose sight of our visible ground, declaring the saying: "Blessed are those who do not see and yet believe" as a mere wit, and always continuing to infer from appearance to being, we naturally arrived at atheism or at least at skepticism. The sophist as well as the philosopher, the one who loves truth as well as the one who loves himself above truth, were restricted and confined in the sensually apparent world, and when the atheist said quite brazenly: "There is no God!"—Why?—"Because our globe is without proportion and without symmetry"—our good and religious Bernardin de Saint-Pierre wrote his *Études* as a refutation and depicted the appearance of harmony with warmth and talent. Dissatisfied with French philosophizing, led to Hamburg by circumstances and business, I sought to console myself in my skepticism with some arguments from Cicero and Fontenelle; however, the axiom of the latter, with which he had lived for 100 years, did not help me either as long as I remained inactive, and it truly helped me only when and to the extent that I interpreted it in a manner suitable to my temperament. I spoke to Fontenelle thus: Yes, as you say, "Everything is possible and everyone is right," it is possible that I understand Kant and I am right to try to understand him, and, since Fontenelle had nothing against it, I took Kant under my arm, went to Wansbeck and rented a room there for both of us, where I spent the summer in his company, entirely alone.

I lived with this man for a couple of years and gradually became acquainted, to a certain degree, with his mind, so that I was at least able to free myself from the empirical procedure and to comprehend what philosophy as a science would have to consist of, if such a science were possible at all. The undeniable Being, according to Kant, was the non-nothing; but for us it was merely the non-nothing; for in and for itself it was the absolute Being, i.e., that which had to be presupposed by all possible doubting and affirming, by all possible human representation, without having to presuppose all of this in order to be, but merely in order to be represented. In the Being that was only believed and never to be positively investigated, truth therefore had to consist, for since nothing was absolute outside this Being, no particular harmony could be called the absolute truth: truth in the positive sense. But the true Being and the truth of Being was for us an X, and philosophy as pure science was impossible and forever! — From Kant, whom I had understood mainly with Reinhold’s help, I came to Reinhold’s view and studied for several years in succession the philosophical spirit of this venerable and conscientious man and his various attempts to represent truth in itself, as consisting in the agreement of the three inseparable characters of Being.

Some time ago I came to the idea that the so-called philosophical justifications of criminal law known to me up to that point would hardly withstand a deeper critique, and they aroused in me a sincere aversion to all engagement with this philosophy. — But the more I devoted myself to historical investigations, and in particular came to know, alongside Roman law, the very interesting Germanic and ecclesiastical criminal law, the more convinced I became that all positive systems of criminal law serve a common root in an idea, which appears differently to man depending on his standpoint. — I further found that this idea of punishment is the truly immanent and eternal element of punishment, and that punishment is therefore not something invented by men and devised for some purpose of utility.

Our local situation is very similar to our former one in Jena; only nature must not be compared with the sterility of Jena. We already have ripe grapes, and the vegetation is not so lush in our fatherland as it is here. I dare not describe the poetic landscape, as it has already been sung and praised by so many poets and travel writers. Our social circle is still limited to Thibaut’s, Wilkens, Martin, Heise, Voß, and a few other families. Thibaut, together with his wife, stands highest in the estimation of us all, especially also of Emmi; Wilkens are also very dear to us. Prof. Wilken is particularly remarkable to me because he is the first scholar I have seen in my life who does not look like a scholar. He has a talented, interesting wife, a daughter of Tischbein. Besides, we have learned women of all kinds here. Madame Chezi from Paris, a second Liebeskind: only in a more pleasant external form. Frau von Helwig, the sister of Lesbos, a vain fool or, as Thibaut says, a Madonna to be seen. Frau von Wohlzogen, who, however, has returned to Weimar for a few months and will come back in the autumn.

Pending more serious dispatches, I had the Prussian Legation deliver to you and to a few other persons biographical notes on Fourier, which I had printed since my return. This is the continuation of my address to the Academy that I gave you in Berlin. These notes, combined with the address, will give you some idea of one of the best men and most eminent spirits I have encountered in my life, I who, as you know, have a fairly happy hand. They may also interest you by offering little-known details of the great period of the Revolution and the Empire. The style is a bit neglected. It is a great difficulty to write details: the style must not give them too much importance, and it must not take away from their interest either. One must recede, but not too much; in biography there must be a little history and not too much history. You should really tell Monsieur de Varnhagen to pass on his secret to me. Do not spare me the criticisms either; for I have biographical projects, of which I have spoken to you, I believe. I want to give the three great revolutionaries in philosophy, Socrates, Descartes, and Kant; and perhaps also what I call the organizers will come after, Plato, Aristotle, and Leibniz. If I have time left, Proclus will provide me with a high life of a commentator.

Settle it firmly in your mind, dear Hegel, that my entire soul is always devoted to philosophy. That is the foundation of the poem of my poor life, as I was telling you; politics only fills in the episodes. Upon my return, I had to compose a report on my mission. This report is nothing but the continuation of the letters I had written from Frankfurt, Weimar, Schulpforta, Leipzig, Berlin, and Bonn to Monsieur de Montalivet, which I limited myself to supporting with supporting documents and the necessary elaborations. Five letters have already been printed, which amounts to more than one hundred pages. Those that relate to Prussia will not see the light of day and hardly deserve to do so, for the reasons you know. If I believed that all my pedantic writings could interest you in the slightest, I would send them to you. In any case, whether for you or for others, I direct you to the Revue de Paris, Volumes 29 and 30.

so that the field can be worked through in its entire scope. And, what pleases Mr. Van Ghert no less than me: the students of this college are making extraordinary progress; but especially they are, which I least expected in the first year, taken with the philosophical subjects that I teach, with the exception of the history of philosophy. Mr. Van Ghert, who attended an examination on logic that I arranged, admired the happy progress that these pupils have made in so short a time; but he also recognized at the same time that I philosophize in the Hegelian method; which pleased him greatly. Mr. Van Ghert, like me, awaits with impatience Your Excellency’s philosophical Encyclopedia, 2nd edition, and Your Excellency’s Philosophy of Religion. It must concern me all the more; since I have begun to lecture weekly for 3 hours to the Germans in this college, whose number is about 80, on the history of philosophy from Kant to Hegel. In this semester I will conclude with the Jacobi system, but in the next school year I will develop the Schelling and Hegel systems. The subject of the history of philosophy is indeed not assigned to me, but to another professor; nevertheless, since I have been requested by the Germans to present to them the newer and newest systems, I complied with them all the more willingly; since it is to be hoped that in a few years Your Excellency’s system will take deeper root here than at several German universities, to which I also count Bonn.

That His Archbishop of Cologne (from Münster), in connection with the all-powerful Secret O. R. R. Schmedding (from Münster), wanted to force me into the Cathedral Chapter of Cologne, is known to Your High Excellency, as is also the fact that this would make room for Prof. Hermes of Bonn (from Münster) and the Informator and Chaplain Ritter in the house of the Hon. G. O. R. R. Schmedding. However, this act of force, which perhaps has no precedent in the Prussian University Annals, did not succeed; and I may assure Your High Excellency that I am here, under the protection of the strong Belgian government, very satisfied; all the more so, since I have a very beautiful sphere of activity. I now ask Your High Excellency to recommend me most highly to the Hon. Secret Senior Government Councillor Dr. J. Schulze. Otherwise, I am, as I always have been, with intimate reverence, Your High Excellency’s most obedient Seber Prof.

How sad the state of the educational institutions of the Catholic clergy, and consequently of the education of the clergy, is in the Kingdom of the Netherlands, Your Excellency has seen with your own eyes. And how detrimental such a clergy must be and is to the state, is likewise known to Your Excellency. Mr. Van Ghert has therefore long been occupied with the idea of establishing a philosophical college for the Catholics of the entire Kingdom who wish to devote themselves to the clerical state. He carried out this idea, despite the opposition of the higher clergy and even of some statesmen, to the astonishment of all, with great success. This college now counts 230 students, and in the coming autumn perhaps 400; so that in a few years it will already reach the number of 1000–1200, for which it is calculated. His Majesty the King, the High Ministry, and even many opponents are extremely satisfied with this institution. The premises selected by Mr. Van Ghert for this purpose, the General Seminary built by Emperor Joseph, which accommodates a good 14–1500 students, is not only very suitably located, but also very pleasant and beautiful. In these premises, not only are the lectures held, but the students belonging to the college also have their residence and board here. The paying students pay 200 Dutch guilders annually; the indigent receive royal scholarships, with which this sum is covered. Indeed, I know no larger state that is so willing to provide support, and that expends such large sums, as the Belgian one. The internal (domestic) management of this college is entrusted to a Rector, two Sub-rectors, and an Economist. The number of Sub-rectors will be increased with the increase of students. The gentlemen Curators have the general supervision, but the highest and decisive authority lies with Mr. Van Ghert, to whom this college has grown deeply into his soul. As well as provision is made for food and lodging, as well as for domestic order, so little is lacking in the academic subjects. Here are taught: Low German language, Hebrew language, Latin, Greek, general, Low German, and Church history, Logic, Metaphysics, Moral Philosophy, History of Philosophy, Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, and Canon Law. It will also soon be arranged that the philosophical

The lines you so infinitely kindly devoted to my grief have fully achieved their noble purpose. I scarcely thought it possible that anyone, other than myself, would perceive the Deceased in all her relationships in such a manner, and to the man who has restored to my heart, in a faithful and living image, the beloved being that has departed from me, I need not say how infinitely beneficial these expressions of the most delicate, yet strongest and most sublime, sympathy are to me. Just as in the beloved Deceased all that was noble and grand manifested itself in the most unassuming attachment and veneration, so too did her relationship with you form and become ever more firmly established. She placed great value on you, and had the warmest and most delicate concern for everything concerning you and your esteemed wife. All the more precious to me is the monument she has in your heart, which you have erected through your expressions about her. You have also correctly grasped my feeling. Grief still barely allows a friendly light for the harsh fate that has befallen me. I lack the being who, in the hardest blows of fate, helped me win the friendly light as a protecting angel. My greatest pain is that I cannot separate myself from the idea of still seeking comfort in her now, and that with the certainty forcing itself upon me that this no longer exists for me on this earth, I awaken to an all the more painful feeling of irreplaceable loss.

What I wrote about Sina is based on a viewpoint and principle that I have already stated in my lectures on world history since 1804, and which I also published in writings and essays in 1807 and 1813... Therefore, I assure you on my honor that I am not aware of the slightest influence of your lectures on the philosophy of history, that the work is entirely my own, and that no use whatsoever has been made of your notes. I have therefore in no way deserved such a hostile mention.

In any case, it demands serious attention and deep love in order not to fail in one's conduct toward these directions; specifically, from the side of philosophy, the recognition of the content cannot be repeated too often, and subsequently, the essence of the form and its appearance in the differentiated stages cannot be made sufficiently recognizable and intuitive to consciousness. Yet I feel that I am precisely prevented from expressing myself adequately by such generalities. Hopefully, I will find another opportunity to obtain detailed and specific instruction from you on this point. However, I cannot close without first having made the confession to you, my very revered Professor, that in literary matters I have for some time been occupied with the too-often interrupted attempt to present my own professional science in an intuitive manner in the light of speculative philosophy, albeit only aphoristically, as it were scene by scene; it is particularly important to me to have living images in order to simultaneously enliven our dead practice. Therefore, I look around for historical content to give the book both content and life at the same time, specifically to meet my professional colleagues with points of reference that can facilitate understanding, when the unknown is linked to the known, and through this, the known itself is renewed, rejuvenated, and enlivened. In conclusion, I may well express the hope for future personal acquaintance; hopefully, it is not the last time that I sign myself with deep respect and veneration as your obedient and grateful C. Fr. Göschel.

An urgent wish is that you be with us already in the next winter semester, and that the lectures you intend to give be announced in the lecture list, which is printed in the month of August. I therefore request your answer to the question made above as promptly as possible. As for the travel costs to here, you will, as I have been written, either be granted a reasonable flat rate, or, if you prefer, your actual expenses for this purpose could be reimbursed. Regarding the widow's and orphan's allowance, a regulation was made in the year 1810, which concerns all civil servants without distinction and provides sufficient reassurance. I hasten so that this letter may go to the post today, and I ask you to kindly excuse my generally hastily written letter. If I live to see you belonging to the University of Heidelberg, which I love like my foster mother and shall love until the end of my life, then a pure and refreshing ray of light has fallen into my life. With truly sincere respect, your most devoted Daub, d. Z. Rector.

Now that I have finally found a point of rest here, I am compelled to give you, dear friend, at least a brief report concerning what affects you. In strict accordance with the instructions you gave me, I spoke of you and about you in Berlin. I was unable to create an opportunity to do so with Minister von Schuckmann himself, no matter how diligently I sought it. On the other hand, an entirely uninvited (though not unwelcome) opportunity first presented itself with State Councillor Süvern and finally with State Councillor Nicolovius, which I was able to use all the more unreservedly, precisely because it was entirely uninvited, to your advantage according to your wishes. I may certainly assume that after these conversations, if your answer still allows for negotiation, a firm vote will be cast in your favor; and I even imagine that the inquiry directed to you would have turned out quite differently than it actually did, had I been able to speak beforehand. I have found the course of affairs of this kind no better in general there than in a certain elsewhere; everywhere God has loved the same arrangement, to secure praise in the mouths of children and young infants, and the whole difference might come down to the fact that he here and there allows the devil to interpose a little Satan, who must sometimes, against his will, do his will as well. In the meantime, it does help here and there if a proper schoolmaster steps in among the minors and gives a solid blow on the desk with the ruler. In this manner, more or less, I have conducted myself, and I may almost believe that the ears of one or the other are ringing a little. — Please let me know soon how your affairs stand.... No one can rejoice more sincerely than we do in your good fortune. The same love and attachment from us will accompany you everywhere, if we must accompany you throughout.

I am literally with you day and night, and you must sometimes feel and know that I am devoting all my strength to you. May it be granted to me to live with you for a longer time and to come even closer to you over matters that are equally important to us both. Perhaps that will come to pass, but until then, do not doubt for a moment that I love you warmly and that your well-being is my earnest prayer to God. Please also tell me when I may hope to see your Philosophy of Spirit appear, which I greatly desire.

My best regards to Friend Schulz. He, too, is as quiet as a mouse. This, however, should not prevent me from expressing my gratitude to him soon. Farewell, and think of us with love. May God grant you health and cheerfulness forever, as He grants it to me, so that I cannot thank Him enough, especially for my eyes. With all my heart, yours, Windischmann. I also thank you for the friendly reception of Mr. Ludowig. His poor aunt, Mrs. Hirn, is truly in a lamentable situation, which she endures with a strong soul and a submission that is exemplary. Her most painful complaint is that someone was benefited by her action, which she had not foreseen, as her only fault in the matter was placing too much trust in the son.

Beloved, revered Friend! If you thought of me as often as I think of you, I should by now have heard a word from you telling me what you are doing, whether you love me, and how you received my dispatch in October 1823. Nevertheless, do not believe that I am not convinced of your concern, since, for example, I recognize your involvement in the Minister’s reply and wish to do so; I also know very well that you, like me, are in the midst of the pressure of work; but it is good to hear from a man so intimately revered that even what one has written with good and strict intent regarding the truth is not entirely unworthy in his eyes. Moreover, I confess that I can learn most from you, and from you above all contemporaries who bear the name of philosophers, however much I know that we still differ on a main point. I make this confession in full earnest, the more I am convinced of the intellectual sharpness of your investigations and deeply respect and revere you in my soul for this strict, grand penetration into the truth. To whom God has given so much, as He has given to you, He will also help to complete what has already been carried so far.

to set forth the Protestant educational institutions of the Kingdom. The Ministerial Resolution mentioned at the beginning, says N., contains in particular two provisions which I must hold incompatible with the educational requirements of the Protestants: a) the lowering of the age of entry into the Progymnasium from the 12th to the 10th year of life; b) the complete abolition of the subject teachers of Mathematics and of the philosophical preparatory studies in the Gymnasiums. In the former respect, it is convincingly demonstrated that in a primary education of only two years, instead of the previous four-year one, the requirements to be met for entry into the Progymnasium could not be fulfilled, and that as a result of the lowering to an age level two years earlier, the pupils would complete the Gymnasium at the age of sixteen years without having attained the maturity necessary for university study. Here, reference is likely made to the old Catholic educational arrangement, according to which the Lyceum was placed between the Gymnasium and the University, which in a two-year philosophical course (called Logic and Physics) led the young men over to the University. In the same manner, N. continues, the Protestants would be placed at a disadvantage by the other innovation, whereby they, who have no Lyceums, would be deprived of the necessary preparation in such important subjects as Mathematics and the philosophical sciences, since young men who, in their 16th year of life, enter the University with an incomplete Gymnasium education, cannot be kept in a state to examine the grounds of faith with their own judgment, and to learn to understand the Holy Scripture in the original language as the Protestant Church indispensably requires of its teachers. Accordingly, the same person first submits the request that the decided change of the curriculum not be extended to the Protestant educational institutions in Ansbach, Bayreuth, Nuremberg, and Augsburg, and secondly, after setting forth how little the presence of a single councilor of their confession in the Commission, consisting of 4 ecclesiastical and 1 secular Catholics (not counting the head), could serve to reassure the numerous Protestants of the Kingdom, the other request to arrange the extraordinary Commission appointed for the revision of the previous curriculum in such a way that the responsibility falling on the petitioner thereby be eased.

There is so much that has deeply interested me and urges me toward a more extensive outpouring, but there is too much material for me to be able to deal with it thoroughly at present, and it is too important to be disposed of in a few words; I therefore reserve all of this for another occasion. The general world events and expectations, as well as those of the nearer circles, mostly lead me to more general reflections, which push the individual and the immediate, however much it interests the feeling, further away in thought. I hold to the fact that the world spirit has given the time the command word: to advance. This command is obeyed; this being advances like an armored, tightly closed phalanx irresistibly, and with as imperceptible a movement as the sun advances, forward, through thick and thin; countless light troops flank it on all sides, for and against it, most of whom know nothing at all about what it is about, and only receive blows to the head as if from an invisible hand. All lingering flattery and wise-guy airiness avails nothing against it; it may reach this colossus perhaps only up to the shoe laces and smear a bit of shoe polish or dirt on them, but it cannot loosen them, much less pull off the god-shoes with the—according to Voß, see mythological letters and others—elastic spring soles, or even the seven-league boots, if he puts them on. The safest (namely internally and externally) party is probably to keep a firm eye on the advancing giant; thus one can even stand by, and for the edification of the whole busy and zealous company, even help smear on shoe pitch, which is supposed to hold the giant fast, and to one's own mental enjoyment promote the serious activity.

To His Excellency, Professor Hegel in Berlin.

Most Revered Friend!

The purpose of this letter is to recommend the bearer, Dr. Port from Denmark, who has stayed here for a few months, to your goodwill, and to give you a sign of life from me; both on the assumption that I still stand in your good memory. And may I not assume this? I have not ceased to love you; I am, especially since you left us, occupied by you daily, indeed almost hourly, and have been in your company almost uninterruptedly, and only now do I fully know the greatness of our loss through your departure. — I have studied your Logic with the utmost exertion, and only then has the content of your Phenomenology of Spirit finally become entirely clear to me. It was for the sake of Dogmatics and Morals that I valued it; now I believe myself prepared, and will confidently proceed to the elaboration of the system of the former; for the latter I look forward with the liveliest joy to your Natural Law, which I have heard is soon to appear. The surroundings, the external life and its rarities were long since, and even before your presence here, indifferent to me; but through you, Great, noble man! I have, since the last two years, truly become at home in science, and I hope that if the inner life is granted me a few more years, I shall still be able to prove by deed that strict science flourishes in the South as in the North. Better, of course, it would be to attach the proof itself to this letter instead of the expressed hope; that would be a real sign of life from me. I ask you to maintain your goodwill and am, with the warmest respect and love, your most devoted Daub.

Since our Julius arrived at your place, not a sound from you, my dear friends and godparents! That is almost a bit too much or harsh! But I do not intend to be deterred by this from making myself heard on my side. So, first of all, I remind you of what Julius, if he has not forgotten it, will have suggested; namely, that you would like to write to me just 2 lines about how many and what kind of candidates showed up at your examination.... Second, I am also curious to hear whether you have not perhaps heard something further in the meantime about the Mehmelsche Vocation)); nothing further has come to my ears about it myself. As proof of what can be expected in cases of settlement for the University of Erlangen, it may serve you that Mr. v. Zlentner! wants to place the withered branch") in Harle's place, which he has long wanted to get rid of in Landshut! (But I ask that nothing be let out about this yet). — Third, my main business now comes up. Just as worms, frogs, and other vermin often follow the rain, so do the Weillers and consorts follow the gloomy day that spreads over the entire civilized world. In the general (Sünd-Fluth, in which all that is outdated flows back, this literary and pedagogical, like the rest of the rabble, believes it has found its moment; and

I have known it so far only from an issue of the Heidelberg Journal containing the continuation of a review. From this very fact I already conclude that it is masterly and that you have said things about the essence of philosophy that had not been said before. I cannot yet judge the whole; but do not believe that it is delay on my part; rather, I am ready, as soon as you send it to me and desire it, to share my detailed judgment with you. So much I already see, that your work has gone deeper than before, and that insofar as I regard it as free thoughts on the subject, I find it exemplary. Your view will certainly act very beneficially against the shallow spirit of today’s fashionable philosophy, for nothing seems to me more unworthy of the German sense of truth, which has always revealed itself in thoroughness of research and in honest expression, than the charlatanry of Schelling and his associates, which is nothing but methodlessness and unproven chatter, hiding hypocritically behind a petty enthusiasm. Besides, I know him only very little, but enough to find him disagreeable. Besides, you will certainly have found, as I have, on reviewing the systems from antiquity onward, that given the complete inconsistency they all have, it is not to be wondered at that philosophy is still in its swaddling clothes, and that history does not show us the result from it that it will certainly have once the spirit of truth has fully brought it forth. It pleases me that, when I compare your ideas with mine in thought, I foresee in advance that we, although walking on different paths, are not walking on opposite ones, and that we will, I believe, meet in most of the results. It would please me very much if this bond of truth also strengthened our old friendship, for the others are no more, and of those who shared with us the view of truth, you are the only one who has remained to me.

Goethe was here in November and December. He is now healthy, and was particularly lively and cheerful. We also got to know the poet Werner during that time, and admired several of his sonnets, which he does especially well. I heard him read his “Cross on the Baltic Sea” at Frommann’s, which has many excellent passages, and the motives are also very praiseworthy. You must read it. Tomorrow, on the Duchess’s birthday, a tragedy by him, Vanda, will be performed, which has already been highly praised to us, and he is said to have endeavored to observe brevity, which is not easy for him. Now I have chattered on long enough. Farewell, and remember your friend Th. Seebeck. Have you heard nothing of the knights and the Munich proceedings regarding the dowsing rod? I have received hardly any news from him for half a year. Schelver is quite satisfied, and promises to send me his Philosophy of Medicine shortly. He inquires of me where you are.

How are you, my dear friend? I have not received any news from you for quite a long time. You have received my reply to your first letter, I presume? Frommann told me that you were satisfied with your present situation; this pleases me, yet I wish you could return to your former sphere of activity. For Jena, there is little to hope for at present. It was recently said here that Berthier had written to Henry that something would certainly still be done for Jena. May Heaven grant that this may prove true. How is the second part of your System coming along? Have you already begun the printing? — Last summer I continued the experiments on light, and arrived at some not uninteresting results, which I shall present to you at some convenient time. Perhaps we may be able to discuss them orally next spring, if you are then still in Bamberg...

The review of De Wette's work has been delayed; I am sighing under a burden of business; to this are added domestic sufferings, which more or less extend their influence to this day. I would gladly have given it a greater degree of perfection; but the brevity of the time I could devote to its preparation did not permit this; and I did not wish, nor could I, delay any longer. May it not be entirely unworthy of your approval. Heaven grant that I may finally come to concentration in my position or within it. The administration of a fairly large church fund, numerous presbytery affairs, the inspection of 11 teachers, the work occasioned by the school commission, a parish office — that and other similar things are too much, if one wishes to live undividedly for science. Mr. Minister von Altenstein has given me some hope in this regard. His friendly words read in a letter of July 1st of this year: “I shall be all the more glad to take into consideration your wish to obtain an appropriate sphere of activity at a university here, the more sincere is the respect which I have dedicated to you on the basis of your previous literary works.” I certainly thank you for this pleasing expression also for your kind cooperation. My most heartfelt thanks for it! Perhaps I shall reach the longed-for goal.

I can be very satisfied with the success of my first lecture, which was attended by a very large number of people. My listeners endured it, and I may hope to have exerted some beneficial influence on them. At least, in many cases, the fear of studying philosophy has been overcome, and thus some counteraction has been provided against the activities of an unscientific faction, which is also resident here. I have sent you the speech with which I opened the lecture via the book trade. Not that I would dare to place great weight on it; but in the hands of my most deeply revered teacher, I wished to place all my literary productions. Even if they are insignificant, you, I know this, will receive them kindly, and this touching matter shows at least to some extent how I view academic teaching. May God preserve you to the entire scientific fatherland for a long time yet! I am, with unchanging love, your revering J. Rust. P.S. May I perhaps soon enjoy a few lines?

Regarding the other point, I note that the printing of this work had already been completed during my journey in Italy. Therefore, having just arrived at the Rhine, my first business is to let this letter precede the dispatch of the copy, which I shall receive from Erlangen. You will tell yourself how often I have thought of you, dear sir, with my friends in Italy; I merely add here the request that you recommend me and my wife to your celebrated wife, and excuse me if I trouble you with the further handling (by post) of the enclosed letter. In that most distinguished esteem, the measure of which is given by the matter itself, which is not hidden from free and willing insight, and in the modest hope of soon hearing something from your dear hand, Yours — Christian Kapp. I shall be in Erlangen before the middle of October.

Winzingen near Neustadt on the Haardt

Most Honored Professor!

I have taken the liberty to dedicate to you a small treatise: On the Origin of Mankind and Peoples according to the Mosaic Genesis, and therefore I ask your indulgence both for this in general, and in particular for the fact that this announcement reaches you only now. If, in excusing the former, I refer to the Hebrew meaning of your name in connection with the Old Testament subject of the work, I know that I am simultaneously excusing this point by having allowed myself to transfer the custom, according to which the refusal of a request for baptism and godparenthood is considered ungodly, to the present case. Do not count this as a fault against the free and open admirer, who cares for the truth regardless of (but with recognition of) the person; a sentiment which, even where it expresses itself clumsily, can only be misunderstood by the rabble.

From that time on, van Ghert lived as a private citizen in The Hague until his death, occupied with literary work and philosophical lectures, with public-spirited efforts to improve popular education, and occasionally with magnetic cures, the treatment of which he had learned in Jena and which he had then applied with good success first in Amsterdam and Brussels. A few weeks before his death, he began a cycle of lectures on H.’s Aesthetics. Distinguished by philosophical education and religious tolerance, he has left behind in his fatherland a highly respected memory as both a statesman and a writer.

Peter Gabriel van Ghert, a Dutchman by birth (178 and raised in the Catholic faith, went as a young man, driven by the urge for philosophical knowledge, to Jena to acquaint himself with German philosophy. But since he did not even understand German, he first attended Ulrich’s lectures on logic, which were held in Latin, though he did not find them helpful. Thereafter he listened to Hegel, without understanding him, until the latter, moved by the open confession of his listener’s inability, introduced him to his philosophy through oral conversation. From then on, van Ghert studied it with zeal and success and remained its faithful follower throughout his entire life.

I truly do not know what to make of the aforementioned news, as I cannot think of any positions that would be suitable only for poor heads. — On the other hand, I also do not understand how it comes about that the second part of your divine Phenomenology, along with the Philosophy of Nature, is not appearing. — However it may be: fear has overcome me, and I shall have no peace until you have the kindness to honor me with your own letter. — If you are truly as unfortunate as the news suggests, I might occasionally be able to be of assistance to you in my fatherland. — The universities will soon be reorganized, and if you perhaps have the genius to become a professor in Holland, where the lectures are (at least until now) held in Latin, then I would spare no effort to ensure that you obtained a good position. — I am a Doctor of Law and a Clerk at the Ministry of Public Worship in Amsterdam — the Minister, whom I know very well and who does much according to my suggestion, will appoint some professors, and so I could always put your name forward — the annual salary is 6000 Dutch guilders.

to tell. Nuremberg, September 20, 1826. First Bulletin. Honored Sir and Friend. The first thing this Bulletin must begin with is the regret we felt at having missed your wife in Leipzig: she had departed a few hours before our arrival. We would gladly have given her a foretaste of good news from Berlin, yet on the other hand it was pleasing to us to know that your state of straw-widowerhood had ended earlier than you yourself had supposed. After I had greeted the trade in Professor Wenck), I hastened likewise to Professor (commonly called Councillor)-Wendt to salute Leipzig philosophy and to negotiate for the Literary Gazette. I found a small man who, in the mythology of the Leipzig university system, belongs to the more historical persons, i.e., to the professors of newer foundation, who as such have the right to follow the movements of the times, what is statutorily forbidden to the professors of older foundation of all 4 nations"). Professor Wendt seems to be an eclectic, to whom much that does not go together is right at the same time, but who for the Literary Gazette might nevertheless be of use. As concert director of Leipzig, as city aesthete, and as leader of the concert-giving ladies, he will in any case be familiar with the popular manner, as it is desired by us. Professor Wendt took a dinner-supper with us in the evening at the Hotel de Saxe, and here a bottle of good wine completed the courtship begun in the morning. Professor Wendt had some misgivings against Mr. von Cotta, which the honorarium of 20 thalers soon removed. The man is otherwise well acquainted with the book trade; in Leipzig the booksellers seem to publish the works with the authors; their initiative is rarely followed by a veto on the part of

In Nuremberg, where we have been since the day before yesterday at noon, we did not fail to visit the family of your wife, who are in the best of health. We also found Zeune and his wife from Berlin there. The numerous curiosities of Nuremberg occupied us for two full days, and the place is beginning to please me very much, as I am just having to leave. Among the paintings, a Dürer is probably the most distinguished, which we saw at the house of Mr. von Holzschuher through the kind mediation of Mr. von Tucher. While Hotho finds great nourishment here for his immediate studies, I enjoy it here too, without immediately turning what I have seen into the constraint of study.

9. The organic state in which Munich finds itself, despite all its offensive boasting, drew me away without having fundamentally clarified anything. Such was the situation upon my arrival. Cotta was in a dilemma, revealed the Bavarian circumstances to me, and wanted me to find a way out; I could suggest no other course than the termination of all negotiations, whereby I pointed out to him how uncertain the Munich venture was, and how treacherous the conduct toward us would be: I must, however, give Cotta the credit of having decisively rejected this latter point; he merely lamented constantly over the dual venture, one of which would kill and undermine the other. Finally, he produced his way out, asking whether the two ventures could not be combined, and thus the unfortunate schism eliminated. I agreed to this combination, but only on the condition that the Munich men would be gladly seen and admitted as collaborators in our Literary Gazette: I proposed to go to Munich with this intention. Cotta consented only too willingly, and so this evening the contract, with minor modifications, as prescribed by the Society, was signed by me and Cotta. This contract will serve in Munich to either make the gentlemen, who in any case act prematurely, desist from their venture, or to bring us in the capacity of collaborators. Tomorrow morning I depart for Munich, accompanied by many letters written by Cotta. Thence I wish to receive further instructions on conduct from the honored Society, which I intend to await in any case. Since the contract is signed, the game is much lighter here. While I humbly request these letters of instruction, I am your devoted Gans. I ask you to greet all members of the Society.

Gans. Second Bulletin. Stuttgart, September 26, 1826. Honored Sir and Friend. This Bulletin, which is rather a dispatch that I submit to the honored Society, is of a more serious nature than the previous one, in which I had to cover the lack of content with all manner of arabesques. I arrived here late in the evening on the 23rd and announced myself to Mr. v. Cotta, who fortunately had just returned from a journey. A letter from him to Weimar, which summoned me to a conference in Augsburg or Munich, had not reached me, which, as you will see, was a good thing. Here, namely, I found entirely unexpected obstacles for our matter. Mr. v. Cotta had had an audience with the King of Bavaria a few days prior, and the King had urged him to publish a literary journal for the new University of Munich. Thiersch, whom the King apparently used as a grand faiseur, had just been here to carry out the Royal wish immediately. Cotta found himself in a peculiar embarrassment. He did not wish to break off his negotiations with Berlin, nor to disavow them; yet he seems to be in such relations with the King of Bavaria that they do not allow a refusal; finally, he saw that two undertakings of the same kind in his publishing house cannot coexist. Fortunately, in my last letter I had reported that I intended to recruit Thiersch and Niethammer in Munich as collaborators. Cotta showed this letter to Thiersch, while at the same time revealing to him how far he had already gone with Berlin. Thiersch, whether it was the vanity that he had been thought of, or the un-

Your Excellency had Professor Wilken ask me which courses I intend to read this winter, as you wish to alternate with me. Such an arrangement would also be very agreeable to me, provided it suits your convenience. Until now, I have read Logic every winter, along with another course from a cycle I have established, comprising an outline of the whole of Philosophy (similar to your Encyclopedia), Ethics, Jurisprudence, Politics, and Aesthetics. I do not have sufficient knowledge of the natural sciences, and I am doubly pleased that you will take up this field here. For this winter, I have provisionally determined to read Politics, as I am currently reading Jurisprudence. However, I am happy to leave it to depend on how many listeners, prepared by the previous courses, I can expect.

The eagerness of a partisan rushes into the fire where the situation tempts him. But you can count on me only to the extent that enemies meet me on my official path, where my profession lies. If you wish to accept me under this condition, then enter my name in your roll. — I have communicated your letter to Mr. v. Roth. However, he has not replied to the invitation; and therefore, to press him further, I have found to be beyond the limits of my mandate. On the other hand, with regard to your announced notice of Hamann’s works, he has instructed me to write to you: that the collection of works is to be considered closed with the 7th volume, since the 8th volume will actually contain only the indexes, and at most a few minor additions of little importance; that the appearance of this 8th volume is not to be expected soon, and that he intends to postpone it all the more, after the announcement of your notice of the work, in order to keep open a small space in it for the possible case regarding your notice; specifically, however, that you would yourself find the reason why Hamann has been so little understood and will be, in the fact that he often took a very high standpoint, as for example in his judgment on Homer. For my part, I look forward with great eagerness to your judgment on Hamann’s works. I find his standpoint to be of such a nature that I expect from a thorough judgment on him a resolution of the discrepancy in which, according to common opinion, philosophy and history stand to one another. But I do not consider the resolution to be easy. That Hamann, in the comparison of his time with ours, stands as a seer above his contemporaries, will hardly be disputed.
