But our time — if one will allow this honorific name to the rabble — understands him even less than his own time did. It is therefore perfectly time that one comes who is able to remove the cataract. I welcome him from the bottom of my heart!

As for the philosophy, which you were perhaps a little put off by, it is not really of much consequence, and it may well be considered blind here, which I am quite happy about, because I would like to make all the Heidelberg philosophers invisible—not so much blind, for they may well be that, but rather invisible—so as to draw you, dear friend, all the more visibly to that great cask, which the idealist Johann Jacob Wagner would almost prefer to his own philosophy if it were full.

The newly created Professor (I believe I may call him so, as he is already working on his reading catalogue with scholarly enthusiasm) receives a salary of 2,500 florins, and will therefore, if one adds the honorarium for spreading printed and oral light, lose nothing. But I ask you to keep this beautiful secret still secret. We too, Emmi and I, are seeking to prepare ourselves in a worthy manner for academic life, and have thrown ourselves, with the greatest possible exertion of mind, upon the Flegeljahre. May Heaven grant that Emmi finds no "Quod Deus vult" among the Heidelberg students, otherwise her resolve to be a homebody might waver. I cannot conceive where the Theory of Colours may have gone, but I hope it will soon come to light again, for it has been handed over to someone. I will certainly come to Nuremberg. But you must certainly come to Ansbach; and now; for we shall only be able to mount the red horse in a few weeks. The gentleman asks you to accept his best regards and to thank you for your prophetic good wish. Emmi also graciously recommends herself. Your friend from the heart, Caroline P. Is v. Hoven still in Nuremberg?

Regarding Fragments, I am not far from providing new ones, but only for ancient Philosophy. I would include my two biographies of Xenophanes and Zeno, which I sent to you. Did you receive them? You should certainly point out their defects to me, for I am going to reproduce them, and I could still benefit from your critiques. I am staying in Paris during these holidays and I intend to use them for the publication of these new Fragments. And you, what are you doing during these holidays? How are you? What have you done? And where does Philosophy stand in Berlin? I have rarely seen Mr. Michelet, whom I found very formalistic. He did not seek me out much, and I did not have the time to run after him. I hope that Gans and Hotho, if they return, will be less flighty. Tell them kindly that they will always find me the same. Van-Gheert, who is mad about philosophy and your philosophy, wrote to me that you authorized him to ask me for Hotho's notebooks. I therefore sent them to him. But please tell Hotho clearly that I released nothing except under the positive assurance required and given that you authorized Van-Gheert. My responsibility is saved. I thank you for this communication, which reminded me of Berlin and of conversations whose memory is very dear to me.

The fault is, apart from the noted compliance of the Curator, that there are too few dissenters here (Leonhard means well by us, but keeps to a neutral stance), and that Daub is too passive in practical matters. He always thinks that, if he quietly despises that empiricism here as if it did not exist at all, that is enough. This is recently the history of my total defeat. — I console myself with the quiet study of Plato, Aristotle, and the others — but I cannot conceal two things: that I now feel your loss doubly — we two would have unseated the Munkians — and that, if I could come to a university — where it would be better, and where the wine would not be too expensive — I would leave here today.

What happened? The Empiricists allied themselves with Paulus and the young Voß; they declared that they had been appointed by the government as editors for six years, and that they had signed the contract with Oswald. Yes, Paulus even threatened the Curator with a lawsuit before the Grand Ducal Government—and they prevailed. Munke is the general editor, and Paulus and Voß direct the rest (Schlosser, Daub, and Thibaut no longer review anything at all). Now Paulus had a complaint against me inserted in the Yearbooks, because he felt offended by a passage in the preface to the 4th volume of the Mythology—and the Curator allowed this article to pass censorship. But now you should see the arrogance with which the insignificant Munke puffs himself up, and how he, together with the other Physicists, mocks in societies everything that is not empiricism in their manner; how Goethe is no poet, Seebeck and other genius men are no scholars, etc. etc.

Most venerable Professor,

Please forgive me for daring to appear before you in writing once again. I now have a double reason for doing so. First, I cannot refrain from respectfully offering you my congratulations on the Royal honor that has been bestowed upon you, for I took all the more lively part in your elevation to the rank of Knight, as I consider it an external recognition of your principles regarding the general estate (§ 205 et seq.). You will therefore certainly excuse me if, in relation to this event concerning your person, I enclose a small occasional piece on the Order of the Red Eagle, which I hastily composed a year or two ago for my father’s official jubilee. I would have presented it to you along with my congratulations earlier, had I not simultaneously wished, secondly, to add the Herald’s voice to Goethe’s Faust, which I can only send to you today, and to which I most humbly recommend your kind indulgence. These sheets were written three years ago; I lacked the time to revise them thoroughly; nevertheless, they seemed to me to contain moments that might be worth sharing, and therefore I preferred to let them go out in this imperfect form rather than have them lost entirely.

The work I hinted at to you earlier, which I cannot contemplate without a sense of fear because it exceeds my powers, is an investigation into magic that has been pursued for several years and is now in the painful throes of birth. Circumstances compel me to submit even the unfinished work, and if it is then only a seven-month-old infant, that it may at least last a while and have a slight effect. In itself, such an investigation must proceed hand in hand with your Phenomenology of Spirit; any other treatment is merely a collection of materials. You will find what I was able to accomplish and judge it fairly. Everything rests on the fundamental idea that the temporal, the finite, the becoming, and whatever else it is called, is the Eternal itself, which is engaged in its development, education, and self-recognition, and that the unfathomable Spirit must individualize and shape itself in infinite and infinitely diverse, but most sharply graspable within itself, moments, whereby just as many kinds of one-sidedness and enchantment become possible and effective, all of which lie on the path of the development of the Spirit and must find their discussion through the investigation, from the first full magical power of the Impenetrable (Nature, which wells up everywhere) over man, through the isolation and entanglement of the moments, to the penetration, transfiguration, and complete magical power of the Spirit itself, which dissolves all enchantment and is clear and free life itself. That in such an investigation the most peculiar and notorious stuff occurs, which requires great dexterity in treatment, you easily understand, as well as that with proper treatment and understanding of the matter, something great must come out for the true liberation of man from himself. Consider now how my heart trembles in the face of such a task and how I never approach the work except with fear, and yet I would like to do something according to my powers, especially for the instruction of educators and physicians.

Mr. Brendel brought me, encouraged me to write to you, which I am further compelled to do by something else. For I have been in one of the worst states of mind for about 14 days, into which I was thrown by a nearly apoplectic fit. My already oppressive situation thereby became a rock on my chest: a deep hypochondria and almost half-paralysis had taken possession of me; everything I have pursued and written disgusts me, and least of all would I have undertaken a work, of which I shall yet speak to you. I must get rid of this tiresome state, and I cannot do so more thoroughly than by forcibly casting aside everything else and again devoting myself solely to science, and now, studying the System of Science anew, no longer hesitating to consult its author and to learn from him, according to his serious and clear understanding, whether he considers what I wish to hint at here worthy of being carried out, or not. In any case, you will heal me if you tell me the truth unreservedly: for you do not believe how deeply I feel that I have done and can do so little useful, and how very much I wish to begin all study again from the beginning, in order to pursue it now more to my satisfaction.

Dear Friend! I may well address you thus, for the former is truly earnest with me, and the latter may well be spoken when one finds that they have long been one in the most essential respects. I have long wished to tell you this and much more, and I have once already spoken with you through Schubert (though I am uncertain whether he delivered my greeting and errand); yet I always doubted that I possessed anything worthy of being disclosed to you. Now, however, you have, through the friendly greeting that you

The study of your System of the Will has convinced me that this work will one day, when the time of understanding comes, be regarded as the elementary book of the liberation of man, as the key to the new Gospel of which Lessing foretold. You naturally understand what I mean by this, but recognize also what this work is to me (not as a writing, but as a work) and that few have felt it so deeply. I wanted to say this aloud and publicly and could only hint at it, as I was denied the acceptance of my entire review (this was what I had Schubert report to you) and so the view of the matter stands unfinished). I therefore enclose the reflections on the preface and the significance of the whole work that remained with me, all the more so as in the latest philosophical piece of the Heidelberg Yearbook, p. 149, a Dr. Bachmann unknown to me speaks of me so unjustly, that I must have had good reasons to remain silent about that preface. I have sent a note to Heidelberg in which I declare myself on this matter and state plainly: the coldness toward everything philosophical prevented the printing of the whole in Jena. I will get into trouble over this with the excellent Mr. Eichstädt, but that does no harm, he must know it once, for it is not the first time: the review of Schelling’s work was arbitrarily mutilated and torn apart for me. And then that frivolous defamation by Dr. Bachmann now stirs me more keenly than before. Send me back the enclosed sheets soon with your judgment on them. Naturally, my review would have been more thorough had I studied the matter more often. Now I believe I understand you and hold to this understanding as a special comfort.

The present work now (according to the preface:) serves partly as a corrective, partly as a justification of my earlier work. * As I no longer have a copy of it at my disposal, but rather a kind of systematized compilation of the main ideas in that work (though the chain of thought from the theory of self-consciousness has turned out too meager in it): I am so free as to let this literary work follow here. And, alas! once again in a form dictated by the taste of my surroundings, which, for spirits formed in your school, is likely to have little appeal. Nevertheless, I do not insist at all that one of yours (much less you yourself, great teacher) should waste your precious time reading a southern product, of which you are perhaps convinced in advance: rather a stumbling block for your master than building materials for your system. I said: “that I do not insist”; indeed! because with the sending of these lines and their attachment I intend nothing else: but to give room to the feeling of gratitude in my heart towards you, most worthy master! For once again let it be said: I owe you much! And should the mood strike you to convince yourself of this, the end of my work before its beginning might give you more insight than the beginning without its end.

However, I shall always be grateful for any remark from you or from your side; because I assume so much honesty on your part that none of you will join in the usual chatter (which brands me as an idealizing theologian of my church or as a theological speculator for it). To that end, I only wish to add: that I was by no means (as is indeed often the case) sent on travels to the land of philosophy by Catholic theology (at regimental expense); but rather, conversely, the sense for serious research from childhood brought me, the prodigal son of the time, to results in speculation that compelled me (just as my life circumstances (I was a tutor in an Austrian princely house) changed) to take the sacraments in the church. So much from my life; and it is not fiction but truth.

It is therefore now most gratifying to us that the Burschenschaft here has now been completely uprooted. New laws, which are being prepared, will also make its return impossible, and to the satisfaction of all the other students, who had previously had to suffer infinitely under the arrogance of the presumptuous ones. The Prussians have conducted themselves so nobly on this occasion that they cannot be praised enough. An hour ago I received the news that your excellent wife is here. I hastened to her at once. What joy! If you see Gans, please give him my warmest greetings. For six months I had been trying to write to him properly, but one hindering day after another kept pressing in. I repeat here at the end, once more and most urgently, the request with which I began this letter, as your most devoted from the bottom of my heart, A. F. Thibaut.

Mr. v. Henning, however, should in my opinion appear somewhat more vigorously, and at least properly reprimand such presumptuous fellows as the reviewer of his *Principles of Ethics* in the *Hermes* (I know of no other work by him), whom I have also kept in view a few times. In the meantime, I also regret having received the second edition of your *Encyclopedia* only after the completion of my work and even only after the dispatch of the preface; the character of calmness that spreads over the part of the introduction now added would have had an influence on me as well. However, irony, which I have not omitted here and there, may also have its good side. — One of the most difficult pieces in your Logic, as I am happy to admit, was always for me, perhaps due to an error of conception at the first attempt, the treatment of pure reflection and its movement, which precedes the treatment of the determinations of reflection, whereas in its concrete occurrence in the doctrine of Essence it had much fewer difficulties for me. Therefore, before I was yet clear in all details with your presentation, I took an attempt, on the occasion of a note where I nevertheless wished to clear up this subject, to develop and deduce the matter for myself, and, after having done this, also believed to see everything clearly only with you. You will surely see this approach and attempt in my presentation; but it would please me if you find that I have come closer to the track of these thought-tricks and windings. — I would also have to apologize that I have not dedicated my work to you above all others; however, I did not want to set you the judgment of your own work, and wish to please you once with something else, which you should not be able to vindicate so closely to yourself. What I owe you in philosophy, i.e., everything and myself, I have gratefully acknowledged in the preface.

Honorable and deeply revered Teacher and Friend in Science! If one of your oldest students finally makes a public appearance in a larger work, and strives to accomplish something on the path of science that you have shown, it is perhaps time that he does so and, in the testimony of science, also gives testimony from you; but it is also to be wished that, the longer he has remained silent and restrained himself, the better the matter may have been digested in him, and that it not come to light as a still disorderly fermenting agent. The accompanying first part of a larger work I have in mind, which comes to you like a grandson to a grandfather, and in its pure piety also seeks and appeals for a benevolent reception in the spirit of family love, may now justify itself before you for its genuine descent, and will do so if the father is a true son. I will therefore not make many words about it. You will find that I immediately ventured, for my beginning, on your Phenomenology, at least a part of it, and have worked after you, with what freedom and independence and with what success, I await your gracious judgment. It seemed to me that the investigation should be directed immediately with all emphasis on the truth of knowledge in and for itself, especially against those who are unable to detach themselves from external objects and representation, and I have therefore particularly highlighted this side from the very beginning, also with the help of external reflection, that, however we may arrange ourselves, we can never escape the fate of having the objects differently than we know them, and therefore consciousness only needs to satisfy itself and to take care of the inner truth of its knowledge. I have therefore still had much to do with the old opponents, with Krug’s, Fries’s and similar philosophy, which in these lands is still considered great wisdom by many, and with the Rationalists, while figures like Mr. Schleiermacher, and especially Mr. Tholuck, seem to have had even less success with us.

Knight) has recently written to me again, and first announces two letters to Abbot Amoretti, which are to be printed shortly, and soon thereafter his journal: “The Siderism, or New Contributions to a Closer Knowledge of Galvanism” is to begin. He has now also received confirmation of his discovery from Winterl, Hauy, Orstedt, Hülsen, etc. The latest result is as follows: “That the will of the experimenter, and without the need for any mixed-in assistance, can become the complete substitute for external stimuli, and that it, in the form of premonition, conjecture, wish, and pre-determination of the outcome from any theory, and in how many other forms still, is so easily achieved in the ordinary experiments with pendulum, wand, balance, etc. Hence the difficulty of finding faithful mere organs of nature, hence the ease of being so easily exposed to deceptions, confused outcomes; hence the best means for the one who wants to become a mere deceiver. And yet in all of it nothing but the most brilliant confirmation of a long-fermenting principle in physics and physiology, namely this: that the stimulus of the will has equal dignity with the ordinary physical one.” Hereby he reminds me of the electric fishes and what he had already said earlier in his Contributions, last delivery. — He is also on the way to objectively demonstrate the power of the will. “Already, he says, I have reached the point where, for frog preparations of a specific stage of excitability, I can place my fingers different, indifferent, or conversely different, by the mere will. But that is only a beginning, and once I am finished with the “real” side, I will also further cultivate this “ideal” one.” — On this occasion he does not hide from me either that he is convinced that so much secret mistrust may have taken possession of me. But he knows how not only to remove it, but also to explain it, and tells me that I will be satisfied with him, especially if it leads to things that few would even suspect now. He is currently reading a private course on the physiological part of Galvanism to Mr. Jacobi, Schenk, Schelling, Baader, etc. Have you already heard news from Niethammer in Munich? I hear that it is supposed to be very expensive there still.

I shall probably not leave Jena until peace, which hopefully will not be long in coming after such decisive battles, is achieved, nor shall I make any decision regarding my future place of residence. I am to convey many greetings to you from my wife and also from the children, as well as from Maj. v. Knebel, who was just with me and who specifically instructed me to ask you to devote yourself to humanities, i.e., letter-writing, rather than to philosophy; for the latter helps him nothing, and he longs for news from you. I also ask you to write to me again soon, and if you wish to write something truly pleasant to me, let it be that you are returning to us soon. Your faithful friend Th. Sk. Do you already know that Reizenstein has had to hand over the curatorship of the University of Heidelberg again? This frequent change will certainly not serve to strengthen the confidence of the gentlemen professors there. Do not make any inconvenience for yourself regarding the money. Farewell.

And so let our effort be directed not merely to today and the passing morning, but to that true morning or spring of spirits, and we shall gladly console ourselves if you do not understand us, you who, still entirely bound in time, must still await deliverance from your whirlpools, well knowing and considering that for these too that morning of eternity will one day dawn. — Besides, it is of course true that for us this light can at first only powerfully emerge from the earlier mist of things, and not everything and anything can immediately stand before our eyes in the same clarity and distinctness of form, which I must at least say to myself, because I see how we, though very much in agreement in the principles, do not always meet in exactly the same way in some further downward-lying consequence. — Let us only remain faithful to that duty of strictness in the innermost spirit! Then everything will one day again arrange itself properly, and science will continue and complete its victory! Your friend will tell you more about my activity here and its hindrances and cares. But his participation and yours have given me new courage, and so I will faithfully continue my daily work; — and the rest and more external — Gecor With heartfelt affection, yours J. E. Berger.

Your letter reached me here, and after careful consideration, I will send it accompanied by a letter to Schuckmann, but I will have it delivered by my friend Link, who, as I know from him, has voted in favor of your appointment to Berlin. What effect this may have is entirely uncertain; in no case will it be harmful, since the occasion of the essay as well as its promotion is entirely harmless. More important is the content itself, and of this I must believe that it will appeal favorably to the Minister; first, because I have come to know him closely for years in very manifold relationships; second, I must judge so because your views have appealed to me so much. — In general, after reading your essay, it struck my conscience as if I had had merely selfish intentions in the whole proposal; for undeniably I gain first and most. Admittedly, the new turn of philosophy has produced so many ideas and views that do not want to fit into the old framework, and which, if merely mechanically mixed with the old, give only a bad porridge, no substantial nourishing food. Now those (there are probably only a few left) who strictly adhere to the old are as wrong as those who reject it entirely; at least both appear to me equally inadmissible given the historical direction of my mind. A twofold task would seem necessary, namely a scientifically strict processing of the present, now become living, and the remaining living material into a strictly closed whole, so that the hovering and mistiness and the pretentious, contentless arbitrariness may cease, and the law may prescribe a true course to the overestimated forces acting eccentrically in individual directions. Furthermore, we need a historical demonstration of the course of development and how we have come to the present position. For Greek philosophy, the necessity and naturalness of all stages and turns is certainly very beautifully to be demonstrated, even if it has not yet been done; for the modern, it may be harder, but if one does not lay too much weight on the small pertinence pieces which make exaggerated claims to entirely peculiar and full sovereignty, it should be possible and certainly very instructive.

Especially harmful is the current presumptuous dominance of craft-like letter-philology, which, as you rightly observe, can only be the first stage, and which, without historical and philosophical illumination, with its petty pedantry, becomes a true bloodsucker of all youthful energy. I have already had many disputes about this, even in professional relationships, and I would have been even more severely criticized if I had not fortunately also once passed through these philological antechambers—though only run through them. Personally, I was especially pleased by your highlighting of the Philosophy of Spirit alongside the Philosophy of Nature; for while the magnet and the galvanic battery had gained so much space, it seemed that no place was left for the former, and while scientific physics expanded to infinity, at least many students never thought of clarifying the secrets of their own breast. Nothing, for example, is now more generally neglected at universities than the study of ethics, and although many so-called scholars were willing to sacrifice and did sacrifice their lives for the state, they lacked the first concepts of state and church.

I break off so as not to weary you with attempts to acquire your own views by learning them; it is also externally difficult at this moment, as on the left a wretched singer and on the right the servant beating out the skirts are doing violence to my ears. I very much wish, however, that with this one letter our relationship not be entirely ended and dissolved. After the current wandering about, more lasting rest should set in, and I intend to let it rest with this second journey, just as with the first journey description. When this comes into your hands, think of me kindly in connection with it. My traveling companions recommend themselves to you and your dear wife just as I do. Your exceedingly kind reception gave the stay in Nuremberg the best charm, and we shall gladly look back on those evenings in favorable and unfavorable circumstances. v. Raumer.

A great advantage of our apartment is that it is excellently situated for optical experiments, in which, as is known, we are very strong. We have already observed the moon and light shadows in their full beauty. Only without the moonlight does the experiment not yet succeed for us. Please occasionally ask our countryman Pfaff where the error lies. Privy Councillor von Bajard smoked his pipe with us last Sunday and drank a glass of beer with it. He is as jolly as a bachelor, not a misanthrope, and hopes that the seat of the local district will soon be moved back to Nuremberg.

Ungstein, near Dürkheim in the Royal Bavarian [region].

Most reverently honored Professor!

From a great distance, I allow myself to recall my remembrance of you. The accompanying work is the first literary product to appear under my name. To whom could I send it sooner as proof of my deepest respect and veneration than to you, the man who has so decisively influenced my education and under whose beneficial guidance I first learned to truly love science? I give myself up to the friendly hope that you will graciously accept and judge with forbearance the modest gift of your former pupil, who will never cease to be devoted to you with his whole soul. I have investigated impartially, and what I have found, I have spoken without fear. That your spirit, i.e., the spirit of true scientificity, has not entirely departed from me, I may believe all the more, as the disposition of my work, it seems to me, belongs to it, while especially the sixth section is rooted in it. If I mentioned your revered name here and there and allowed myself in the cited section to hint at your great merits for science and its construction, this was done on the one hand because I found in you the most distinguished authority for my view, and on the other hand because I wanted to declare myself without fear against the shallowness of many speakers of our days. If the views set down in my work, and especially the laws of scientific progress followed therein, were to receive your approval even in general, this would be the most beautiful reward for me. The longer I occupy myself with science, the dearer it becomes to me; but unfortunately, my external circumstances are not the most favorable for its cultivation. Crushed by a rather protracted illness, I had to give up my teaching position in Speyer five years ago and withdraw to the country. Here I now live (9 hours from Heidelberg on the Upper Rhine) in a very beautiful region, but almost excluded from all literary intercourse. My health has been restored, but the goal that I had earlier, encouraged by you, most honored Professor, set my eyes on, namely the goal of becoming an academic teacher, has receded further than before.

It is true that I might not find it so difficult to obtain an extraordinary professorship in my Bavarian homeland; but it is most likely that this would be without any salary at all, or with such a small one that I could not support my family. And yet, I am always drawn back to the lectern. It is an unpleasant situation. Do not take this confession amiss. I still see in you the dear teacher to whom I may speak openly. I intend to work diligently; perhaps I shall nevertheless reach the desired goal; if not, I have loved a friend in science who becomes lovelier every day and whose company continually attracts me more and more. — That Schuster, also one of your pupils, died in Paris, where he had stayed last year to continue his chemical studies, you have probably already learned. His unfortunate mother is profoundly depressed by this sad and unexpected event to everyone. Mr. Consistorial Councilor Schultz in Speyer is, as far as I know, quite well with his family. Last year he had joined with me in the editing of a theological-churchly journal, but special circumstances have delayed its publication until now. I close with the heartfelt wish that my lines may find you and your esteemed family in the best of health. With the highest respect and love, I am your revering J. Rust.

My heavy debts of correspondence must not carry over into the year 1816, which I would long since have gladly paid off, had I not been in the same situation as the father, who instructs me to tell you: he would certainly have written to you if he had known anything sensible. Unfortunately, I realize that if one were to wait for such things, one would have to give up writing altogether. It is truly no longer possible to expect any salvation from that arch-dull human race, especially since it has performed a somersault into German stupidity and has adorned itself with crosses of all kinds, by which no devils can be exorcised; or if even one is exorcised, 1,000 others and worse ones come back, and one is in a worse state than before.

Faster than I thought possible, your matter has been decided. I have the order to inform you that you have been appointed Professor of the philosophical preparatory sciences and at the same time Rector of the Gymnasium in Nuremberg, and that it is desired that you arrange your journey so that you arrive in Nuremberg, where your presence will be urgently required, at the beginning or at the latest in the middle of the following week, in order to put into effect, under the guidance of Mr. District School Councilor Paulus, the new study organization, insofar as it concerns the Gymnasium. I wish myself, you, and the matter good luck, and remain with the known sentiments of high respect, your devoted Niethammer, K. B. Senior School Councilor. P. S. I request you to issue a similar one in my name to Mr. Huscher in Wartenfels.

With sincere gratitude for the interest you take in Schubart’s fate, I have informed this distinguished man, though somewhat diminished by certain peculiarities, of this. How grateful and willing he is to avail himself of the favor shown to him is evident from the enclosed letter. Whether it would be advisable to fulfill the wishes he has expressed, I leave to your kind judgment, and therefore ask for some gracious instruction. The previous delay is thereby explained and, I hope, excused. Please have the kindness to continue to maintain the favorable disposition initiated for his benefit. He is one of the younger men whom I still wish to see introduced into civil daily life.

I read your literary papers with great interest, although, as you know my sentiments and views, you will easily imagine that I shake my head here and there. This much-praised self-knowledge has, for some time now, led only to self-torment and self-destruction, without the slightest practical advantage in life having resulted from it. The Weimar friends of literature and art are preparing something that I have all the more reason to share sooner or later, as, owing to a heavy burden of work, the next piece on art and antiquity will be delayed longer than usual.

What is happening in Spain, and what is now happening in England, you will be able to inform us about better than I can write to you. Our Hereditary Prince, who recently intended to pay a visit to Emperor Napoleon in Paris, first learned in Mainz that the latter had already departed for Italy. On the day of his return, Prince William of Prussia arrived in Weimar, who also had intended to go to Paris. He has now departed for Homburg. Goethe has been here for 14 days, and I see him often. Seebeck is also often with us.

September. I am entirely at your disposal, and I leave the plan for this campaign to you. Just count on my punctuality. On the day, at the agreed hour, I shall be wherever you please. The best, certainly, would be to come to Paris. If I spoke to Gans, I would tell him: put yourself in Berlin by diligence on the 1st of Sept., on the 10th you will be in Paris. You will stay there 15 or 20 days and on the 1st of Oct. you will be in Brussels. We will remain a dozen days in Holland and the Netherlands and on the 15th of Oct. you will be in Berlin. But this rapidity and this precision of movements would tire you too much, and if you come to Paris, count on a journey of two months. You cannot do it in less. But why would you not put this time into it? I would take great pleasure in showing you the honors of Paris, dear Hegel. You will stay at my house, you will lodge at my house and we will spend some more good fraternal days. You will have at your disposal my Governess who is German, my secretary who is German, and me who loves you with all my heart. I would see you off via Brussels to the banks of the Rhine. But for all this, it is necessary to leave Berlin in the first days of September. For later Belgium would no longer be very beautiful; and the coolness of the evenings could do you harm, and the slightest worry of good Madame Hegel would weigh on my conscience. In any case, tell me promptly your intentions.

Please thank Madam Milder very tenderly for me and tell her that I still love her just as much. You do not speak of Madam Bloch. She no longer writes to me, and I am anxious about everything that concerns her. Please tell me a word about her. Why would she not also go to Ems? Now, a few lines about Philosophy. Do not fail to send me the notebooks of Mr. Hotho via Mr. Panofka. My young German will copy them, and I am awaiting your Encyclopedia. I will always catch something from it and try to fit some scraps of your great thoughts to my size. An article by your hand on my Fragments would please me greatly, and I do not consider myself discharged of this debt. Congratulate me on having finished Proclus. The sixth volume must have reached you with a piece on Eunapius. But all my efforts are concentrated on Plato: it is on this card that I stake my philosophical reputation; and I also stake my determination to complete such a painful undertaking. Within a month, a new volume will appear, which I will send to you via the uncle of Mr. Hotho. I want you to have my entire translation before your eyes so that you may tell me your opinion frankly. I do not say goodbye to you, and I await a word from you promptly.

Most Honored Professor! The great kindness you showed me during my all too brief stay in Berlin made it my duty for a long time to express my heartfelt thanks to you. But since even in the realm of freedom an external occasion must not be lacking, I believe I have found one in the sending of the enclosed small treatise, which, although written in a language that you perhaps do not read, nevertheless rightfully belongs to you; for you frequently find your writings cited in it, and whatever good may be in it belongs to you more than to myself. It concerns a dispute over freedom and necessity, which is being conducted at this moment in Copenhagen, and that among very distinguished men, who, however, cling more or less to the abstract sides of the relationship, without being able to rise to the concrete of the concept, so that the whole dispute, as I have also noted in my treatise, resembles a carnal rebirth of the third Kantian antinomy. I therefore believed I was undertaking a not unmeritorious task by drawing the attention of the philosophers of my fatherland to the fact that they were moving in a circle, like mill-horses, without getting any further through their exertion; by trying to drive them out of their narrow circle into the domain of truth, which, according to my most intimate conviction, is to be sought and found only in the sphere of conceptual philosophy opened up by you, — a doctrine that does not yet seem to have spread to Denmark. I hope soon to be able to do more toward the same purpose, when my German-written outlines of the system of aesthetics, as a speculative science, which are being printed in Schleswig, come to light, a treatise for which I only regret that I know your interesting and deeply penetrating lectures on this subject only from imperfect lecture notes, which were shared with me in Berlin.

In earnest, I think it well that you have found such a resource in these times of bread, estate, and understanding scarcity, and I commend your undertaking. With wisdom, truly, little is served and few, and in the end best, when we serve ourselves. However much I am convinced of this truth, I do not see how I, who otherwise can serve myself and others little with wisdom, could be particularly serviceable to you, even without it.

Jena, September 11, 1807. Indeed, dear friend and philosopher, you have fulfilled our wish somewhat late; nevertheless, we were not entirely without news of you, and we rejoiced when we heard that you were well and that things were going well for you. It is therefore at least pleasing to us that we know you are well housed for the time being, and verily the heavenly nectar, or the Nepenthe, brewed in Bamberg, will not be of slight importance to our wishes for your well-being.

Indeed, dear friend, I think you should address your needs to Mr. Falke; he lives with several and many different people, and would probably be happy to take on your request. It seems to me that, under your supervision, he would be the man for it, and you could make use of him. Now I would rather speak with you about your latest philosophy—if only I had read it. Seebeck gave me the preface to it, and I admired your deep, thinking spirit. What remains a wish for me, and, it seems, for some friends as well, is that you had laid down the fine net of your thoughts, which at places appears clear and lovely, in a way that is sometimes more sensibly graspable for our duller eyes. Truly, we consider you one of the foremost thinkers of our time; but we wish that you had given more bodily form to your spiritual power. What I say here is perhaps bold, perhaps not sufficiently supported by reasons; but you must forgive a poetic wish, if I would also like to see the serious drawn over into the realm of the beautiful—without thereby just becoming a Lucretian didactic poem. Your similes are excellent, just like your thoughts.

The spouting and psychologizing by which one can so easily decompose the existing dogma tickles the self-love of the dullest and of those who have learned nothing most of all. Hence the running and pushing toward where one eats the broad prose with spoons—while the auditoriums of the others become emptier. Even Daub is no longer listened to so eagerly. Seeing this fuss—one would like to flee with the satirist beyond the glacial ocean. I am annoyed about it daily, although the nuisance affects me less directly. What the German (Stuttgart) Observer has been eager to report about me this winter will be known to you. But the following you do not know: that Voß has discovered it and has confidentially told the travelers how Daub and I have taken a professorship with a reservation and consequently belong to the secret converts, to whom it is permitted until a certain deadline to play Protestants, in order to work more effectively within the body of the heretical church to undermine Papism! You must tell this to the friend Marheinecke, and if he still accepts greetings from such crypto-Papists—you should also greet him very kindly on my behalf. He was called to Breslau in 1822 as extraordinary professor of philosophy on H.'s recommendation.

Most venerable Teacher and Friend! I take the liberty to use the occasion afforded by the submission of the review of Krug’s Fundamental Philosophy, i.e., Fundamental Unphilosophy and Folly, to enclose a few lines to you. — This book is a masterpiece of exemplary absurdity. I had to keep laughing while reading it, and therefore, in the review, I knew of nothing better to do with such incomprehensible stupidity—which, nevertheless, long deserves a strong reprimand and chastisement for its arrogance—than to play with it while laughing and to make fun of its author through continuous irony. If Mr. Kr.’s chatter and shouting should ever be taken into account, and if, in the first place, an external purpose is to be achieved with a not insignificant effect, I know no way I would consider more appropriate than the one I chose; I have partly turned the opponent’s own weapons against him, certainly sought to show him to be superior, but did everything in the impartiality that dialectic absolutely needs in order to become and remain master of the subject. However, it was necessary here to go through every particular and into everything, in order to let the worthless appear even in its own self-destruction; thereby, of course, the review has become somewhat long, longer than Mr. Kr. is worth considered in himself, especially since there is no question of a higher scientific interest in the matter anyway, and only this must be valid for it, that the unscientific shallowness and self-aggrandizing philosophical ignorance be given the proper defeat. However, if the tone and form of my work should cause some offense in the editorial office because of their unusualness, I ask you to take a little interest in the matter and to let your decision be applied; if one thing or another should be found too striking and strong, especially in a speech in which I let reason itself speak against Mr. Kr., I am by no means against such passages or expressions being struck out and replaced by something better, although I am ready to take everything upon myself and to fight it out. —

Yet it is noteworthy that the word of tradition has grown weaker; for indeed, this summer the little group of those who listen to Hinrichs has become smaller. It is admirable and truly touching to see the effort the man makes, and with what iron diligence he, for example, this winter, alongside his other tasks, has studied Greek philosophy and has patiently swallowed even the dryness of the verbal jargon with which I in the philological seminar handle and must handle the texts of the old philosophers. — But on the other hand, it is also not quite possible to see where it is all leading for him — his domestic and economic situation is strained — since I became his godfather together with Daub and Schlosser, I have come to know more about it. If he teaches with approval and success, as has generally been the case up to now, then those are — as and where you know — letters of disrecommendation, and the door to office and bread closes ever more tightly. This state of affairs is beginning to weigh on our hearts.

Natural Law, and you will prepare proper study weeks for the friend Daub, who often asks about it. I think it will now soon come to light, and as an outsider I shall at least have to rejoice over the embarrassments in which philosophers and jurists will find themselves. — I have established a regular factory of Greek and Roman gods. Do not be alarmed when next month you will receive a tenth volume of more than 1000 pages. It is just a lengthy business with all that mythological stuff. In the meantime, I have personally met Professor Ritter. A charming man. You will find that I have also read his writings. He is now going to Berlin, where southern Germany must deliver up its best heads. — But our Professor Cousin has not behaved nicely toward me. What good do all the flatteries do? — You know, of course, that he himself said he understands no Greek. Now he demanded of me a) that I hand over my collections on Proclus to him — for 500 florins — without the trouble — b) that I find him a German publisher so that he could publish Proclus. I thought that no answer is also an answer, and had an announcement printed. Now he comes with his Latin translations of pieces of Proclus — most of which are in Fabricius — sends out I do not know what from Tiedemann and Tennemann — and assures the public that my Proclus will not appear in eternal time. I therefore had to tell the public that indeed my edition is being printed, and that Mr. Cousin assures more than he can know and about which no one has asked him. You will receive this Greek book in the autumn, and I ask for a kind reception. — My wife has again endured a hard sickbed. The other acquaintances and I myself have remained healthy. Farewell. With heartfelt greetings from Daub and Schlosser. Your Creuzer.

Schlosser thinks he should go home, that a nourishing position is certainly waiting for him there, and that it offers him enough leisure to make himself known through writings, which could secure him appointments. For the time being, he intends to try his hand at writing here. — Things looked more cheerful recently in Stuttgart. We were four (Daub, Thibaut, Leonhard, and I) who went over during the Easter holidays, and were witnesses to the wedding festivities. The Boisserés are established in the most proper manner, and everything around them looks quite royal, including the livery servants who are subject to them; and the pictures are distributed in a splendid suite throughout the palace. There is no lack of good hosts either — but all three are ailing, and especially Bertram has not yet quite accustomed himself.

Here, where I am so close to Berlin that it is hardly possible to be closer in Bavaria, this neighborhood alone might prompt me to remind you, my dear friend, once again of myself and of us. However, this accidental circumstance would not be enough to break such an outdated and almost hardened silence, if I were not at the same time particularly occupied with you here. You will hardly guess what I might still have to do with you today on a commission trip in Bavaria, so I will simply say at once that my traveling companion is your Natural Law. Even if I am only left with an occasional isolated hour for conversation with this traveling companion, it is still more than I was allowed at home. But the main thing is that I prefer this conversation to any other I find on this trip. First of all, I delight in the sharpness and penetrating nature, and I take pleasure in the paragraphs that are such as Jacobi wished them to be from you). Of course, he would not have found all of them corresponding to his wish, but much, even in the stricter form, would have pleased him as well. I would certainly have many things to ask, if it were so easy to ask and answer in such close proximity; but with all the hesitation I may find, I tell myself that it was time to deal with the dullness and flatness, not only of our political schemers, but of our political scientists themselves, and if you do not deserve thanks from these, you are all the more certain of it from others. — That Julius has not yet personally thanked you for this gift, please excuse him. It was truly, I can testify, his serious intention to write to you through the Dane Hjort — who must have been with you in the meantime and will have greeted and spoken of us — but since he is to be forcibly absorbed by the Chamber of Finance, he has so much to do to assimilate himself that he truly deserves an excuse.

If a young man from here, Mr. Simrock, should attend your lectures or seek your acquaintance, I ask that you receive him well. He is a diligent, estimable man; not a talent of distinction, but good, and I should like him to be protected by a higher interest from the idleness of the jurist’s life, and to come, on the path of serious thinking, to the insight that he still lacks something essential and that he must spend his life inquiring into and working on himself... We greet you all from the heart. I am, with reverence and friendship, yours, Windischmann. One more thing! I recently told the young Dr. Esser, who now seems to be turning to me with confidence, how senseless his attack on your logic had been (namely in his so-called System of Logic). He seemed to see it too, and I hope he improves.

In Paris, a certain faction was preparing a sort of ovation for me, which I refused for more than one reason. I found everyone furious against Prussia. They would have liked me to thunder a pamphlet against it and its police. Certainly, I do not like this police; but after having been moderate towards it in Berlin, it did not suit me to suddenly take it into my head to get angry in Paris, 300 leagues from the danger. I therefore remained calm, free in my remarks, according to my principles and my habits; but without violence. I even dared to say that life in Berlin was quite bearable, and this caused great outcry, especially from a Prussian, full of genius, if you will, but mean and troublesome, who would have been delighted if I had turned all of Berlin into ridicule. Finally, for fifteen days I surprised and displeased the lovers of scandal. Then everything passed as everything passes in Paris.

As for the government, I will tell you that it has been satisfied with my conduct there and here. Mr. de Damas understood me and does me justice. He has even managed to obtain from one of his colleagues that next year, at the start of the term (for we are now on vacation), I be placed back on the Faculty list, which I desired, as you know. If this comes to pass, and there is every appearance of it, I shall be as before, and that is all I need for the moment. But do you believe that Mr. de Damas has not yet been able to obtain a copy of my examinations? The finest letters are written to him on my account; but no examinations. I insist, and I will always insist. But I doubt that the ordinary slowness of your Minister will match my impatience. You know that the French Government has made a decisive publication regarding me in the Moniteur, and if it restores me to my former situation, it is doing all that is in its power. Between us, I add that Mr. de Damas made me offers which I had to reject, but which at least prove his goodwill. Let us wait, and not anticipate the future. Farewell, my dear friend, I have only space left to ask you to convey my greetings to the good Mrs. Hegel, and our excellent friend Bloch.

However, you understand that my true friends, Human and Royer Collard, approved of my conduct, and with them the very small number of statesmen of the opposition; except for the intriguers and the meddlers and some false friends who had been looking for some time for pretexts of ingratitude and betrayal; the public, which does not stop at the chatter of cliques, has understood the whole of my conduct. This whole affair has proved two things, that I was invariably attached to the cause of liberty, but that no one was able to drag me into any folly. Those who, by their denunciations, have provoked this persecution against me, and those who hoped to exploit my resentments, are discouraged by the firmness and moderation of my attitude; and in general my situation is approximately what you could wish for me in my country, and with my principles, which are still, my wise friend, a little younger than yours.

Passing through Leipzig, I instructed my bookseller’s agent to send you a copy of my edition of Descartes. Did he do so? I also instructed him to send a copy to Mr. de Henning, to whom I wrote a covering letter from Fulda, with a thousand thanks for all the care he had shown me in Berlin, and the request that I be remembered to his charming wife, to Mr. and Mrs. Forster, and to Mr. Michelet. I fear that Hesse has kept my note, and I ask you to serve as my interpreter with Mr. de Henning and his friends. In Weimar, I saw Goethe once, who received me because of you, although he was ill; I was deeply touched by this, and I thank you for it. In Frankfurt, I sought out Carové, who remains very attached to you, although he has somewhat departed from your philosophical method. One may have a more extensive and firmer understanding; one cannot have more loyalty and a better heart. I love him very sincerely. I also found Mr. de Rheinardt in Frankfurt, who overwhelmed me. He taught me much about my situation; and Humann in Strasbourg gave me new insights, so that I arrived in Paris with a preconceived notion and a plan made: I followed it inflexibly.

It has been generally suspected that I did not quietly sever my family ties in Berlin—that I even demanded my dismissal. However, a quiet resolution was impossible.... I had to leave—I say this still now, after having had nearly five weeks to consider, and after having enjoyed Jena’s mountain air and Jena’s riding track for four weeks for the pleasure of body and mind. I demanded my dismissal out of a kind of cowardice, if I am to call the thing by its proper name. In Berlin, namely, I could not stay—the manner of my

Since I am once again in the position of having to justify my conduct, I cannot refrain from mentioning an accusation that has been made against me from Berlin. I have been charged with a lack of propriety for not stating the true reason for my departure from Berlin in my letter to the Minister, in which I requested my dismissal. A simple and natural line of reasoning would have stopped at the fact that, once I had achieved what I wanted, I had no interest whatsoever in exposing the details of family circumstances in an indiscreet manner in an official petition.

The departure left me, regarding what was to happen to me next, at the discretion of the Minister, if I wished to remain in Prussia — since I was now far too proud not to have been half dead with anger had they, after I had become an Extraordinary Professor in Berlin, offered me an extraordinary professorship at another university, perhaps even in Greifswald — since, furthermore, for the present moment and for the next four or five years, as long as I had all the time to myself, I was financially completely secure, I preferred to cut off such humiliations by myself requesting my dismissal.

I have also (which has likewise been said of me) made no reproaches to Herr von Altenstein for not having enabled me to marry earlier — I had been in that state since Michaelmas without needing any further financial means; if I nevertheless sought them, it was partly out of reasonable consideration for the future, and partly out of a just pride; it must have incensed me to see myself paid, for having devoted half of my young and fresh strength to the scholarly day-labor of the library, like a secondary school student for private lessons; I felt something stirring within me, which one calls individual

Your Excellency, I feel compelled to express how much your letter has pleased me. That you so intimately penetrate my will and achievements, whatever they may be, and give them full, reasoned approval, is a great encouragement and benefit to me. Your letter arrived at precisely the right moment, as I, stirred by the latest treatment of entoptic colors, am once again reviewing my older chromatic papers and cannot help but feel that I must bring many matters closer to public view through careful editing.

Before the Gymnasium came the Progymnasium as a secondary school, just as the Real Institute was preceded by the Real or Burgher School, and as the first preparatory stage, a lower and upper primary school, which together with the Progymnasium represented the various classes of the modern Bavarian Latin school. Above the Gymnasia stood the Lyceums as the transitional stage to university studies, though not without special additional provisions: both for the completion of general education in general, and for instruction in theological special or professional studies. A special position among these was held by the Lyceum in Munich, which, as an educational institution replacing the general university section, was limited to philosophical and general subjects and was to be in connection with the Royal Academy of Sciences in Munich.

This is expressed from the outset in the following definitions: The Gymnasium Institute is to occupy its pupils primarily with scholarly language study and the introduction to the speculative study of ideas; the Real or physico-technical Institute is to occupy its pupils primarily with scholarly subject study and the contemplative study of ideas. For the Gymnasium, as is still the case in Bavaria today, a four-year course of instruction was prescribed, according to the division into Upper, Middle, and Lower classes, with two years allotted to the Middle class, or in four classes, where the Middle class was divided into two as lower and upper, as this, however, occurred only at the Gymnasium in Munich.

Mephistopheles (meaning the late Mother) must transform himself for you into a female Martha (or 1I 2). Otherwise, with all the gold of the — School Fund! — you could not make ends meet here. She intends, however, to inquire after a very slow-moving Nuremberg woman. The gentlemen Idealists keep us, from above, completely pure from all that material, dirty business of Mammon. God damn all the Idealism. To Mr. GR. v. Bayard, Fuchs, Huscher, and all friends, including female friends — the most suitable. Your Am. On the margin is written in the hand of Mrs. Paulus: Emmi is very sensitively offended that you are putting off your coming here for so long. I will say nothing about myself. Hnns Unglüg! The value is worn out and written illegibly. She is the owner of the Bamberg newspaper, Paulus's wife, Karoline. Syriac: the thousands or the mistress (Prof. Aug. Köhler). P. Beautiful and talented daughter, Sophie Karoline Eleutherie, born 1791, first called Karolinchen in the family, then Emmi, later Sophie. See about her Reichlin-Meldegg, Paulus and his Time 1, 429.

Today the Emperor visits the battlefield of Jena and will take breakfast on the Napoleon Hill, where he bivouacked on the night from the 13th to the 14th of October, from where a hare hunt will also be prepared for him in the area around Apolda. The sky favors these pleasures, for we have had the most beautiful weather since today and yesterday, such as we have not had for a long time. Farewell! P.S. I wrote the above, dear friend, this morning, still rather tired, only in a hurry. Use from it what you may deem good — only do not compromise me in any way! — Afternoon. Seebeck has just returned from the Napoleon Hill, who sends you his warmest greetings, and has seen Emperor Napoleon and the other high dignitaries there again. The former was exceedingly kind, and showed Emperor Alexander from the height of the hill the arrangements that had been made during the battle. He has also, it is said, promised the local deputies to replace the damage which the city suffered at that time through the fire. At the hunt itself, the Emperor is said to have been very cheerful. A small temple had been erected on the height of the hill for the Emperor — although only of wood, for we do not have marble here, nor the means for it — where the breakfast was taken. The wretched epigram on it, which our pedants set, I will only recite to you, but do not let it become known further!! Praesentes Divos nune prisca Thuringia junxit, En novus attonitos junget amor populos 1IIII! It is supposed to be an acrostic! Forgive my haste!

Dear Friend, I am just returning this morning from Weimar, where I was yesterday to see the arrival of the great Emperor Napoleon and the other monarchs and princes who now shine under the Thuringian sky. A hunt on the Ettersberg was prepared for the great Emperor Napoleon before his arrival in Erfurt; the Ettersberg, as you know, lies on the road from there, about an hour and a half from Weimar. Both emperors, for the Russian one has also been in Erfurt for several days, arrived together in a four-horse open carriage, preceded by the Duke of Weimar, accompanied by a very brilliant retinue, at about two o'clock at the scheduled driven hunt, where a spacious canopy had been erected quite elegantly and appropriately for the high guests. The other monarchs soon followed, among whom I particularly noticed the King of Bavaria, the King of Saxony, and Württemberg. All eyes were fixed on the great emperors, and especially on Napoleon, who, by the sight of a great, thinking, ever-active man, although in simple attire, inspired the entire crowd. One also admired the grace and condescension of Emperor Alexander; so that one could say without exaggeration that one saw in a single carriage together what the world can only show in high and crowned form.

University of France. Ministry of Public Instruction and Worship. Paris, October 15, 1831.

Here is another word from me, my dear friend, along with a small package that the Ministry will have delivered to you, and I ask you to distribute the various pieces exactly as follows. These pieces are: 1. For you, the sixth volume of Plato containing the Phaedrus, the Meno, and the Symposium, with a prospectus. 2. Also for you, the opinion of Mr. R. Collard on the hereditary nature of the Peerage.

Your valued letter of 9 March of this year. As I hoped, so it is. For the treatment of theological morality, your jurisprudence has the greatest consequences, but its effect also extends to dogmatic theology. If only some professional jurists (craft is what it is called in Hesse) had studied it as diligently as I have, the state of positive law would soon be quite different and better than it is now and has been until now. Had I been in Berlin this summer, I would, with your permission, have attended your lectures on the philosophy of religion. A single note to your philosophy of law on § 14 has accomplished more than I have with all my notebooks, entitled Judas Iscariot; hopefully you, dearest friend, will leave them unread, for what could possibly confront you from them, to where and beyond which you are not long since? And where was the logical method for me at that time? In your writings! Only since then have I, through unceasing study (not without great, sustained exertions for my aging), become somewhat master of it. I gave lectures on your Phenomenology this summer. I intend to work through the introduction to it during the vacations just beginning, and have it printed, in order, if possible, to bring the work to the theologians, who, without this science and its study, have nothing further in their theology than the bare name. The first volume of Schleiermacher’s Dogmatics has been in my hands for about 14 days. I have read the preface and table of contents; Creuzer (he is now on a trip to Ulm) shared your letter with me, in which you designate Dresden as the city in which we could, during the vacation time, perhaps most conveniently and most pleasantly meet together. I was in Karlsruhe when I received this letter, as a member of the Synod for the church union, and already looked forward with joy to our reunion. May we only bring the thought to execution! And why not? You have stimulated it, I will not give it up again. Heartfelt greetings from my family to you and your wife. With the most intimate reverence and love, your faithfully devoted Daub.

It was very pleasing to me to hear that you and your family are well; I had just previously heard that you were somewhat unwell. May God preserve you and allow you to work much longer for the promotion of the truth, in the knowledge of which you will surely come to know Him ever more intimately and devote yourself entirely to Him as His possession. The bearer of this letter is the nephew of Mrs. Hirn, Mr. Wilhelm Ludowigs from Cologne, the son of a pious family that does much good and is now the only support of the poor, oppressed woman...

Dearest Friend! Your kind letter of August 23rd, which was a true proof of your care for a poor suffering widow and no less of your friendly disposition toward me, gave me genuine joy, for which I thank you heartily. I have communicated the passage concerning Mrs. Hirn to her, and she was deeply moved and grateful for your efforts. These efforts seem already to have borne fruit, as the Crown Prince has inquired about the glass paintings. Up to now, an offer of 9,000 thalers has also been made from another source. I must also correct my previous statement regarding the valuation of 19,000 thalers, clarifying that this was not the judicial valuation, but one given by connoisseurs. I believe that everything will be sold for around 10,000 thalers. I must also note that the Crown Prince of Bavaria has also made an inquiry.

My own request, with which I wished to trouble you, is to have it inquired at the Royal Library there whether an editio princeps or any other edition prior to 1513 of Frontinus's two books on aqueducts is to be found there, and whether I can obtain such a copy? Chief Librarian Reuss in Göttingen has kindly sent me several editions from 1518 onwards, as well as the editio princeps of Frontinus's Strategematicon; however, Göttingen does not possess the editio princeps or the other two oldest editions of the work on aqueducts, and I have asked other libraries in vain, so that only Berlin and Dresden seem to me to be worth inquiring with. If you could help me in this matter, I would be very grateful; at least one is reluctant to give up such a wish as long as the last resort has not been tried. I have newly edited, translated, and extensively commented on this hitherto misunderstood work, which presented the greatest difficulties regarding the text, initially with the intention of showing that the Vitruvius we have is an interpolated writer from the Middle Ages who did not even understand the old fragments he compiled. Furthermore, I intend to show what a precious piece of antiquity we possess in Frontinus, without having known it. You will surely see how important it is to me to do everything possible for Frontinus's text. Since my work has progressed so far that any comparison can be completed as quickly as possible, I can immediately return the books that might be entrusted to me for this purpose within the requested time. Please kindly send my warmest greetings to Prof. Wilcken, who will probably have the kindness, in such a case, to send the shipment by post and to collect the postal expenses from me at the same time.

What you wrote to me about Schelling is unknown here. However, it is by no means unlikely to me; for in Erlangen, although no principal chair has become vacant due to Abicht’s departure, everything is now to be ranked higher on one hand; — on the other hand, Sch. is here, as I have already written to you, dissatisfied, about which there would be much to say. His approval among the students is, however, so unanimous that it has ended with Wagner and his clamoring, to everyone’s relief! The latter has no lecture at all, while the other has barely managed to get one going with 20 listeners, whereas Schelling has an auditorium of nearly three hundred and fifty students. An even worse end came to another attempt at antagonism, made by a most shallow-headed and lowly partisan, the so-called Spanish Fisherman — a man like a Spanish wall, which can be set up around any privy — out of devotion to the higher authority (namely Count Thürheim); yet without being in the least instigated by the latter, but solely because it had been reported that Sch. had upset the Count with a strong letter. As he launched out at philosophy with crude insults (N.B. in an Aesthetics which he patches together from Sulzer), Brother Studio — who did not see, or did not want to see, the perforated Spanish wall which the Spaniard had deliberately placed so negligently around his intention, that he could indeed hide behind it in an emergency, but his seat on the privy was quite visibly presented — felt he had to save the honor of his idol and stop the mouth of this Pharisee. So whole crowds gathered in the Spanish auditorium, and since the actor nevertheless allowed himself some more crude remarks during his hour, there arose such a scuffling, whistling, and uproar that he really had to stop and leave the lecture hall.

If I have understood your letter correctly, you wish to postpone not only the consummation of the marriage, but even the public announcement of your union, until your promotion to Erlangen has been effected. I cannot approve of this in any way. Your promotion is, according to my knowledge of the circumstances, so little doubtful that I cannot doubt it even in the case that I were to leave my position. But I can also, according to my knowledge of the circumstances, hardly think that this promotion will occur earlier than with the beginning of the next academic year, since this Easter has passed before anything has been done for the University of Erlangen. Why would you then still delay a full half-year to arrive at the full enjoyment of your happiness? Do you perhaps consider yourself as Professor and Rector of the Gymnasium in Nuremberg not respected and worthy enough to be publicly and solemnly received as a member of a family that, in the former glory of the Imperial City of Nuremberg, indeed occupied a very respected position? I must almost fear something similar, since not only the marriage itself, but even the public announcement of the union is to remain suspended for the time being! — To speak plainly! I consider this to be an equally wretched and unfounded timidity on your part. In a time in which kings themselves are no longer required to present ancestors in order to obtain the right to court princesses, in a time in which personal merit and self-acquired rank, without any ancestors, ennobles more than all proofs of ancestry — public opinion cannot be afraid of a union such as yours. Besides, I am of the opinion that, even measured by the past dissolved former circumstances, the rank you have as Rector and Professor of one of the most respected royal Gymnasiums, which places you alongside a royal district councilor, is not below the line that would even formerly have opened to you entry into the family to which you now belong.

I also cannot imagine at all (and my wife, who became better acquainted with your bride’s family last year and, in her letters from Nuremberg at that time, highly praised the modest seclusion and domesticity she found there, agrees with me on this point) that you should have been given any reason for such timidity by that family. Therefore, please do not let yourself be deterred from bringing your engagement to a conclusion as soon as possible by such vain anxieties—or, to put it more plainly, by a certain vanity on your part, which suits a philosopher so poorly.

However, I have another reason that makes it a matter of concern for me to advise against the delay. The permission to marry, which you—having been classified as a civil servant—must receive directly from His Majesty the King, you will in fact obtain much more easily as Rector in Nuremberg than you could obtain it as a Professor in Erlangen. The reason is quite simple. The main consideration regarding the marriage permission to be granted concerns the widow’s pension guaranteed to all civil servants by the general service statute, and always gives rise to the question of the fund from which the pension would have to be paid in the event of your death. This consideration is now far less problematic for the already regulated budget of the educational institutions than for the not yet regulated fund of the University of Erlangen. For this reason, I must doubly wish that you may soon be in a position to apply for the marriage permission, so that difficulties do not ultimately arise from this side and—the last deception becomes more grievous than the first.

Lost, my highly esteemed friend, by no means has the important letter gone, which brought us the first news of your happiness. That it is already 14 days today since this pleasing letter has been in my hands, without my having replied a single syllable to it until now, would give you the right with anyone else to conclude a cold reception of such news, but not with me and not with my wife. More intimate joy, warmer sympathy, more heartfelt wishes than ours, this news could not have aroused in any of your friends, and I may assume that you are convinced of this without special assurance. But I have already been so close for two times 14 days to obtaining a decision on my own affair, that I thought each day I was only allowed to wait 24 hours for certainty, and therefore also thought of postponing my congratulatory letter to you by only 24 hours each day. Thus these 24 hours of hesitation have gradually already exceeded the

To the Honorable Professor Hegel in Jena.

Highly esteemed Friend! You have probably been waiting impatiently since last Friday for a reply from me. Although I would have been only too glad to comply with your wish, it was not granted to me, because the small matter on which the decision still depended refused to be settled. Following a new recollection that occurred to the Privy Councillor von Bayard yesterday, I am at last in a position to submit the following more definite information to you.

You must give shelter to my misery and cover it with the mantle of your wealth and your friendship. I will not send you my translation of Tennemann, which would be of no use to you and whose preface concerns only France. If, however—say a word. Philosophy is progressing quite well here. I am turning over in my head a project that could serve it and naturalize in France the spirit of that great and admirable movement which has been constantly growing in Germany for 40 years. I am thinking of undertaking a translation or rather a recasting of Kant. As long as Kant is not known, nothing is done and Germany is not for France. The father known, on the contrary, the children and grandchildren will soon be known. But what an undertaking! My courage recoils!—However, one idea supports me, which is that Kant, once put into French and a little cleaned up, could present himself to everyone and go to England, Italy, America, and the Indies. But I stop and ask you for your opinion on this idea! Write to me at will in German or in French, but write to me. Yours entirely from the heart, Victor Cousin. By the way, I send you my very best compliments on your Rectorship. Hail, most distinguished man.

I am sending you, my dear friend, Mr. Girardin, one of the most distinguished editors of the Journal des Débats, who is going to Prussia to study your provincial system and who is also interested in literature and philosophy. You will take great pleasure in conversing with him about the state of France, and he will give you detailed news of mine. Your last letter, which Mr. Raumer delivered to me, found me barely recovered from that abominable winter, as you very justly call it, and from the loss of my mother, who succumbed after a long and painful agony. The avowed reason for the interruption of my course is the true one; and I would resume it at Easter, if my strength permitted. But it seems wise to postpone it further. In any case, if I am too weak to withstand the strain of public lectures, I am already strong enough to work, and I intend to use the leisure of this summer to advance my translation of Plato.

The nature of the subjects I treated in writing, or perhaps also my own subjective character, made it impossible until now to strictly follow the rigorous philosophical method that you have discovered and demonstrated, and of whose value and validity I am perfectly convinced; therefore, I fear the reproach of having often merely applied your teachings externally to the subjects, and treated the latter in an inadequate manner according to those teachings. The consciousness of not having proceeded arbitrarily, but of having been guided by inner necessity, is not sufficient to protect me from these doubts, however vividly it lives in me, for often an inner necessity drives us to error, only to lead us to the truth by roundabout ways. In any case, I am aware that I can only be enabled to continue on a path, which I have not entered without serious enthusiasm, with firmer self-confidence and purified insight, through lively communication and intellectual exchange with men who have a voice in the high tasks of thinking. I may therefore well hope for forgiveness if I ask you to grant some interest to the present writing and to my scholarly striving, and to receive with goodwill the assurance of sincere admiration and deeply felt reverence, which your spirit and your works have indelibly impressed upon me. Your Excellency’s most respectfully devoted Christian Hermann Weiße.

This letter, my friend, will be handed to you by Mr. Dr. Panofka, one of your compatriots who has spent a few weeks here on his return from Italy, and to whom I am extremely indebted for the kindness he showed in giving me a few lessons in Archaeology on the ancient monuments of our Museum. Mr. Panofka seems to me quite worthy of your acquaintance, and I am paying my debts by introducing him to you. You must have received the third and final volume of Descartes. I am now buried in Proclus, which I hope to be able to finish by Easter. The printing of the third and final volume is very advanced. That, my dear friend, is my campaign of Moscow. If I get through it, all will be well. But what pains the copying and collation of the manuscripts cost me!
