I hope that this third volume will be a little better than the others, and that Germany will be willing to do justice at least to my zeal.

I. All things are through God, but not all things are from God or created from His own essential being. This is my conviction against Pantheism. I distinguish the Son of Time (man) from the Son of Eternity (Jesus Christ). The former can fall and has fallen. The latter cannot fall, but has humbled Himself in order to raise up the fallen Son. II. The law of justice is the law of equality of contradictory things. I believe you have yourself set this out in one of your treatises, as for example the equality between crime and punishment, whereby the crime is reduced to 0: — 1+E 1 = 0)).

V. That Jesus Christ reconciled justice was a voluntary act, or an act of mercy (which is why He Himself says: “No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” John 10:18). VI. Not everyone is redeemed by his death, but only those who believe in Him (He desires love in return for love). VII. Love for Jesus Christ can hardly be attained outside the Catholic Church. (Since the Protestantism, love has grown cold in the world; lukewarmness and indifference have taken the place of religion and the fear of God.)

III. The crime of the Fall is the creature’s striving to become equal to God (according to Revelation and according to the knowledge of sin in me and outside me). IV. If a nothing seeks to rise to the equality of God, then according to the law of justice a God must humble himself to nothing. By this means the crime is destroyed. If man is to be reconciled with God and satisfaction is to be given to the justice of God, then Jesus Christ had to suffer for the sin of men.

Dear Doctor Hegel! I have found this sheet among my papers, which you were kind enough to lend me, but which I forgot to return to you; I ask your forgiveness for this. I recently learned from Ritter that you are still in Jena; because I have led a wandering life since my departure from Jena, it seems to me that I cannot be sure of finding anyone in their old place, otherwise I would have returned your manuscript to you sooner. Ritter wrote to me that you are very occupied with physics; since we last saw each other, I have mostly occupied myself with the study of theology, and my wish to become Catholic, which you probably already know, has been fulfilled. It would perhaps be possible for me now, more so than at the time when I last spoke with you in friendship about this matter, to set my faith in Jesus Christ in the light; not to prove or demonstrate it, for it is before all proof and above all proof, and the core of my existence; and in trust of the patience with which you have usually listened to me, I will venture to present my view to you briefly and simply.

What you say critically and polemically in the Preface about non-philosophy, especially what you say against the fear of form, against nature philosophy, against the arrogance of mathematicians, and what you also say in the Introduction against Kant and his critical philosophy, I find entirely excellent and there is hardly anything that I would not be willing to sign. In the style and the presentation, I have recognized you and your zeal, which has a flaming sword at its disposal, and I have thought of the times of the League of our Spirits, from the midst of which fate has snatched the others away from us. As far as you say in the Preface and Introduction about the Phenomenology, I believe that you allow it to count in its entire presentation only as an introduction to the standpoint of construction. This also agrees with my system insofar as I, although I did not myself take this path, nevertheless presented it as a possible one, but as the longer one and one necessarily linked in advance with certain assumptions, and thus insofar as less evident. — I proceed immediately to the philosophical construction from the fact of doubt in general, where I am alone historical and not constructing, but narrating, in that I show that there is only one, and hypothetically posit this one, which seems to me all the more correct as the most general view one has of science in general is that of a hypothesis in life. But I say (§., one could also develop the one doubt from everything, and this path seems to me to be the one your Phenomenology takes; for although you do not properly start from doubt, you do start from the uncertainty of things, from sensory perception, which is actually doubt in concrete, the experienced doubt, and since you did not once take the path of construction, you could not leave the standpoint of experience, which presents the schema of truth still in the whole and without its distinctions.

Dearest Friend! Your letter gave me true pleasure. Your judgment of my work is as friendly as it is substantial. Your invitation is very dear to me, and I shall seek to make use of it. It will please me to get to know your wife, and to find in her the person you have deemed worthy of your choice. Until then, I shall also keep all our explanations on metaphysics in reserve, for, as I hope, if Heaven grants me the joy of this meeting, our conversation will be serious and beneficial. In the meantime, I wish to tell you a few things that can prove to you that I have considered your works, and that I believe we are not walking on paths far apart from one another. There is no need to fear that mutual misunderstandings arising from such an imperfect communication could create mutual prejudices that should not disappear, especially once I have more thoroughly penetrated your work, in an immediate and lively clarification. First of all, I feel that you would have wanted to judge the beginning of your work only from the whole that is yet to be completed, and this judgment must in any case be suspended in its full extent. But considered as an introduction and beginning, it is already in itself capable of judgment and especially of comparison, which I have all the more gladly made with my system, as I regard this, because it is finished, as my standard. I will therefore share with you a few things, though without prejudice, of what I thought about it, to demonstrate my friendly earnestness and zeal, and to fear less haste than showing a false discretion in doing so.

I conclude by entrusting you with a hundred thousand affectionate regards for your wife, for your children, for Bloch, for his wife, and for Mrs. Milder, whom I still love despite her whims. I say nothing to you, for it has been a long time since everything has been said between us, and I content myself with embracing you once more with the tenderest part of my heart. V. Cousin. P.S. See that the copy of your lectures, which I have requested, is clean and accurate. The history of philosophy and universal history, that is what matters most to me for the present. — Among your new collaborators, do you have anyone who is particularly interested in ancient philosophy? That would be a very useful correspondent for me.

Descartes is finished, and I am delving into Plato. This is where your advice will be indispensable, and when you have paid what you owe in way of friendly severities to my preface, I shall claim the same debt in favor of my Plato. For the moment, I ask nothing of you and send you gratis the third volume, which has finally appeared, and which contains, as the main piece, the Gorgias. One day, you will have to read me in full. Now, read only the Dedication. There is a phrase about your Police that did not seem to me too sharp when I

I have sent you my Fragments, that is to say, the preface, which alone is readable, and on which alone I solicit and await your reasoned opinion. It is an account of my philosophical attempts from 1815 to 1819. Come down a little from the heights and give me your hand. There are four points in this small writing: 1. the Method, 2. the application to consciousness or Psychology, 3. the passage from Psychology to ontology, 4. some attempts at a historical system. Drop something from your good head on these four points. Be all the more merciless because, determined to be useful to my country, I shall always allow myself to modify, according to the needs and the state, as it is, of this poor country, the directions of my masters from Germany. I said this strongly to our excellent friend Schelling, and I believe I also wrote it to Dr. Gans; it is not a question of creating here in a greenhouse an artificial interest for foreign speculations, no, it is a question of implanting in the bowels of the country fertile germs that develop there naturally, and according to the primitive virtues of the soil; it is a question of giving France a French movement that then goes of its own accord. No consideration will make me abandon this line of conduct. Consequently, my friends up there can be all the more severe with me because they must not fear dragging me blindly down here into ill-calculated steps. I shall measure the force of the wind by that of the poor lamb; but as for me, who am not a lamb, I beg the wind to blow with all its force. I feel my back firm enough to support it; I ask for mercy only for France. Hegel, tell me the truth, then I shall pass on to my country what it can understand of it.

How are you? How is dear Mrs. Hegel? And your children? — Your soul is at peace, Hegel. Mine is suffering. I spend my life regretting my prison. But I do not forget that I am not with you, alone, at night, on your sofa; and it is not at a distance of 300 leagues that we can converse intimately. Sorrow hounds me; but it will not have to deal with a coward. I endure everything and I work. My external situation is tolerable for the time being; they have restored my title and my half pay and I am as before my journey. My entire occupation is to study and translate Plato, and the Philosophy of Alexandria. That is my only and serious business; and in the intervals I correct the proofs of my edition of Descartes. You know my life as if I lived near you. From time to time, I contribute a few articles to the Journal des Savants, and I remain in contact with many of my former students. Farewell. Love me always and do not fear that I will ever forget you. I do not pass a day without thinking of you; let us hope that we shall see each other again: I need it, in every respect. Farewell, my friend. I embrace you with all the strength of my arms and my heart. V. Cousin. P.S. Have you received my Edition of Descartes, and a volume of Proclus? Where are you at?

My dear friend, I do not want Gans to leave here without carrying a few lines from me that remind you of me, and that scold you very severely for your silence and that of all my friends in Berlin. I wrote to you twice, once by post and once by opportunity; no answer. I did the same to Bloch and his wife; the same silence. I had written to Mr. Henning of Fulda in Hesse. Mr. de la Motte Fouqué wrote me some pretty verses to reproach me for my laziness: I replied with bad prose, but at least very long. He was briefer; for he did not answer me. I willingly forgive you; but try to give some signs of life, or I shall go back to prison at the Stadtvogtey to rekindle your friendship! No; for I believe it, and from the bottom of my heart; and neither time nor absence nor silence will extinguish my faith.
